fallacies.name: Ad Hominem
fallacies.shortDef: Attacking the person instead of their argument.
fallacies.definition: Rejecting a claim because of who makes it (their character, motives, background or track record) instead of engaging with the reasons or evidence they offer.
howToSpot: Is the reply about the person or about the point they made?
Would the rebuttal still work if someone else made the same claim?
Insults, motives or past slip-ups offered in place of counter-evidence
fallacies.classicExample: Why would we take budget advice from Dev? He can't even keep his own desk tidy.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Pointing out a real conflict of interest or a poor track record is fair when a claim rests on someone's word alone, but it's a reason to check the evidence, not to reject the claim.

contrast.fal_tu_quoque: Ad hominem attacks the person's character or motives; tu quoque deflects by saying the critic does the same thing.
contrast.fal_guilt_by_association: Ad hominem targets the person making the claim; guilt by association targets who they're linked with.
contrast.fal_genetic_fallacy: Ad hominem targets the person arguing now; the genetic fallacy dismisses a claim by its origin or history.

fallacies.name: Genetic Fallacy
fallacies.shortDef: Judging a claim or practice by where it came from, not by its merits.
fallacies.definition: Accepting or rejecting a claim, idea or practice because of its origin or history, such as who first proposed it, where it began or why it started, instead of how well it holds up now.
howToSpot: Is the idea judged by its origin story rather than by current evidence?
Ask whether a good idea could come from a bad source, or the reverse
Watch for 'it started as...' offered as the whole case
fallacies.classicExample: Handshakes began as a way to show you weren't holding a weapon, so they're pointless now.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Origin matters when the source is the only evidence, like an anonymous rumor. Once independent evidence exists, or the original reason is checked against today's facts, judge that evidence.

contrast.fal_ad_hominem: The genetic fallacy dismisses a claim by its origin or history; ad hominem attacks the person currently making the argument.
contrast.fal_guilt_by_association: The genetic fallacy looks at where an idea came from; guilt by association looks at who supports or is linked to it now.

fallacies.name: Guilt by Association
fallacies.shortDef: Rejecting a claim or person because of who they're linked with.
fallacies.definition: Judging a claim, product or person as bad because of a link to a disliked person or group, such as a shared supporter, user or venue, instead of evaluating it on its own merits.
howToSpot: Is the claim judged on its reasons, or on who else backs it?
Ask whether the idea would look fine if someone you liked endorsed it
Watch for a disliked group or person dropped in where evidence should be
fallacies.classicExample: The rival club across town supports the new bike lanes, so they must be a bad idea.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Associations can be fair evidence about risk, like a repeated partnership with people caught misreporting, but they justify a closer look at the evidence, not a verdict on the claim.

contrast.fal_ad_hominem: Guilt by association taints a claim through someone else it's linked to; ad hominem attacks the person making the claim directly.
contrast.fal_genetic_fallacy: Guilt by association points to disliked supporters or users now; the genetic fallacy points to where the idea originally came from.

fallacies.name: Red Herring
fallacies.shortDef: Changing the subject to dodge the real question.
fallacies.definition: Introducing a different topic that may sound related but doesn't bear on the question at hand, so attention drifts away and the original issue goes unanswered.
howToSpot: Restate the original question; does the reply actually answer it?
Notice when the topic shifts to something easier, nicer or more exciting
Ask whether the new point would change the answer to the old question
fallacies.classicExample: Asked why rent went up 20%, the landlord talked about the beautiful new art in the lobby.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Raising a new point is fair when it bears on the question, like a mechanic noting other needed repairs, or when you answer the original question first and then add context.

contrast.fal_straw_man: A red herring changes the subject; a straw man stays on the subject but distorts the other side's position.
contrast.fal_tu_quoque: A red herring shifts to any unrelated issue; tu quoque shifts specifically to the critic's own behavior.

fallacies.name: Straw Man
fallacies.shortDef: Distorting someone's position into a weaker one, then attacking that.
fallacies.definition: Restating someone's argument in an exaggerated, oversimplified or extreme form, then refuting that distorted version as if it were what they actually said.
howToSpot: Compare what was actually said with the version being attacked
Look for dropped qualifiers: 'some' becomes 'all', 'less' becomes 'none'
Ask whether the original speaker would accept this summary of their view
fallacies.classicExample: Jen wants to cut the snack budget by 10%. So she wants everyone starving at their desks?
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Summarizing someone's view and showing where it leads is fair when the summary is accurate and they'd recognize it, ideally checked with them or quoted in their own words.

contrast.fal_red_herring: A straw man distorts the opponent's actual position; a red herring drops the topic and brings in a different one.
contrast.fal_false_dichotomy: A straw man misrepresents one side's view; a false dichotomy pretends there are only two options to choose from.

fallacies.name: Tu Quoque
fallacies.shortDef: Dodging a criticism by pointing out that the critic does it too.
fallacies.definition: Rejecting a criticism or argument by claiming the person making it is inconsistent or guilty of the same thing, instead of addressing whether the criticism itself is correct.
howToSpot: Does the reply answer the criticism, or turn it back on the critic?
Would the point be wrong even if the critic behaved perfectly?
Watch for the critic's own behavior showing up right where an answer should be
fallacies.classicExample: You're telling me to stop texting while driving? I've seen you check your phone at red lights.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Pointing out inconsistency is fair when the question is someone's credibility or fairness, like rule-makers exempting themselves, as long as the original point is still judged on its merits.

contrast.fal_ad_hominem: Tu quoque deflects by saying the critic does it too; ad hominem attacks the critic's character, traits or motives in general.
contrast.fal_red_herring: Tu quoque turns attention to the critic's own behavior; a red herring shifts to any other topic that dodges the question.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Consequences
fallacies.shortDef: Judging whether a claim is true by whether we'd like its consequences.
fallacies.definition: Arguing that a factual claim must be true because believing it leads to good outcomes, or false because accepting it would be unpleasant, when those outcomes say nothing about what is actually the case.
howToSpot: Is the question what's true, or what we should do about it?
Ask whether the facts would change if the outcome were different
Watch for a finding rejected because accepting it would be painful or costly
fallacies.classicExample: The bridge can't be unsafe. Closing it would wreck the downtown shops.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Consequences are the right test for decisions, like whether to close the bridge or limit its traffic. They just can't settle facts, like whether the bridge is actually safe.

contrast.fal_appeal_to_emotion: Appeal to consequences ties truth to good or bad outcomes; appeal to emotion stirs feelings without needing any claim about outcomes.
contrast.fal_slippery_slope: Appeal to consequences rejects a claim because its results would be bad; slippery slope predicts an unsupported chain of events from one step.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Emotion
fallacies.shortDef: Using stirred-up feelings in place of reasons to win agreement.
fallacies.definition: Trying to make a claim seem true or a choice seem right by provoking feelings such as pride, guilt, disgust, outrage or loyalty, when those feelings don't bear on whether the claim holds up.
howToSpot: Strip out the emotional words; is there still a reason left?
Ask what evidence would support this if you felt nothing about it
Notice vivid imagery, guilt or pride doing the work that facts should do
fallacies.classicExample: Picture your daughter's face on her birthday. You can't put a price on that, so the deluxe package it is.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Emotion is fair when it's proportionate and rides on real reasons, like telling one student's story alongside the cost data, so the feeling motivates the argument instead of replacing it.

contrast.fal_appeal_to_pity: Appeal to emotion can use any feeling; appeal to pity specifically asks for sympathy for someone's hardship.
contrast.fal_appeal_to_fear: Appeal to emotion covers pride, guilt, disgust and more; appeal to fear works by making you afraid of a threat.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Fear
fallacies.shortDef: Using scary, exaggerated or unsupported threats to push a conclusion.
fallacies.definition: Pushing a belief or action by making people afraid of a danger that is exaggerated, unsupported or unrelated to the choice, so fear does the persuading instead of evidence about the real risk.
howToSpot: Is the danger backed by evidence, or just vividly described?
Ask how likely the threat is, and whether the choice actually prevents it
Watch for urgency and worst cases standing in for numbers
fallacies.classicExample: Buy our premium alarm today. Burglars could be watching your street right now, and next time your kids might be home.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Warning about danger is fair when the risk is real, sized honestly and actually reduced by the action, like urging carbon monoxide detectors in homes with gas furnaces.

contrast.fal_slippery_slope: Appeal to fear scares you with a threat; slippery slope claims one step will trigger an unsupported chain of further steps.
contrast.fal_appeal_to_emotion: Appeal to fear works through dread of danger; appeal to emotion covers any feeling, like pride, guilt or disgust.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Pity
fallacies.shortDef: Asking for sympathy instead of giving reasons a claim is true or fair.
fallacies.definition: Arguing that a claim should be accepted, or a judgment changed, because someone's hardship makes us feel sorry for them, when that hardship doesn't bear on the question being decided.
howToSpot: Ask what is being decided, and whether the hardship changes that answer
Separate 'I feel for them' from 'they're right' or 'they met the standard'
Watch for a sad story arriving right where evidence should be
fallacies.classicExample: I know my essay is two weeks late and has no conclusion, but I've had such a rough semester that I deserve an A.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Hardship is relevant when the decision is about need or fairness, like an extension for a documented illness, or when the rules explicitly make room for circumstances.

contrast.fal_appeal_to_emotion: Appeal to pity relies on sympathy for someone's hardship; appeal to emotion can use any feeling, like pride, guilt or outrage.
contrast.fal_red_herring: Appeal to pity swaps reasons for sympathy; a red herring swaps the topic for an unrelated one.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Authority
fallacies.shortDef: Treating someone's say-so as proof, especially outside their expertise.
fallacies.definition: Accepting a claim because an authority figure endorses it when that person lacks expertise in the topic, speaks against the consensus of their field, or offers nothing beyond their status.
howToSpot: Is the authority an expert in this specific topic?
Do other experts in that field agree, or is this one voice?
Is there evidence behind the endorsement, or just a title or fame?
fallacies.classicExample: A famous quarterback swears by these magnetic insoles, so they must fix back pain.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Relying on experts is reasonable when they speak within their field and reflect its consensus, like trusting independent structural engineers about a crack in your foundation.

contrast.fal_bandwagon: Appeal to authority leans on one esteemed source; bandwagon leans on how many people believe or do something.
contrast.fal_genetic_fallacy: Appeal to authority accepts a claim because of who vouches for it; the genetic fallacy judges a claim by its origin or history.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Nature
fallacies.shortDef: Assuming something is good because it's natural, or bad because it isn't.
fallacies.definition: Arguing that something is healthy, safe or better because it is natural, or harmful because it is artificial, synthetic or processed, without evidence about its actual effects.
howToSpot: Is 'natural', 'chemical' or 'lab-made' doing the work of evidence?
Remember many natural things are harmful and many synthetic ones help
Ask what the evidence says about effects, not about origins
fallacies.classicExample: These herbal sleep drops are 100% plant-based, so they must be safer than anything from a pharmacy.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: 'Natural' is fair as a description, or when backed by evidence about effects, like choosing a mineral sunscreen because it irritates sensitive skin less.

contrast.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Appeal to nature prizes what's natural or unprocessed; appeal to tradition prizes what's old or customary.
contrast.fal_is_ought: Appeal to nature says natural means good or safe; is-ought jumps from any fact about how things are to how they should be.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Tradition
fallacies.shortDef: Assuming something is right or better because it's always been done that way.
fallacies.definition: Arguing that a practice or belief is correct, or should continue, simply because it is old or long established, without showing that the reasons behind it still hold today.
howToSpot: Is age or habit the main reason given?
Ask why the practice started, and whether that reason still applies
Watch for years, generations or founding dates standing in for results
fallacies.classicExample: We've posted paper flyers for every bake sale since 1987, so there's no reason to try social media.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Long use can be evidence when it reflects a tested track record, and it's fair to find out why a rule exists before scrapping it. Age alone just isn't a reason.

contrast.fal_appeal_to_nature: Appeal to tradition prizes what's old or customary; appeal to nature prizes what's natural or unprocessed.
contrast.fal_bandwagon: Appeal to tradition says it's always been done; bandwagon says lots of people do it right now.

fallacies.name: Bandwagon
fallacies.shortDef: Treating something as true or good because many people believe or do it.
fallacies.definition: Concluding that a claim is true, or a choice is right, because it's popular, trending or what most people do, when popularity isn't evidence about the question being asked.
howToSpot: Is the main reason how many people believe, buy or do it?
Ask what evidence those people had, and whether it applies to you
Watch for sales figures, trends or lines out the door standing in for reasons
fallacies.classicExample: Three million people have downloaded this diet app, so it must actually work.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Popularity is fair evidence when the question is about popularity itself, like which time slot most families prefer, or when many users report on something they judge directly, like comfort.

contrast.fal_appeal_to_authority: Bandwagon leans on how many people agree; appeal to authority leans on one esteemed source.
contrast.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Bandwagon says lots of people do it now; appeal to tradition says it's always been done that way.

fallacies.name: Anecdotal Evidence
fallacies.shortDef: Letting a personal story outweigh broader, systematic evidence.
fallacies.definition: Using a vivid personal experience, or a friend's, to dismiss or outweigh systematic evidence such as studies, surveys or large datasets. One case can be real and still tell you little about what usually happens.
howToSpot: Is a single story being set against studies, surveys or larger data?
Would one exception really change what's true on average?
Is the story's vividness doing the work that evidence should do?
fallacies.classicExample: My grandfather smoked every day and lived to 95, so the health risks of smoking are exaggerated.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Personal experience is fair as one data point, a reason to look closer, or a counterexample to an absolute 'always' or 'never' claim, as long as it isn't treated as outweighing the larger evidence.

contrast.fal_hasty_generalization: Anecdotal evidence sets a personal story against systematic data; hasty generalization builds a broad claim from too few cases.
contrast.fal_cherry_picking: Anecdotal evidence leans on one personal story; cherry picking selects the favorable data points from a larger set.

fallacies.name: Cherry Picking
fallacies.shortDef: Citing only the evidence that supports you and ignoring the rest.
fallacies.definition: Presenting the data points, studies, quotes or time periods that favor a conclusion while leaving out or waving away the available evidence that cuts against it, so the case looks stronger than it is.
howToSpot: Is this all the evidence, or just the best-looking slice of it?
Why does the time period, group or sample start and stop where it does?
What would the full dataset, average or overall rating show?
fallacies.classicExample: Our fund returned 31% last year! (The small print: losses in two of the four years before that.)
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Focusing on a subset is fair when the rule for choosing it is set in advance and applied evenly, such as excluding low-quality studies, and when including everything wouldn't change the conclusion.

contrast.fal_texas_sharpshooter: Cherry picking hides or ignores unfavorable evidence; the sharpshooter finds a cluster after the fact and treats it as the target all along.
contrast.fal_hasty_generalization: Cherry picking chooses the favorable cases from many available; hasty generalization leans on too few cases to begin with.

fallacies.name: False Cause
fallacies.shortDef: Treating a correlation between two things as proof one causes the other.
fallacies.definition: Concluding that A causes B because the two tend to occur together, without ruling out a third factor that drives both, the cause running the other way, or plain coincidence.
howToSpot: Is the evidence just that two things go together across people, places or times?
Could a third factor explain both, or could the cause run the other way?
Was anything assigned at random or compared with a fair control group?
fallacies.classicExample: Towns that sell more ice cream have more drownings, so ice cream must make swimming dangerous.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: A correlation is a fair clue worth investigating. It becomes good evidence of cause when a randomized trial or a careful comparison rules out hidden factors and reverse causation.

contrast.fal_post_hoc: False cause reads cause into things that go together across many cases; post hoc reads cause into one thing simply following another in time.
contrast.fal_texas_sharpshooter: False cause misreads a real correlation; the sharpshooter hunts through data for a cluster and then treats it as meaningful.

fallacies.name: Gambler's Fallacy
fallacies.shortDef: Believing past random outcomes change the odds of independent future ones.
fallacies.definition: Thinking that a run of one outcome makes a different outcome 'due', or a repeat less likely, when each event is independent, like coin flips, dice rolls or fresh random draws. Chance has no memory.
howToSpot: Is each event truly independent, like a fresh roll, flip or random pick?
Is someone saying an outcome is 'due', 'owed' or that luck must even out?
Do past results actually change the physical odds of the next one?
fallacies.classicExample: Red has come up seven times in a row at the roulette table, so black is bound to hit next.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Past outcomes do matter when events are dependent, such as cards drawn without reshuffling or parts that wear out with use. Then the odds really do shift with history.

contrast.fal_false_cause: False cause invents a causal link between things; the gambler's fallacy imagines past random results pushing future ones to even out.
contrast.fal_hasty_generalization: Hasty generalization draws a broad rule from few cases; the gambler's fallacy expects a short run of luck to reverse itself.

fallacies.name: Hasty Generalization
fallacies.shortDef: Drawing a broad conclusion from a sample that's too small or unrepresentative.
fallacies.definition: Generalizing about a whole group from a few cases, or from a sample that doesn't reflect the group, such as one visit, a handful of people or a self-selected crowd of fans or complainers.
howToSpot: How many cases is the claim based on, and how big is the group it's about?
Were the cases picked in a way that skews them, like volunteers or fans?
Does the conclusion say 'all' or 'always' when the evidence says 'some'?
fallacies.classicExample: The two people I met from Port Ellis were rude, so people from Port Ellis are rude.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Generalizing is fine when the sample is large and representative, like a random survey, or when a small random sample shows a result so extreme that chance can't explain it.

contrast.fal_anecdotal_evidence: Hasty generalization leaps from too few cases; anecdotal evidence lets a personal story outweigh systematic data that already exists.
contrast.fal_composition: Hasty generalization goes from some members to all members; composition goes from the parts to the whole thing they make up.

fallacies.name: Post Hoc
aliases: After this, therefore because of this
fallacies.shortDef: Assuming that because B followed A, A must have caused B.
fallacies.definition: Concluding that one event caused another simply because it came first. Timing alone can't rule out coincidence, a shared cause, or a change that would have happened anyway, like a cold clearing up on its own.
howToSpot: Is the only evidence that one thing happened right after another?
Would the outcome have happened anyway, through recovery, seasons or a bounce back?
Did anything else change around the same time?
fallacies.classicExample: I started wearing my lucky socks on Monday and we've won every game since. The socks are working.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Timing is a fair first clue. It becomes good evidence when the effect repeats, appears and disappears with the suspected cause, or holds up against a comparison group.

contrast.fal_false_cause: Post hoc relies on one thing following another in time; false cause relies on two things going together across many cases.
contrast.fal_anecdotal_evidence: Post hoc infers cause from timing; anecdotal evidence lets a personal story outweigh broader data, whatever the timing.

fallacies.name: Slippery Slope
fallacies.shortDef: Claiming a small step will inevitably snowball into disaster, without support.
fallacies.definition: Arguing that a modest first step will lead, link by link, to an extreme outcome, while giving no real evidence that each link is likely. The chain is presented as inevitable instead of being shown.
howToSpot: Count the links: is each step supported, or just asserted?
Watch for 'next it'll be', 'then', 'before you know it' piling up.
Could an ordinary decision stop the chain at any step along the way?
fallacies.classicExample: If we let students redo one quiz, soon they'll expect to redo every test, and grades will mean nothing.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Predicting a chain of consequences is fair when each link is backed by evidence, such as a contract clause, a precedent or data, and the likelihood is stated honestly rather than as inevitable.

contrast.fal_appeal_to_fear: A slippery slope lays out a chain of steps to a bad end; an appeal to fear just stirs up dread, with or without a chain.
contrast.fal_false_cause: False cause misreads one link from a correlation; a slippery slope stacks a series of unsupported links into a runaway chain.

fallacies.name: Texas Sharpshooter
fallacies.shortDef: Spotting a pattern or 'hit' after the fact and treating it as meaningful.
fallacies.definition: Sifting through data or events until a cluster or match appears, then treating it as a real pattern or a successful prediction, ignoring that the target was drawn around the hits and that chance alone produces clusters.
howToSpot: Was the pattern predicted beforehand, or found by looking afterward?
How many other patterns, places or variables were checked along the way?
Would a vague prediction have 'come true' whatever happened?
fallacies.classicExample: A man fires at a barn, then paints a bullseye around the tightest group of holes and calls himself a sharpshooter.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Spotting a cluster is a fair starting point. It becomes evidence when the hypothesis is stated in advance and then tested on new data, or when chance is properly accounted for.

contrast.fal_cherry_picking: Cherry picking leaves out unfavorable evidence; the sharpshooter draws the target around whatever cluster turned up after looking.
contrast.fal_false_cause: False cause misreads a genuine correlation as cause; the sharpshooter's 'pattern' may be nothing more than chance found by searching.

fallacies.name: Appeal to Ignorance
fallacies.shortDef: Concluding a claim is true because it hasn't been proven false, or the reverse.
fallacies.definition: Treating a lack of evidence as if it were evidence: deciding something is true because no one has disproven it, or false because no one has proven it, when nobody has looked hard enough for the gap to mean much.
howToSpot: Is "no one has shown otherwise" doing the work that real evidence should do?
Has anyone looked in a way that would have found evidence if it existed?
Could the honest answer simply be "we don't know yet"?
fallacies.classicExample: No one has ever proven that ghosts don't exist, so they must be real.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Absence of evidence counts when a thorough search would have found something if it were there, like a full inspection that finds no termite signs in any beam.

contrast.fal_burden_of_proof: Appeal to ignorance draws a conclusion from missing evidence; burden of proof demands that others do the disproving.
contrast.fal_false_dichotomy: Appeal to ignorance treats "not proven false" as "true"; it's like a false dichotomy that leaves out the option "we don't know yet."

fallacies.name: Burden of Proof
fallacies.shortDef: Making a claim and demanding that others disprove it instead of supporting it.
fallacies.definition: Putting forward a claim and then insisting that doubters prove it false, instead of giving evidence for it. Whoever makes a claim owes the reasons; skeptics don't have to disprove it first.
howToSpot: Who made the claim, and have they offered any evidence for it?
Is the speaker asking critics to disprove something they never supported?
Does doubting the claim get treated as if it were a rival claim needing proof?
fallacies.classicExample: My lucky socks help the team win. If you think they don't, prove it.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Asking critics for counter-evidence is fair once you've already supported your claim, or when the critic is making a claim of their own, like asserting a well-tested product is dangerous.

contrast.fal_appeal_to_ignorance: Burden of proof hands the job of proving to critics; appeal to ignorance concludes a claim is true (or false) because it hasn't been disproven.
contrast.fal_moving_the_goalposts: Burden of proof dodges supporting a claim at all; moving the goalposts raises the bar after evidence has been provided.

fallacies.name: Circular Reasoning
fallacies.shortDef: Supporting a claim with a reason that already assumes the claim is true.
fallacies.definition: Offering reasons that only work if the conclusion is already accepted, often by restating it in other words or by letting two claims vouch for each other. The argument loops and gives no independent reason to believe it.
howToSpot: Strip the wording: is the reason just the conclusion said differently?
Would someone who doubts the claim accept the reason?
Trace the support: does it eventually point back to the original claim?
fallacies.classicExample: The reviews on this site are trustworthy because the site only publishes trustworthy reviews.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Restating a claim to clarify it is fine, and so is stating a definition. It only becomes a fallacy when the restatement is offered as evidence for the claim.

contrast.fal_loaded_question: Circular reasoning argues for a claim by assuming it; a loaded question tucks the assumption into a question instead.
contrast.fal_no_true_scotsman: Circular reasoning assumes its own conclusion; no true Scotsman redefines a group after the fact to exclude a counterexample.

fallacies.name: False Analogy
fallacies.shortDef: Drawing a conclusion from a comparison that fails on the point that matters.
fallacies.definition: Arguing that because two things are alike in some ways, what is true of one must be true of the other, when they differ in exactly the way that matters for the conclusion.
howToSpot: What property is being carried over from one thing to the other?
Are the two alike in the way that actually produces that property?
Name one relevant difference, then check whether the conclusion survives it.
fallacies.classicExample: A company is like a ship, and a ship has one captain whose word is final, so employees should never question the CEO.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: An analogy is fair when the two cases share the feature that drives the conclusion, like predicting results at one warehouse from another with the same layout, shelving and order volume.

contrast.fal_false_equivalence: A false analogy infers a conclusion from a flawed comparison; false equivalence simply declares two unequal things the same.
contrast.fal_composition: A false analogy compares two separate things; composition assumes a whole has a property because its parts have it.

fallacies.name: False Dichotomy
fallacies.shortDef: Presenting two options as the only ones when others exist.
fallacies.definition: Framing a decision as either/or, so that rejecting one option seems to force the other, when reasonable alternatives, combinations or in-between paths have been left out.
howToSpot: Can you name a realistic third option the speaker skipped?
Does rejecting one choice really force you into the other?
Ask whether both options could be combined, delayed or done partly.
fallacies.classicExample: Either we ban phones in class completely, or we accept that students will never pay attention again.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: It's fair when the two options truly exhaust the possibilities, like a motion that either passes or fails, or when the other options have already been ruled out with stated reasons.

contrast.fal_middle_ground: A false dichotomy hides the other options; middle ground assumes the option between two extremes must be the right one.
contrast.fal_loaded_question: A false dichotomy offers too few choices; a loaded question slips an unproven assumption into the question itself.

fallacies.name: False Equivalence
fallacies.shortDef: Treating two things as equal when they differ greatly in a way that matters.
fallacies.definition: Presenting two things as the same, or as equally bad, risky, costly or credible, because they share some feature, while ignoring large differences in scale, severity or strength of evidence that matter to the conclusion.
howToSpot: What do the two things share, and is that the part that matters here?
Check the scale: are they really similar in size, severity or evidence?
Put rough numbers on each side and see whether "the same" still holds.
fallacies.classicExample: Sure, he emptied the club's bank account, but she once took printer paper home from the office. We all cut corners.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Calling two things equivalent is fair when they really match on the dimension that matters, like two phone plans with the same price, data and coverage, or two generic pills with the same active dose.

contrast.fal_false_analogy: False equivalence declares two unequal things the same; a false analogy draws a conclusion from a comparison that breaks on the relevant point.
contrast.fal_middle_ground: False equivalence gives two sides equal weight; middle ground goes further and assumes the answer lies halfway between them.

fallacies.name: Loaded Question
fallacies.shortDef: Asking a question that presumes something unproven, so any answer concedes it.
fallacies.definition: Building a disputed or unproven assumption into a question, so that answering it directly seems to accept the assumption. The question does the arguing, and the hidden claim never gets supported.
howToSpot: What must already be true for this question to make sense?
Would a direct answer admit something you never agreed to?
Is the assumption supported anywhere, or only implied by the wording?
fallacies.classicExample: Have you stopped wasting the team's budget on that software yet?
fallacies.legitimateVersion: A question with a built-in assumption is fine when the assumption is established or agreed, like asking "When did the leak start?" after everyone has seen the water damage.

contrast.fal_false_dichotomy: A loaded question hides an assumption inside a question; a false dichotomy openly limits you to two options.
contrast.fal_circular_reasoning: A loaded question presumes a claim while asking; circular reasoning offers a conclusion as the proof of itself.

fallacies.name: Middle Ground
fallacies.shortDef: Assuming a compromise between two positions must be the correct answer.
fallacies.definition: Concluding that the truth or the best choice lies between two positions simply because it is in the middle, without showing that the middle is better supported. Sometimes one side is just right, or both are wrong.
howToSpot: Is the middle option defended on its merits, or only for being in the middle?
Could one side simply be right, or both be wrong?
Would splitting the difference still make sense if one position were absurd?
fallacies.classicExample: One mechanic says the brakes are fine and another says they're shot, so they're probably about half worn.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: A compromise is reasonable when it's justified on its own merits, such as evidence that the moderate option works better, or when splitting a shared cost is fair because both sides benefit equally.

contrast.fal_false_dichotomy: Middle ground assumes the in-between option is right; a false dichotomy pretends there are only two options at all.
contrast.fal_false_equivalence: Middle ground splits the difference between positions; false equivalence treats two very unequal things as if they were the same.

fallacies.name: Moving the Goalposts
fallacies.shortDef: Raising or changing the standard of proof after the original one has been met.
fallacies.definition: Demanding new or tougher evidence once the evidence originally asked for has been provided, so the claim never has to be accepted. The bar keeps shifting instead of the conclusion being reconsidered.
howToSpot: What standard did the speaker set at the start?
Was that standard met before the new demand appeared?
Would any evidence ever be enough, or does the bar keep moving?
fallacies.classicExample: Show me one study that says it works. Okay, that's one; show me ten. Fine, but were any of them done in this country?
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Asking for more is fair when the original request wasn't actually met, or when new information reveals a real gap, like a test that didn't cover the case you care about.

contrast.fal_no_true_scotsman: Moving the goalposts raises the bar for proof; no true Scotsman redefines a group so a counterexample stops counting.
contrast.fal_special_pleading: Moving the goalposts shifts a standard after it's met; special pleading exempts one case from a standard that still applies to others.

fallacies.name: No True Scotsman
fallacies.shortDef: Redefining a group to exclude a counterexample instead of revising the claim.
fallacies.definition: Defending a sweeping claim about a group by declaring, once a counterexample appears, that the counterexample was never a "real" or "true" member, so that nothing could ever count against the claim.
howToSpot: Did a counterexample appear just before the group got redefined?
Was the "real member" condition stated beforehand, or invented on the spot?
Is membership now defined by fitting the claim itself?
fallacies.classicExample: No real fan leaves before the final whistle. Your brother left early? Then he was never a real fan.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Excluding a case is fair when it fails a definition that was set beforehand and is widely agreed, like pointing out that a "vegan" cupcake made with butter isn't vegan.

contrast.fal_special_pleading: No true Scotsman changes who counts as a member; special pleading keeps the rule but exempts one case from it.
contrast.fal_moving_the_goalposts: No true Scotsman redefines a group to dodge a counterexample; moving the goalposts raises the bar for proof after it was met.

fallacies.name: Special Pleading
fallacies.shortDef: Exempting yourself or a favorite from a rule without a relevant reason.
fallacies.definition: Applying a rule or standard to others while carving out an exception for oneself, one's group or a favored case, without giving a difference that is actually relevant to the purpose of the rule.
howToSpot: Is a rule applied to others but waived for the speaker or a favorite?
What makes this case different, and is that difference relevant to the rule?
Would the speaker accept the same excuse from someone else?
fallacies.classicExample: Everyone should pay their parking tickets on time. Mine are different, though; I was only running in for a minute.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: An exception is fair when there's a stated difference that's relevant to the rule's purpose and would apply to anyone in the same spot, like waiving late fees because the payment system was down.

contrast.fal_no_true_scotsman: Special pleading exempts a case from a rule; no true Scotsman redefines a group so a counterexample no longer counts as a member.
contrast.fal_moving_the_goalposts: Special pleading carves out an exception to a standard; moving the goalposts raises the standard after someone has met it.

fallacies.name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
fallacies.shortDef: Continuing something because of what's already been spent, not what's ahead.
fallacies.definition: Letting money, time or effort that is already spent and can't be recovered drive a decision about the future, instead of weighing only the costs and benefits still to come.
howToSpot: Is the main reason to continue what has already been spent?
If you were starting fresh today, would you still choose this?
Does continuing recover the past investment, or is it gone either way?
fallacies.classicExample: This movie is awful, but we paid $18 a ticket, so we're staying until the end.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Continuing is reasonable when the remaining benefits outweigh the remaining costs, like finishing a nearly done renovation because the last step adds more value than it costs.

contrast.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Sunk cost keeps going because of what has been invested; appeal to tradition keeps going because it has always been done that way.
contrast.fal_appeal_to_consequences: Sunk cost looks back at what was spent; appeal to consequences judges a claim by whether its outcome would be pleasant.

fallacies.name: Composition
fallacies.shortDef: Assuming that what's true of the parts must be true of the whole.
fallacies.definition: Concluding that a whole has a property because each of its parts has it, when the property may not carry over: small effects can add up, parts can interact, and a whole can behave differently from its pieces.
howToSpot: Is a trait of each part being stamped onto the whole?
Could the parts add up, clash or interact once they're combined?
Does the trait depend on scale, like 'small', 'safe' or 'unnoticeable'?
fallacies.classicExample: Every player on our team is a star, so we'll obviously be the best team in the league.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Some traits do pass from parts to whole, like 'made entirely of steel', or 'gluten-free' when every ingredient is and nothing else gets in. It's fair when the trait truly transfers.

contrast.fal_division: Composition goes from the parts up to the whole; division goes from the whole down to its parts.
contrast.fal_hasty_generalization: Composition stamps the parts' traits onto the whole they form; hasty generalization stretches a few members' traits to all members.

fallacies.name: Division
fallacies.shortDef: Assuming that what's true of the whole must be true of each of its parts.
fallacies.definition: Concluding that a part or member has a property because the whole or group it belongs to has it. A top-ranked school, a winning team or a high average can still contain weak or struggling parts.
howToSpot: Is a trait of a group, team or total being pinned on one member?
Is an average or overall result treated as true of every individual?
Could the whole have the trait while some of its parts lack it?
fallacies.classicExample: Ashford is a wealthy town, so everyone who lives there must be wealthy.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Some traits do pass from whole to parts, such as a recall covering a whole batch or a rule covering every unit. It's fair when the trait applies to each part by its nature or by definition.

contrast.fal_composition: Division goes from the whole down to its parts; composition goes from the parts up to the whole.
contrast.fal_hasty_generalization: Division assumes a part shares the group's overall trait; hasty generalization builds a claim about the group from too few members.

fallacies.name: Equivocation
fallacies.shortDef: Shifting between two meanings of the same word within one argument.
fallacies.definition: Using a key word or phrase in one sense in one part of an argument and a different sense in another, so the conclusion seems to follow when it only follows because the word sounds the same.
howToSpot: Find the key word and ask what it means each time it appears.
Swap in a precise synonym each time: does the argument still work?
Watch technical words with everyday meanings, like 'significant' or 'theory'.
fallacies.classicExample: The sign said 'fine for parking here,' so I figured parking there was fine.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Using a word with several meanings is fine when its sense stays fixed throughout, or when the speaker spells out which meaning applies and reasons from that one.

contrast.fal_straw_man: A straw man distorts someone else's position; equivocation shifts the meaning of a word inside the argument itself.
contrast.fal_false_analogy: A false analogy compares two things that differ in key ways; equivocation treats two meanings of one word as if they were the same.

fallacies.name: Is–Ought Fallacy
fallacies.shortDef: Concluding what should be done purely from facts about what is.
fallacies.definition: Moving from a description of how things are (what's legal, typical, profitable or possible) to a claim about how they ought to be, without stating or defending the value premise that would connect them.
howToSpot: Do the premises only describe facts, while the conclusion says 'should' or 'fair'?
What value premise is missing, and would people actually agree with it?
Does 'can', 'does' or 'is allowed' quietly become 'ought to' or 'it's fine'?
fallacies.classicExample: Our software can record every keystroke employees make, so we should be recording them.
fallacies.legitimateVersion: Facts belong in moral and policy arguments. The step to 'should' is fair when the value premise is stated openly, like 'we've committed to protecting student health', and the facts are applied to it.

contrast.fal_appeal_to_nature: Appeal to nature says natural means good; the is–ought fallacy slides from any kind of fact (legal, typical, profitable) to a 'should'.
contrast.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Appeal to tradition says it's right because it's always been done; is–ought jumps from how things currently are to how they ought to be.

items.passage:
Lena: I compared three printer leases. Ours is $410 a month; Inkhaven is $260 for the same volume and includes toner. Sheet's attached.
Dev: Lena's the one who showed up to the client lunch in hiking boots. Not sure I want her picking our vendors.
Rafi: Can we at least open the sheet?
items.cue: Lena's the one who showed up to the client lunch in hiking boots
items.explanation: Dev answers Lena's price comparison with a jab about her shoes. Her footwear has nothing to do with whether Inkhaven is cheaper, and the numbers in the sheet go unexamined.

whyNot.fal_tu_quoque: Dev isn't saying Lena is guilty of the same thing she's criticizing; he's mocking her to brush off her numbers.

items.passage: Saw a sports dietitian going viral for saying most gym-goers could skip protein shakes and get enough from regular meals. Respectfully, the man has the build of a coat hanger. I'm not taking nutrition notes from someone who looks like that. Anyway, new 12-week program drops Friday. Link in bio.
items.cue: the man has the build of a coat hanger
items.explanation: Coach Brandt mocks the dietitian's body instead of addressing his claim about protein. Whether regular meals can cover protein needs depends on evidence, not on how the dietitian looks.

whyNot.fal_genetic_fallacy: The post doesn't dismiss the idea because of where it originated; it insults the person who said it.

items.title: Re: Later start time proposal
items.passage: Thanks, Amara, for the research packet. I agree teen sleep matters, and before any vote I'd want to see what a revised bus schedule would cost. That said, Amara has pushed a pet cause at nearly every council meeting this year, so I'd weigh her conclusions accordingly. Happy to discuss Thursday. Gordon
items.cue: Amara has pushed a pet cause at nearly every council meeting this year
items.explanation: Gordon raises a fair cost question, then discounts Amara's research by painting her as a serial crusader. Her reputation at meetings doesn't tell us whether the sleep studies hold up.

whyNot.fal_guilt_by_association: Gordon doesn't tie Amara to a disliked group or person; he attacks her own character and motives.

items.title: Decent worksheets, skip the rest
items.passage: The budgeting worksheets in chapter 3 are genuinely useful, and the tone is friendly without being preachy. But the book's big argument, that most people do better with low-cost index funds than picking stocks, is pushed by a guy who dropped out of business school and still drives a 15-year-old hatchback. Hardly a winner. Two stars.
items.cue: pushed by a guy who dropped out of business school
items.explanation: Harold praises the worksheets but rejects the index-fund argument because of the author's schooling and car. Those facts about the author don't test whether the argument's evidence is sound.

whyNot.fal_genetic_fallacy: Harold isn't tracing the idea's origin or history; he's belittling the author personally to avoid the argument.

items.passage: I've read Ms. Lindqvist's petition and the decibel readings she commissioned from an independent acoustics firm, and I thank her for the effort. But let's be realistic: her back fence is forty feet from the dog run. Of course she wants it moved. I don't think we should redesign a public park around one homeowner's interests.
items.cue: her back fence is forty feet from the dog run. Of course she wants it moved.
items.explanation: Councillor Okafor brushes aside independent noise readings by pointing to Ms. Lindqvist's personal stake. Her motive may explain why she petitioned, but it doesn't make the measurements wrong.

whyNot.fal_genetic_fallacy: The readings came from an independent firm, so this isn't judging them by their source; it dismisses them via the petitioner's motives.

items.passage: Look, I appreciate that Mei filed the ticket with repro steps and a screen recording. But this is the same Mei who flagged a 'critical' memory leak in March that turned out to be her own test config. I'm not pulling two people off the release for this one. Let's keep moving.
items.cue: flagged a 'critical' memory leak in March that turned out to be her own test config
items.explanation: The lead dismisses Mei's bug report because of a past false alarm. Her ticket comes with repro steps and a recording anyone can check, so her track record isn't what decides it.

whyNot.fal_genetic_fallacy: It isn't the ticket's origin story at issue; the lead discounts Mei herself over an old mistake while ignoring evidence anyone could verify.

items.passage: Helmets? I rode my bike to the plant every day for twenty-two years without one and never so much as scraped my head. I'm not against them, but all those head-injury studies get blown way out of proportion. Anyway, who wants another burger?
items.cue: twenty-two years without one and never so much as scraped my head
items.explanation: Ray uses his own lucky record to wave away research on head injuries. One rider avoiding a bad crash says little about what happens across thousands of crashes.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Ray isn't building a rule from a few cases so much as using his single story to outweigh the studies he mentions.

items.title: Ignore the ratings, this car is bulletproof
items.passage: Every reliability survey out there puts the Vantessa sedan near the bottom of its class, and I honestly don't get it. Mine has 140,000 miles and has never needed anything but oil changes and tires. Comfortable seats, decent mileage, roomy trunk. Don't let the ratings scare you off: this car is built to last.
items.cue: Mine has 140,000 miles and has never needed anything but oil changes and tires.
items.explanation: Tom lets his one good car outweigh surveys of thousands of owners. Some Vantessas will run perfectly even if the model breaks down more often than its rivals, so his story can't overturn the ratings.

whyNot.fal_cherry_picking: Tom isn't picking favorable numbers out of a dataset; he's setting a single personal story against the surveys.

items.passage: Every article says adults need 7-9 hours of sleep. I've slept about five hours a night for a decade, I run marathons and I manage a team of twelve. To be fair, people really do differ, and that research describes averages. But in my experience, you can train your body to need less, so stop stressing about the eight-hour rule.
items.cue: in my experience, you can train your body to need less
items.explanation: Kara sets her own routine against broad sleep research and concludes anyone can train themselves to need less. Her experience can be real without telling others what's safe for them.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Kara explicitly weighs her story against the research and lets it win; that's anecdote over data, not just a small sample.

items.title: Re: Remote connection program
items.passage: Thanks for sharing the engagement results. I know the survey of 430 staff found remote employees feel less connected, and I'm not dismissing it. But my remote team is the closest group I've ever managed; we do video coffee every Friday and nobody's quit in two years. Honestly, I don't think the connection program is needed.
items.cue: my remote team is the closest group I've ever managed
items.explanation: Victor's team may be genuinely close, but he uses it to set aside a survey of 430 people. One team's experience can't outweigh what the broader data shows across the company.

whyNot.fal_cherry_picking: Victor isn't selecting data points from the survey; he's countering the whole survey with his own team's story.

items.passage:
Ji-woo: The district report is out: across three years, kids in the ReadUp program gained about 1.5 grade levels on average.
Maria: That's encouraging!
Ji-woo: Maybe. Daniel did a full year of it and his reading didn't budge. Honestly, I'm not convinced it does much, and I'd rather the PTA funded something else.
items.cue: Daniel did a full year of it and his reading didn't budge
items.explanation: Ji-woo's frustration is understandable, but she lets her son's year outweigh three years of district-wide results. An average gain still leaves room for some kids who don't improve.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Ji-woo isn't building a claim from a few cases; she has the district data in front of her and lets one child's story overrule it.

items.source: Resident Glen Harlow · Pine County water board hearing
items.passage: I've read the county's report saying nitrate levels in rural wells along Route 6 have climbed past the safety limit. With respect, my family has drunk from our well for thirty years. Three kids, six grandkids, all healthy as horses. I don't doubt the lab did its job, but I don't see why we need to spend money on filters.
items.cue: my family has drunk from our well for thirty years
items.explanation: Glen's family history feels like strong evidence, but it can't outweigh lab tests of the water itself. Thirty healthy years don't show today's water is safe, especially since the levels have recently climbed.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Glen isn't sampling a few wells; he sets his family's experience against the county's tests and lets the story win.

items.title: The recovery secret of a champion
items.passage: Three-time national sprint champion Dez Calloway wears Magnara copper bands every single day. 'They've completely changed my recovery,' he says. If they work for one of the fastest men alive, imagine what they'll do for your sore knees. Two bands for $39, free shipping this week only.
items.cue: If they work for one of the fastest men alive
items.explanation: The ad treats a sprinter's endorsement as proof that copper bands relieve joint pain. Dez knows sprinting, not medicine, and the ad offers no evidence that the bands do anything.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: The ad leans on one famous athlete's word, not on how many people use the bands.

items.passage:
Grandpa Tunde: Don't install the phone update tonight. My friend Lionel says updates are how they secretly slow down older phones.
Femi: Lionel... your dentist?
Grandpa Tunde: He's a doctor, Femi. A very smart man. If he says it, I trust it.
items.cue: He's a doctor, Femi. A very smart man. If he says it, I trust it.
items.explanation: Grandpa trusts Lionel on phone software because he's a respected dentist. Dental training says nothing about how phone updates work.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Grandpa relies on one person's status, not on how many people believe the claim.

items.title: Thoughts after curriculum night
items.passage: Hi Ms. Duarte, thank you for a great curriculum night. I loved the focus on word problems, and the new homework portal is much easier to use. One concern: bestselling novelist Corinne Hale, whose kids attend Westbrook, has written that this discovery-based math leaves children confused. She's a brilliant thinker, and I'd like the school to reconsider.
items.cue: She's a brilliant thinker, and I'd like the school to reconsider.
items.explanation: Renata asks the school to rethink its math approach because a famous novelist criticized it. Corinne's talent as a writer doesn't make her an authority on how children learn math.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Renata cites one celebrated person, not a crowd; the trouble is that the novelist's expertise lies elsewhere.

items.passage: Day 12 of cold plunges after my morning lift. The first minute is brutal, I won't lie, and my towel budget has doubled. Grandmaster Viktor Sandor, one of the greatest chess minds alive, does it every morning and says cold water 'resets your immune system.' If a mind like that swears by it, that's good enough for me.
items.cue: If a mind like that swears by it, that's good enough for me.
items.explanation: Nadia accepts a health claim because a chess champion makes it. Brilliance at chess isn't expertise in immunology, and no evidence is offered for the 'reset'.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Nadia relies on a single admired figure, not on the popularity of cold plunges.

items.source: Board chair Leonard Fitch · Halverton school board
items.passage: We've heard a lot tonight about sleep studies supporting a later start, and I've read some of them. But I'd remind everyone that Dr. Anjali Rao, a cardiologist who has practiced in this county for thirty years, told us last month that a 45-minute shift makes no real difference to teenagers' health. If anyone understands health, it's her. I'm comfortable keeping our schedule.
items.cue: If anyone understands health, it's her.
items.explanation: Leonard sets the sleep research aside in favor of one respected doctor's opinion. Dr. Rao is a heart specialist, not a sleep researcher, and her view runs against the studies he just mentioned.

whyNot.fal_genetic_fallacy: Leonard isn't judging the sleep studies by their origin; he overrides them with one doctor's standing outside her specialty.

items.title: Analysts raise battery outlook after Kaplan's bold forecast
items.passage: Venture investor Sloane Kaplan, whose early bets on three software giants made her a billionaire, told a conference Thursday that solid-state home batteries will halve household electricity bills within five years. Analysts at Grayfield Research raised their sector forecast the next morning, citing her unmatched record of spotting winners.
items.cue: citing her unmatched record of spotting winners
items.explanation: The analysts raise their forecast because a celebrated software investor made a prediction. Her record picking software companies doesn't make her an expert on battery chemistry or energy costs.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: The analysts aren't following a crowd; they defer to one investor's reputation in a field outside her expertise.

items.passage:
Hiroshi: Physio thinks my shin pain is a stress reaction. She wants me off running for six weeks.
Danielle: No way. The marathon is in five weeks and you've trained all year. It has to be something minor.
Hiroshi: She did press on it and I nearly hit the ceiling.
items.cue: The marathon is in five weeks and you've trained all year. It has to be something minor.
items.explanation: Danielle decides the injury must be minor because a serious one would wreck Hiroshi's race. The race date has no bearing on what's actually happening in his shin.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_emotion: Danielle isn't just stirring feelings; she infers a medical fact from how bad the alternative would be.

items.source: Car buyer to a friend · dealership lot
items.passage: The dealer swears it's never been in an accident, and honestly, it can't have been. We've promised the whole family a lake trip in it on Friday, and I'm not telling the kids it's off. So no, I'm not spending $40 on a history report. Help me pick seat covers?
items.cue: it can't have been. We've promised the whole family a lake trip in it on Friday
items.explanation: The buyer decides the SUV is accident-free because the alternative would ruin Friday's lake trip. Whether the car was ever in a crash doesn't depend on the family's plans.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_emotion: It's more than a feeling on display; the buyer treats an unwanted outcome as proof of a fact about the car.

items.title: Re: FY27 revenue forecast
items.passage: Thanks for the review, Adaeze. You're right that Q3 bookings came in below plan, and I've trimmed the marketing line to reflect that. But I can't accept a forecast showing a 15% revenue decline next year. A number like that would mean closing the Ashby office and telling the board we've lost a year. Our forecast has to show growth, and I'm confident it's there.
items.cue: A number like that would mean closing the Ashby office
items.explanation: Graham accepts the weak Q3 numbers but rejects the decline forecast because of what it would force the company to do. Painful consequences don't make a forecast inaccurate.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_emotion: Graham isn't just stirring feelings; he argues the projection is wrong because acting on it would be painful.

items.passage: Seeing chatter about the university report saying algae levels in Kestrel Lake are unsafe for swimming. Our town runs on summer visitors. If that report were right, half the shops on Shore Road would be shuttered by August, so no, we're not buying it. Lifeguards are on duty all weekend and the ice cream stand opens at 10!
items.cue: If that report were right, half the shops on Shore Road would be shuttered by August
items.explanation: The post rejects the algae findings because accepting them would hurt local businesses. The lake's water quality doesn't depend on what it would mean for the shops.

whyNot.fal_slippery_slope: The post isn't predicting a chain set off by some step; it denies a fact because its implications would be costly.

items.source: Coach Rory Webb · Wrenford Youth Soccer parent night
items.passage: Some of you sent me that article saying kids born in the first few months of the year are far more likely to be picked for elite youth teams. I don't believe it. If a kid born in November thinks his birthday decides his future, he'll quit before he starts, and I won't have that. Hard work is what gets players picked, full stop.
items.cue: If a kid born in November thinks his birthday decides his future, he'll quit before he starts
items.explanation: Coach Webb rejects the birth-month finding because believing it might discourage younger kids. That's a good reason to talk with players carefully, but it says nothing about whether the pattern is real.

whyNot.fal_slippery_slope: He isn't predicting an unsupported chain from a first step; he denies a factual pattern because believing it could discourage kids.

items.title: Rare heron sighting at Fen Marsh sparks celebration, and caution
items.passage: A single photo taken at dusk has Fen Marsh volunteers convinced the great white heron is nesting there for the first time in 30 years. 'If she's back, it means the restoration worked and every muddy Saturday was worth it,' said volunteer chair Silas Pryce. 'So I'm calling it: she's back.' County biologists say the photo is too dark to confirm the species.
items.cue: If she's back, it means the restoration worked and every muddy Saturday was worth it
items.explanation: Silas decides the heron is back because that outcome would vindicate years of volunteer work. Wanting it to be true doesn't make a dark photo any clearer; only a confirmed sighting would.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_emotion: Silas's hope is emotional, but his reasoning goes further: he concludes a fact is true because its implications would be so welcome.

items.title: Because they're only little once
items.passage: Those first walks to the park. Tiny fingers curled around yours. Moments like these deserve the Pellora Glide, with hand-stitched trim and our signature champagne finish. You'd never give them less than your best. Don't start with their stroller. From $1,249.
items.cue: You'd never give them less than your best.
items.explanation: The ad uses tender images and parental guilt to justify a $1,249 stroller. Love for your child doesn't tell you whether champagne trim makes this stroller safer or better.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_fear: Nothing here warns of danger; the ad leans on tenderness and guilt, not fear.

items.passage: Did you SEE what the Fenmoor Gazette wrote about our Kestrels? After everything this team has given Kestrel Point? I've never been so proud to wear the purple. Anyone with an ounce of hometown pride knows they're the best team in the league, period. Game day Saturday, be loud!
items.cue: Anyone with an ounce of hometown pride knows they're the best team in the league
items.explanation: Ray answers a critical article with indignation and team pride. Feeling proud of the Kestrels doesn't show they're the best team in the league; standings and results would.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_pity: Ray isn't asking anyone to feel sorry for the team; he's stirring up pride and indignation.

items.title: Re: Saturday launch support
items.passage: Hi Joaquin, fair questions about whether QA could wait until Monday morning and whether Saturday counts as overtime. The client did move the launch up, so the pressure is real. But remember how this team pulled together when the Ferris account nearly walked? That's who we are. I'd hate for anyone to be the one counting hours when this team needs them. So I'm counting on all of you at 9 Saturday. Kara
items.cue: I'd hate for anyone to be the one counting hours when this team needs them.
items.explanation: Joaquin asks two practical questions, and Kara answers neither; she invokes team pride and the guilt of 'counting hours' instead. Those feelings don't show Saturday work is necessary or fairly paid.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_pity: Kara isn't asking for sympathy over her own hardship; she uses team pride and guilt to fill the weekend shift.

items.source: Trustee Royce Danforth · Fenmoor school board
items.passage: The nutrition panel says the cricket-flour cookies are high in protein, safe and cheaper than the current snack. Fine. But picture your seven-year-old biting into a cookie made of ground-up bugs. I described it to a room of parents last week and watched their faces. That reaction tells you everything about whether this belongs in our cafeterias.
items.cue: That reaction tells you everything about whether this belongs in our cafeterias.
items.explanation: Royce concedes the panel's findings, then asks the board to decide based on disgust. Parents' grimaces don't tell us whether the cookies are nutritious, safe or affordable.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_fear: Royce doesn't claim the cookies are dangerous; he relies on disgust, a different feeling, to override the evidence.

items.passage: You worked thirty-plus years for this. You worked the weekends, you showed up when it was hard. You deserve a retirement that feels like a reward, not a compromise. That's why the Harrowgate Legacy annuity is the right home for your savings. The fee schedule's in your packet, but honestly, what matters is how you want to feel.
items.cue: honestly, what matters is how you want to feel
items.explanation: The adviser stirs pride and a sense of being owed, then presents the annuity as the answer while waving off the fees. Feeling deserving says nothing about whether this product suits your savings.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_pity: The adviser isn't asking you to sympathize with anyone's hardship; he flatters your pride and sense of reward to make the sale.

items.title: Shoppers bristle as Osterbrook market goes card-only
items.passage: Vendors say counting cash cost them hours each week and that 94% of sales were already by card. Longtime shopper Wes Harlan wasn't swayed: 'After all the money we've spent at these stalls, this is how they treat us? Any decision that leaves loyal customers feeling this insulted is the wrong decision, simple as that.'
items.cue: Any decision that leaves loyal customers feeling this insulted is the wrong decision
items.explanation: Wes doesn't dispute the vendors' reasons; he argues the change is wrong because it makes him feel insulted. His hurt feelings are real, but they don't show going card-only is a bad decision.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_pity: Wes isn't describing a hardship to win sympathy; he treats his feeling of insult as proof that the decision is wrong.

items.title: Is someone reading this right now?
items.passage: Every time you join café Wi-Fi, hackers can see your passwords, your bank balance, even your private photos. It happens to millions of people every day, and most never find out until it's too late. Don't be next. Protect every device in your home with Shroudline for $11.99 a month.
items.cue: hackers can see your passwords, your bank balance, even your private photos
items.explanation: The ad paints a vivid, sweeping threat with no evidence of how often it really happens. Most sites already encrypt logins, so the danger is inflated to sell the subscription.

whyNot.fal_slippery_slope: There's no chain of events here; the ad simply inflates one threat to scare you into buying.

items.passage: PSA: please stop microwaving your leftovers. The radiation scrambles your food at the molecular level, and nobody is talking about what that's doing to your body over time. We threw ours out last year and I sleep so much better knowing it's gone. My kitchen reset guide is linked in bio.
items.cue: nobody is talking about what that's doing to your body over time
items.explanation: Mira hints at a vague, unsupported danger to get followers to ditch their microwaves. She offers no evidence of harm, just an ominous suggestion of what might be happening.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_emotion: The post's pull comes specifically from dread of hidden harm, not from pride, guilt or another feeling.

items.title: Action needed: file migration by Friday
items.passage: Hi all, on December 1 we're moving shared files to Coffer Drive. The current server is out of warranty, and Coffer adds the version history many of you requested. Please migrate your folders this week. Anyone who leaves files on the old server is putting the whole company at risk. One ransomware attack and we could all be out of a job by Christmas.
items.cue: One ransomware attack and we could all be out of a job by Christmas.
items.explanation: The email gives solid reasons to migrate, then tacks on a dramatic worst case: everyone jobless by Christmas. That inflated threat isn't supported and replaces an honest account of the risk.

whyNot.fal_slippery_slope: There's no step-by-step chain; the email jumps straight to a single exaggerated disaster to scare people into acting.

items.source: Resident Bernard Lyle · Wrenford parks meeting
items.passage: I support giving teenagers more to do in this town, and the skate park design looks well thought out. But a park like that draws strangers from all over the county, and I won't stand here and pretend our children will be safe once it opens. Ask yourselves if you'd let your eight-year-old walk past it alone.
items.cue: I won't stand here and pretend our children will be safe once it opens
items.explanation: Bernard offers no evidence that skate parks put children in danger; he invites the room to imagine the worst. Fear of strangers stands in for any data about actual risk.

whyNot.fal_slippery_slope: Bernard doesn't lay out a chain of escalating steps; he relies on a vague, unsupported threat to children's safety.

items.title: Sleep coach urges parents to pull bedtime tablets
items.passage: In a survey of 40 families, children who read on tablets before bed fell asleep about 12 minutes later on average. Pediatric sleep coach Talia Prescott says parents shouldn't wait for more research: 'Every night you hesitate, you're gambling with your child's developing brain.' She is launching a screen-free bedtime course next month.
items.cue: Every night you hesitate, you're gambling with your child's developing brain.
items.explanation: The survey found a modest 12-minute delay, but Talia frames it as a threat to children's brains. The alarm far outruns the evidence, and fear does the persuading.

whyNot.fal_slippery_slope: She doesn't trace a chain of steps from tablets to disaster; she inflates a small finding into a frightening threat.

items.passage:
Lucia: Finally opening a high-yield savings account for the house fund. 4.1% at Thimble Bay Bank.
Uncle Desmond: Banks fail more often than they let on. One bad week and your account is frozen and you're standing outside a locked door while your down payment disappears. I keep mine in a safe at home.
Lucia: Isn't the account insured, though?
items.cue: you're standing outside a locked door while your down payment disappears
items.explanation: Desmond paints a vivid scene of a vanishing down payment without weighing how rare bank failures are or how deposit insurance works. The image does the persuading, not the actual risk.

whyNot.fal_slippery_slope: Desmond isn't predicting a chain set off by Lucia's choice; he uses one exaggerated disaster scene to frighten her.

items.passage: Third summer camping at Lake Corrigan, and the locals still swear there's something huge living down there. Scientists have never proven there isn't, so honestly, I'm counting it as real. Bringing the good camera and the canoe this year. Wish me luck!
items.cue: Scientists have never proven there isn't, so honestly, I'm counting it as real.
items.explanation: Wes treats the lack of proof that there's no creature as a reason to believe there is one. Not having disproven something doesn't make it true.

whyNot.fal_burden_of_proof: Wes isn't demanding that anyone disprove him; he concludes it's real because no one has shown otherwise.

items.passage:
Priyanka: It's been a month since we switched to the four-day sprint cycle. Any feedback from your teams?
Byron: Nobody's complained, so I think it's safe to say everyone loves it.
Ji-ho: To be fair, the feedback form link was broken until yesterday.
items.cue: Nobody's complained, so I think it's safe to say everyone loves it.
items.explanation: Byron takes the absence of complaints as proof that everyone loves the change. Silence isn't approval, especially when, as Ji-ho notes, people couldn't easily give feedback.

whyNot.fal_burden_of_proof: Byron doesn't ask anyone to prove the team dislikes it; he reads a lack of complaints as evidence of approval.

items.title: Pebblestep Readers expanding next fall
items.passage: Dear families, we're excited to share that Pebblestep Readers will expand to every K-3 classroom next fall. Teachers enjoyed the training, and families have given the new books great marks. We haven't measured reading scores yet, but nothing so far suggests the program doesn't work, so we can be confident it's raising reading levels.
items.cue: nothing so far suggests the program doesn't work, so we can be confident it's raising reading levels
items.explanation: The positive feedback is real, but Alana admits reading scores haven't been measured, then concludes the program works because nothing shows it doesn't.

whyNot.fal_burden_of_proof: Alana doesn't ask families to disprove the program; she concludes it works simply because no evidence against it exists yet.

items.title: Parks director: new field infill is safe
items.passage: Asked about residents' questions over the rubber infill on the new Nettlefield Park sports fields, the parks director said no study has ever found the product harmful, so families can be confident it's safe. The infill, introduced by its manufacturer last year, has not yet been the subject of any published research.
items.cue: no study has ever found the product harmful, so families can be confident it's safe
items.explanation: The director treats "no study found harm" as proof of safety, but the last line shows no studies of this product exist at all. No harm has been found because nobody has looked.

whyNot.fal_burden_of_proof: The director doesn't demand that residents prove harm; he concludes the product is safe because harm hasn't been shown.

items.source: Councillor Yvette Marchand · Hollis Bay transportation committee
items.passage: I'll be the skeptic in the room. The protected bike lane on Dorsey Street has been open for three months, and so far there is no evidence it has reduced injuries. None. We were promised safer streets. If the data can't show it's working, then it isn't working, and I'll be moving to restore the parking.
items.cue: If the data can't show it's working, then it isn't working
items.explanation: Yvette sounds rigorous, but three months is likely too short to show any effect on injuries. She turns "not yet shown to work" into "shown not to work."

whyNot.fal_burden_of_proof: Asking supporters for evidence is fair; Yvette's error is concluding the lane fails because early data can't yet show an effect.

items.title: Five years. Zero breaches.
items.passage: Thriftwren has helped families track their spending since 2021. In five years, we've never had a single reported data breach, which tells you everything you need to know: your information is completely secure with us. Link your bank accounts in under two minutes and finally see where your money goes.
items.cue: we've never had a single reported data breach, which tells you everything you need to know
items.explanation: Thriftwren treats the absence of reported breaches as proof of complete security. A clean record is nice, but breaches can go undetected or unreported, so it can't show the app is secure.

whyNot.fal_burden_of_proof: Thriftwren doesn't ask anyone to prove the app insecure; it treats the absence of reported breaches as proof of security.

items.title: Sleep the way you were meant to
items.passage: Mossgrove Calm drops blend valerian, chamomile and lemon balm, with nothing cooked up in a lab. Your body knows the difference. Why fill your system with synthetic sleep aids when the earth already grows something better? 30 nights for $24, or your money back.
items.cue: Why fill your system with synthetic sleep aids when the earth already grows something better?
items.explanation: Mossgrove claims its drops beat sleep medications simply because they come from plants. Being plant-based says nothing about whether they work or are safer; that takes evidence.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: The ad never says the herbs are an old remedy; its pitch is that plants beat anything made in a lab.

items.passage:
Kemi: Heads up, the cleaning crew is starting to use a hospital-grade disinfectant in the hallways and laundry room.
Bjorn: Ugh. I'm asking them to switch to plain vinegar. Something that starts out as apples isn't going to hurt anyone, and it'll handle germs as well as anything mixed in a factory.
Kemi: Is that true about the germs, though?
items.cue: Something that starts out as apples isn't going to hurt anyone
items.explanation: Bjorn assumes vinegar is harmless and just as effective because it comes from fruit instead of a factory. Whether a cleaner is safe or kills germs depends on testing, not on what it's made from.

whyNot.fal_is_ought: Bjorn isn't jumping from how things are to how they ought to be; he assumes that coming from fruit, not a factory, makes a cleaner safe and effective.

items.title: Pricey, but the clean caffeine is worth it
items.passage: Tastes like fresh grapefruit, and the can design is gorgeous. The caffeine comes from green coffee beans instead of the synthetic stuff in regular energy drinks, so it's much gentler on your heart. I'm comfortable drinking three a day now. Only complaint: at $3.50 a can, it adds up fast.
items.cue: instead of the synthetic stuff in regular energy drinks, so it's much gentler on your heart
items.explanation: Priscilla assumes caffeine from beans is easier on the heart than synthetic caffeine. It's the same molecule either way, so three cans a day carries the same caffeine load.
