whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Nothing here rests on custom or history; the flaw is treating 'from beans' as automatically gentler.

items.passage: Switched from cushioned trainers to barefoot shoes in January. My calves screamed for a month, so ease in if you try it. But our feet evolved to run on bare ground, so all that foam is just a crutch that weakens them. No more padding for me, ever. Ten-miler this weekend!
items.cue: our feet evolved to run on bare ground, so all that foam is just a crutch
items.explanation: Marco gives sensible advice about easing in, then argues cushioning is harmful because barefoot running is how feet evolved. What feet did naturally doesn't settle what's best for a modern runner.

whyNot.fal_is_ought: It's not a general leap from facts to duties; Marco treats the natural state of feet as automatically the healthy one.

items.source: Parent rep Sunita Varma · Brookside school board
items.passage: The proposal before us replaces the artificially sweetened yogurt in our cafeterias with versions sweetened with honey and fruit concentrate, and I think that's the right call. Whatever the lab reports say about the sweetener, children's bodies are built for real food, not compounds engineered in a factory. Real ingredients are always the healthier choice.
items.cue: children's bodies are built for real food, not compounds engineered in a factory
items.explanation: Sunita sets aside the lab reports on the sweetener and prefers honey and fruit concentrate because they're 'real food'. Both are still added sugar, so naturalness alone doesn't settle which is healthier.

whyNot.fal_is_ought: Sunita isn't moving from facts to moral duties; she assumes natural ingredients are healthier simply because they're natural.

items.title: Community garden votes to allow only plant-derived pesticides
items.passage: Members of the Larkmoor community garden voted 23-9 to ban synthetic pesticides from the plots this spring. Member Imogen Tate, who proposed the change, said sprays 'derived from plants work with the garden's ecosystem instead of against it.' The new rule allows pyrethrin and neem-based products, which members say they will apply more often to compensate.
items.cue: derived from plants work with the garden's ecosystem instead of against it
items.explanation: Imogen argues plant-derived sprays are better for the garden because of where they come from. Pyrethrins are toxic to bees and fish too; effects, not origins, decide ecological harm.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Imogen's case isn't that plant sprays are traditional; it's that coming from plants makes them ecologically gentler.

items.title: Request to reconsider my final grade
items.passage: Dear Professor Achebe, I'm writing about my final grade of C-. I know I missed three labs and never submitted the last report. But this semester has been incredibly hard: my car broke down twice and I've been working 30 hours a week. I really need a B to keep my scholarship. Could you please reconsider? Thank you, Jordan
items.cue: I really need a B to keep my scholarship
items.explanation: Jordan admits the missing work, then asks for a higher grade because of a hard semester and scholarship pressure. A grade measures the work completed; sympathy doesn't change that.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_emotion: Jordan isn't stirring pride or outrage; the request rests specifically on sympathy for a difficult semester.

items.source: Junior player to the line judge · Kestrel Point Open
items.passage: Come on, that ball was in! I've lost five matches in a row, my dad drove all night to get me here, and I've been playing through a sore wrist all week. Please, just give me this one point. I really need it.
items.cue: I've lost five matches in a row, my dad drove all night to get me here
items.explanation: The player wants the line call reversed because of a losing streak, a long drive and a sore wrist. None of that tells the judge where the ball actually landed.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: The player stays on the line call; the problem is offering hardships as the reason to change it.

items.title: Give this family a break
items.passage: Service was slow and my pasta arrived lukewarm. But the owner told us his wife has been ill and he's running the kitchen alone most nights. Honestly, given what this family is going through, the food is better than the other reviews are saying. Four stars, and please go support them.
items.cue: given what this family is going through, the food is better than the other reviews are saying
items.explanation: Linnea's own visit matches the complaints, but she rates the food higher because she feels for the owner. His situation is a reason for kindness, not evidence about the pasta.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: Linnea doesn't change the subject from the food; she lets sympathy for the owner raise her verdict on it.

items.passage:
Pavel: Your PR fails the checkout tests and has no handling for expired cards. I can't approve it yet.
Nia: The expired-card path is maybe 1% of orders. And I've been here until 10 every night this week, and I just found out my lease isn't being renewed. Can we please merge it? I really need a win right now.
items.cue: I just found out my lease isn't being renewed
items.explanation: Nia makes one relevant point about how rare expired cards are, then leans on her rough week to get the code merged. Her late nights and lease don't fix the failing checkout tests.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_emotion: Nia's appeal is specifically for sympathy over her personal hardship, not some other feeling like pride or outrage.

items.source: Builder Samuel Okoro · Larkmoor zoning hearing
items.passage: Before you vote on the variance, I want you to know who's behind this project. My family has run Okoro Builders for three generations. The last two years have been brutal: we laid off half our crew, and my father's health is failing. Yes, the building sits four feet closer to the creek than the floodplain rule allows. This variance is the difference between finishing and losing everything.
items.cue: we laid off half our crew, and my father's health is failing
items.explanation: Samuel asks the board to excuse a floodplain violation because of his family's hardships. The rule exists for flood safety, and his struggles don't change how close the building sits to the creek.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: His story isn't an unrelated detour; it's offered as the very reason to grant the variance, which makes it a plea for sympathy.

items.passage: People are tearing apart Dr. Aldana's report on the Brindle River cleanup, and it's hard to watch. Her funding was cut in the spring, she's been caring for her mother on top of running the lab, and she still got this done. The least we can do is give her findings the benefit of the doubt instead of nitpicking her sampling methods.
items.cue: The least we can do is give her findings the benefit of the doubt
items.explanation: Gail asks readers to accept Dr. Aldana's findings because of her personal struggles. Pushing through hardship is admirable, but it doesn't answer the questions about her sampling methods.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_emotion: Gail's case rests specifically on sympathy for Dr. Aldana's hardships, not on pride, fear or outrage.

items.passage: I've seen the proposal to switch our inventory counts to barcode scanners. This plant has counted stock on clipboards since my grandfather worked the line, and we've gotten by fine. If it worked for three generations, it'll work for us. Let's get the forklifts moving.
items.cue: If it worked for three generations, it'll work for us.
items.explanation: The supervisor rejects scanners because clipboards have been used for generations. Long use shows the method survived, not that it's as accurate or efficient as the alternative.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: He isn't pointing to how many plants use clipboards now; he's pointing to how long this one has.

items.passage: Westbrook football has been played on Friday nights under the lights since 1962. My dad played on that field, I played on it, my son plays on it now. Moving games to Saturday afternoons to save on 'electricity costs' is ridiculous. Some things you just don't change. Go Herons!
items.cue: Some things you just don't change.
items.explanation: Earl rejects the cost-saving move because Friday games go back decades in his family and town. That history means a lot to him, but it doesn't answer the electricity cost question.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Earl's reason is how long the custom has lasted, not how many people currently favor Friday games.

items.title: Re: Spring fundraiser ideas
items.passage: Hi everyone, a few parents suggested replacing the wrapping-paper sale with an online donation drive, and I appreciate the thought. Online would save volunteer hours, that's true. But the wrapping-paper sale has been how Maple Ridge raises money for nearly thirty years, and I don't see a reason to drop something that's part of who we are. Deb
items.cue: has been how Maple Ridge raises money for nearly thirty years
items.explanation: Deborah grants that the online drive would save volunteer time, then keeps the sale mainly because it's a thirty-year habit. Its age doesn't show it raises more money or is worth the hours.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Nothing here is about what's natural; Deborah's reason is simply how long the sale has been a school custom.

items.title: Some recipes shouldn't be touched
items.passage: The new owners at Odile's Diner added oat milk, a veggie hash and online ordering. Food came out fast and the hash was honestly tasty. But they've changed the pancake batter, which has been on this menu since 1958. I didn't even order them. You don't mess with a recipe that's lasted that long. Three stars.
items.cue: You don't mess with a recipe that's lasted that long.
items.explanation: Clement docks the diner for changing a decades-old recipe without even tasting the new pancakes. A recipe's age doesn't tell you whether the new version is better or worse.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Clement isn't objecting to anything artificial; he objects purely because the old recipe had lasted so long.

items.source: Hal Brunner · Osterbrook garden club talk
items.passage: Folks ask whether planting by the moon's phases actually works. My family has farmed this valley for four generations, and every one of them sowed root crops on the waning moon. That kind of knowledge, tested season after season, doesn't need a lab study to back it up. I'll be handing out this year's planting calendar at the door.
items.cue: That kind of knowledge, tested season after season, doesn't need a lab study to back it up.
items.explanation: Hal treats four generations of habit as proof that moon planting works. Repeating a practice isn't the same as testing it; without comparing results, the 'testing' is just tradition.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Hal's case isn't that moon planting is natural; it's that his family has done it for generations.

items.passage:
Grace: Survey says 72% of staff want to drop the business-casual dress code. Most client meetings are on video now anyway.
Hector: Before we scrap it, remember it's been in place since the firm opened in 1984. Policies that survive that long usually exist for good reasons, even if nobody remembers them. I'd keep it.
Grace: Do we know what the reasons were?
items.cue: Policies that survive that long usually exist for good reasons, even if nobody remembers them.
items.explanation: Hector sounds cautious, but he treats the dress code's age as proof it's justified without naming any reason. Grace's question is the right one: what was it for, and does that still apply?

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Hector doesn't appeal to what most firms do; he appeals to how long this policy has lasted.

items.title: Join the 2 million
items.passage: Over 2 million people now start their mornings with Thrivetide greens powder. Your neighbors, your coworkers, the folks at your gym. It's the fastest-growing wellness drink in the country, and that doesn't happen by accident. What are you waiting for? First tub 30% off.
items.cue: It's the fastest-growing wellness drink in the country, and that doesn't happen by accident.
items.explanation: The ad offers sales numbers and growth as the reason to buy, with no evidence the powder does anything for your health. Popularity can reflect marketing as easily as results.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_authority: No expert or celebrity is cited; the pitch rests entirely on how many people are buying.

items.passage:
Owen: Is the take-home quiz open-book? The syllabus says all quizzes are closed-book.
Leila: Literally the whole class is using their notes. If that many people are doing it, it's obviously allowed.
Owen: Or a lot of people are about to lose points.
items.cue: If that many people are doing it, it's obviously allowed.
items.explanation: Leila concludes notes are allowed because most classmates are using them. The syllabus sets the rule, and it says closed-book no matter how many people ignore it.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Leila isn't saying it's always been done this way; she points to how many people are doing it right now.

items.title: Buggy, but there's a reason it's #1
items.passage: Setup took most of an afternoon, and the mobile app crashes whenever I attach large files. Support took four days to reply. That said, this has been the most downloaded productivity app on the store for three years running, so whatever problems it has can't be that serious. Four stars.
items.cue: so whatever problems it has can't be that serious
items.explanation: Paul lists real problems from his own use, then waves them away because the app is the most downloaded. Download counts don't make the crashes or slow support any less serious.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_authority: Paul isn't deferring to an expert; he lets the app's popularity outweigh his own evidence.

items.passage: I've heard from residents on both sides of this, and I know change is never comfortable. But thirty-eight towns in the region have switched to every-other-week trash pickup in the last two years, and more sign on every month. It's clear which way the region is heading, and I don't want Ferncliff to be the last town left behind.
items.cue: I don't want Ferncliff to be the last town left behind
items.explanation: Rafael's whole case is that other towns have switched and more keep joining. That shows the change is spreading, not that every-other-week pickup would work for Ferncliff's households or budget.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Rafael isn't defending an old custom; he pushes the change because most towns are adopting it, which is popularity, not tradition.

items.passage: The line outside Halmeoni's Table has gone around the block every single day since it opened two weeks ago. Thirty-minute waits, sold out by 2. I haven't actually made it in yet, but at this point it's clearly the best Korean food in Wrenford. Sorry to every other spot in town.
items.cue: I haven't actually made it in yet, but at this point it's clearly the best
items.explanation: Ji-woo crowns the restaurant the best Korean food in town based on its lines, without tasting it. Crowds at a brand-new spot can reflect novelty and buzz as much as quality.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_authority: No critic or expert is involved; the verdict rests on how many people are lining up.

items.title: Proposal: unlimited PTO starting in Q1
items.passage: Hi leadership team, as we plan for Q1, I'd like us to move to unlimited PTO. The Larchmont Talent Survey shows 71% of companies in our sector now offer it, up from 30% just three years ago. That tells me the industry has settled the question, and unlimited PTO is simply the better model. I've attached a draft policy for Thursday's meeting.
items.cue: That tells me the industry has settled the question, and unlimited PTO is simply the better model
items.explanation: Monique's only reason is that most companies in the sector now offer unlimited PTO. Its rapid spread shows a trend, not that the policy is better or that it would work for this team.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_authority: The survey is a headcount of which companies offer the policy, not an expert verdict; Monique is following the crowd, not deferring to expertise.

items.passage: Lots of "where's the evidence?" comments on my copper bracelet video, so let me answer once. I said copper eases joint pain, and I stand by it. If you're so sure it doesn't, go find me a study that proves it doesn't work. I'll wait.
items.cue: If you're so sure it doesn't, go find me a study that proves it doesn't work
items.explanation: Lorna made the claim that copper eases joint pain, so it's up to her to support it. Instead she demands that her doubters prove it doesn't work.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_ignorance: Lorna doesn't argue it's true because no one disproved it; her move is handing the job of proving to her critics.

items.passage:
Hugo: Quinlet's new app is copying our onboarding screens. We should have legal send a letter.
Amina: Do we have anything showing that? Screenshots, a timeline, anything?
Hugo: Can you show me they didn't copy us? You're the one doubting it.
items.cue: Can you show me they didn't copy us? You're the one doubting it.
items.explanation: Hugo makes a serious accusation and wants legal action, but when Amina asks for evidence, he asks her to prove the copying didn't happen.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_ignorance: Hugo doesn't conclude it's true from a lack of evidence; he flips the job of proving onto the person who asked.

items.title: Concern about Eli's history grade
items.passage: Dear Principal Sato, thank you for meeting with us last week. I've looked over Eli's graded essays again, and I still believe Mr. Brandt marks him more harshly than his classmates. If the school disagrees, I'd ask you to demonstrate that he doesn't, with a comparison of every essay he graded this term. Kind regards, Colette Ambrose
items.cue: If the school disagrees, I'd ask you to demonstrate that he doesn't
items.explanation: Colette claims Eli is graded more harshly but offers no comparison of her own. She asks the school to prove the unfairness isn't happening instead of showing that it is.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_ignorance: Colette doesn't say it's true because nobody disproved it; she makes the school responsible for disproving her claim.

items.source: Vendor Beatriz Lowell · Grantmere council meeting
items.passage: Thanks for letting me speak. I've run the honey stand at the Saturday market for nine years, and I'm certain the new Route 6 bus schedule is what's keeping shoppers away this summer. Councillor Diaz asked me for numbers. Respectfully, I'm not the one who changed the buses. If the council thinks the schedule isn't the problem, show us that.
items.cue: If the council thinks the schedule isn't the problem, show us that.
items.explanation: Beatriz claims the bus schedule is driving shoppers away, then refuses to back it up and asks the council to prove the schedule isn't the cause.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_ignorance: Beatriz doesn't argue her claim is true because no one disproved it; she declines to support it and hands the job to the council.

items.source: Dr. Corwin Fenn, archaeologist · radio interview about the Wendle Moor stones
items.passage: My critics keep saying I haven't shown the stones were aligned on purpose. Fair enough, but what have they shown? Calling the alignments coincidence is a claim too, so let them prove it: show me the math that rules out design. Until then, we're on equal footing.
items.cue: Calling the alignments coincidence is a claim too, so let them prove it
items.explanation: Corwin is the one claiming the stones were designed, so he owes the evidence. Critics who doubt him aren't making a rival claim, yet he asks them to rule out design.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_ignorance: Corwin doesn't conclude the stones were designed because nobody disproved it; he demands that critics do the proving.

items.title: Two stars until they come clean
items.passage: Camera is still excellent and battery life is fine. But I'm convinced the latest update deliberately slows down older models to push people to upgrade. Support told me there's no such feature. Then they should have no problem releasing internal benchmark data showing it doesn't happen. Until they do, two stars.
items.cue: Then they should have no problem releasing internal benchmark data showing it doesn't happen
items.explanation: Mateus's demand sounds like a call for transparency, but he offers no sign of slowdown himself. He makes the accusation, then insists the company disprove it.

whyNot.fal_moving_the_goalposts: No evidence was given and then dismissed; Mateus never supports his own claim and asks the company to disprove it.

items.passage:
Mateo: Kowalski is the best keeper in the league, end of discussion. Three clean sheets in his last five games!
Ines: He's let in 41 goals this season, more than any other starting keeper.
Mateo: Those last five games show who he really is. The rest is noise.
items.cue: Those last five games show who he really is. The rest is noise.
items.explanation: Mateo builds his case on the five games that flatter Kowalski and dismisses the rest of the season. The full record, not the best stretch, is what shows how good a keeper is.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Mateo isn't stuck with too little information; the whole season is available and he chooses only the stretch that suits him.

items.title: 31% returns. Imagine what your savings could do.
items.passage: Last year the Harborline Growth Fund returned 31%, beating the market by a mile. Our advisors are available seven days a week, and getting started takes five minutes, with a minimum of just $500. *Annual returns 2021-2024: -8%, 2%, -4%, 5%. Past performance does not guarantee future results.
items.cue: Last year the Harborline Growth Fund returned 31%, beating the market by a mile
items.explanation: Harborline headlines its one standout year and tucks the losing and weak years into the small print. Judged over five years, the fund looks far less impressive.

whyNot.fal_texas_sharpshooter: Harborline isn't inventing a pattern after the fact; it simply spotlights its best year and buries the rest.

items.title: Great news from our spring results!
items.passage: Dear families, our spring reading results are in! Grade 3 scores rose 9 points, the biggest jump in the district. That tells us the new literacy approach we introduced in grades 3 to 5 this year is working, and we'll expand it next fall. Thank you, teachers! (Grade 4 and 5 numbers are in the full report on the portal; new tests always take a year to settle.)
items.cue: That tells us the new literacy approach we introduced in grades 3 to 5 this year is working
items.explanation: The new approach runs in three grades, but Mr. Lindahl cites only the one that improved and tucks the other two into a portal report with an excuse. The results he sidelines are exactly the ones that could undercut his claim.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: He isn't short of data: he has results for all three grades and showcases only the one that looks good.

items.title: Sparrowdale says its calendar redesign is a hit with users
items.passage: Sparrowdale Software says its redesigned calendar app is winning people over, pointing to more than 2,000 five-star reviews posted since the update launched. The new layout does load faster, according to independent tests. The company's statement did not mention the app's overall rating, which has fallen from 4.6 to 3.1 stars since the update.
items.cue: pointing to more than 2,000 five-star reviews posted since the update launched
items.explanation: Sparrowdale highlights the glowing reviews and skips the overall rating, which has dropped sharply. A few thousand fans can coexist with many more unhappy users.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: 2,000 reviews isn't a tiny sample; the issue is that Sparrowdale counts only the favorable ones.

items.source: Text thread · Lena (agent) and the Okonkwos
items.passage:
Lena: Seven similar homes sold on Alder Street this year. The three nicest went for $610k to $640k.
Chidi: So where should we list?
Lena: Those three are what buyers will compare yours to, so $650k is realistic. No need to get hung up on the others.
items.cue: Those three are what buyers will compare yours to, so $650k is realistic
items.explanation: Lena has seven comparable sales but prices the house off only the three highest. Buyers and appraisers will look at all of them, so leaving out the cheaper four makes $650k look safer than it is.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Three sales might look like too small a sample, but Lena had seven; she kept only the ones that support a high price.

items.passage: People keep asking if keto beats low-fat for weight loss. I've linked three trials below where keto groups lost noticeably more weight at six months. Yes, the 12-month follow-ups mostly found no real difference, but almost nobody sticks to a diet for a full year anyway. The six-month data is what counts, and it's clear: keto wins.
items.cue: The six-month data is what counts, and it's clear: keto wins.
items.explanation: Rafael acknowledges the longer follow-ups but declares that only the six-month results count, because they favor keto. The fuller evidence, including a year out, doesn't show keto winning.

whyNot.fal_texas_sharpshooter: Rafael isn't spotting a pattern in random noise; he knows the full results and chooses the time frame that flatters keto.

items.title: Small batches. Big flavor.
items.passage: Our single-origin beans are roasted in small batches every Tuesday and shipped within 48 hours. Why do we call it the best coffee in Calder County? Because no other roaster around here comes close to our quality. Try a bag risk-free: if you don't love it, we'll refund you, no questions asked.
items.cue: Because no other roaster around here comes close to our quality
items.explanation: Brambleworth's reason for "the best coffee" is that no one else matches its quality, which is just "the best" said again. The batch and shipping details don't touch that claim.

whyNot.fal_loaded_question: The ad asks a question, but the question doesn't presume anything; the flaw is the answer, which just restates the claim.

items.passage:
Mina: Is the new Halloran thriller worth the hardcover price? Reviews seem pretty split.
Jasper: Definitely. It's the best thing she's ever written.
Mina: What makes it better than her last one, though?
Jasper: It's just a better book, honestly. That's why it's her best.
items.cue: It's just a better book, honestly. That's why it's her best.
items.explanation: When Mina asks why the book is better, Jasper answers that it's better. His reason and his conclusion are the same claim, so Mina learns nothing new.

whyNot.fal_no_true_scotsman: Jasper isn't redefining a group to exclude a counterexample; he simply repeats his conclusion as the reason for it.

items.title: Re: Do we still need weekly status reports?
items.passage: Hi Ana, thanks for raising this in the retro, and I know the reports eat into Friday afternoons. I read the survey comments too. My view is that the weekly reports are worth it, because the hour we put into them every Friday is time well spent. Let's keep them through Q2 and revisit in July. Thanks, Dmitri
items.cue: the weekly reports are worth it, because the hour we put into them every Friday is time well spent
items.explanation: Dmitri is polite and open to revisiting, but his only reason, that the hour is "time well spent," is another way of saying the reports are worth it.

whyNot.fal_loaded_question: Dmitri isn't asking anything with a hidden assumption; he argues for "worth it" by restating it as "time well spent."

items.passage: People keep asking whether my magnesium sleep gummies are "proven." Fair question! Here's how I look at it: this brand only sells formulas that work, and I know these work because the brand wouldn't sell them otherwise. I've linked the ingredient list in my bio if you're curious. Sleep well, friends!
items.cue: I know these work because the brand wouldn't sell them otherwise
items.explanation: Gwen says the gummies work because the brand only sells what works, and the brand only sells what works because it sells these. The two claims prop each other up.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_authority: Gwen isn't deferring to an outside expert; her two reasons support each other in a loop with nothing outside it.

items.source: Ilse Navarro, Chief People Officer · Quillmark Analytics all-hands
items.passage: A few of you asked whether our interview loop is too long. I get it; five rounds is a lot. But look at what it produces. The people in this room are the strongest engineers I've worked with anywhere, and we know they're the strongest because they cleared the toughest hiring bar in the industry. The loop works.
items.cue: we know they're the strongest because they cleared the toughest hiring bar in the industry
items.explanation: Ilse defends the interview loop by pointing to how strong the hires are, but her only evidence that they're strong is that they passed the loop.

whyNot.fal_no_true_scotsman: Ilse isn't redefining "strong engineer" to dodge a counterexample; she uses the loop's own results as proof the loop works.

items.title: The first diet book I actually finished
items.passage: I've tried four diet books and this is the first one I made it through. The meal plans are realistic and the shopping lists save me time every week. As for whether the advice is sound: the author clearly has excellent judgment about nutrition, which you can see from how sensible the advice in this book is.
items.cue: excellent judgment about nutrition, which you can see from how sensible the advice in this book is
items.explanation: Marguerite's practical praise is fair, but she says the advice is sound because the author's judgment is good, and the author's judgment is good because the advice is sound.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_authority: Marguerite isn't relying on outside credentials; the author's judgment is vouched for only by the very advice in question.

items.passage: Huge offseason for the Ridgeback Rovers! We signed the top scorer from the Valley League, the best goalkeeper in the county and two all-star midfielders. With the best player we could find at every position, this has to be our championship year. Rec league, consider yourselves warned. First match is Sunday at 10.
items.cue: With the best player we could find at every position, this has to be our championship year
items.explanation: Tariq assumes a team of strong individuals must be the strongest team. Teamwork, fit and chemistry belong to the team as a whole, so great parts don't guarantee a great side.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Tariq isn't stretching a few examples to a whole group; he's assuming the players' individual quality automatically adds up to the team's.

items.title: Nothing but goodness in every bite
items.passage: Oats. Honey. Dates. Almonds. Coconut oil. Every ingredient in our Meadowgrain Bar is a wholesome, nutritious food you already trust. Put them together and you get a snack that's healthy through and through, so go ahead and reach for one whenever hunger hits. Available in four flavors at stores near you.
items.cue: Put them together and you get a snack that's healthy through and through
items.explanation: Meadowgrain assumes healthy ingredients make a healthy bar. Combined, honey, dates and oil can add up to a lot of sugar and calories, so a bar of good parts isn't automatically an anytime snack.

whyNot.fal_division: Division would go from the bar down to its ingredients; this ad goes the other way, from the ingredients up to the bar.

items.passage:
Nina: We need to save $200k this year. My list: shorter weekend support hours, slower free shipping, fewer seasonal colors, no printed catalog, and a smaller app team.
Greg: Some of those sting.
Nina: Each one is small, and honestly no customer would notice any single one. So customers won't notice the package either.
items.cue: no customer would notice any single one. So customers won't notice the package either
items.explanation: Nina assumes that because each cut is unnoticeable alone, all five together will be too. Small changes can add up to a clearly worse experience once customers run into several at once.

whyNot.fal_division: Nina reasons from the separate cuts up to the whole package, not from the package down to its parts, which would be division.

items.source: Developer Rob Kessler · Ashford planning hearing
items.passage: I've heard the concerns about traffic, and I take them seriously; we've added a turn lane to the plan. But let's be realistic. Each new home adds maybe two cars to the road. Two cars is nothing on a street like Elm. So the 200-home development as a whole won't make a meaningful difference to traffic.
items.cue: So the 200-home development as a whole won't make a meaningful difference to traffic
items.explanation: Rob argues that because one home's two cars won't matter, the whole development won't either. But 200 homes means roughly 400 more cars, and small amounts add up.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Rob isn't generalizing from a few homes to all homes; he's assuming a trait of each home, 'negligible', carries over to the whole development.

items.title: New storage server: reliability
items.passage: Hi Carla, the parts for the new storage server are in. I picked every component for reliability: the power supply, the controller, both fans and each of the 12 drives is rated at 99% availability or better. With every part that dependable, the server as a whole should give us 99% availability too, which meets the vendor contract.
items.cue: With every part that dependable, the server as a whole should give us 99% availability too
items.explanation: Ivan assumes reliable parts make an equally reliable whole. Without redundancy, the server goes down when any one of its 16 parts fails, so overall availability can be well below any single part's.

whyNot.fal_division: Ivan reasons from the components up to the server; division would run the other way, from the server down to its components.

items.passage: My morning stack, since so many of you asked! Vitamin D, fish oil, turmeric, ashwagandha, St. John's wort and a high-dose B complex. I researched every single one, and each is considered safe at its recommended dose. So taking all six together is perfectly safe, too. Links to my favorite brands below.
items.cue: So taking all six together is perfectly safe, too.
items.explanation: Brooke assumes that because each supplement is safe alone, the combination is safe. Supplements can interact with each other and with medications, so the safety of each part doesn't settle the safety of the stack.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Brooke isn't generalizing from a few cases to many; she's assuming a trait of each pill carries over to the combination.

items.passage:
Femi: Heard the new chemistry teacher at Westbrook High started this week.
Claire: Good! Westbrook's ranked the top public high school in the state, so she's bound to be excellent. Nothing to worry about.
Femi: Malik says the first lab went fine, at least.
items.cue: Westbrook's ranked the top public high school in the state, so she's bound to be excellent
items.explanation: Claire assumes a top-ranked school means every teacher there is top-notch. A ranking reflects the school overall, and a brand-new teacher could be anywhere from great to struggling.

whyNot.fal_composition: Claire reasons from the whole school down to one teacher; composition would run the other way, from parts up to the whole.

items.title: The fries are great, people. Relax.
items.passage: Some reviewers here are complaining that the fries are soggy and bland. Come on. Halden Smash House has won Best Burger Joint in the county three years running. A place that good doesn't serve bad fries, so the complaints must be exaggerated. The double smash burger is still the best in town.
items.cue: A place that good doesn't serve bad fries
items.explanation: Dev assumes that because the restaurant as a whole is award-winning, every item it serves must be good. An award for burgers says little about the fries.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Dev isn't generalizing from a few cases; he's pinning the whole restaurant's reputation on one item it serves.

items.passage: Picked up the Velta X2, and it's earned the hype: Circuit Weekly named it Phone of the Year, and the screen and speakers are excellent. A few people are griping about the selfie camera online, but if it's the best phone of the year, it has the best selfie camera of the year. Simple as that.
items.cue: if it's the best phone of the year, it has the best selfie camera of the year
items.explanation: Ollie assumes the phone's overall award applies to each feature. A phone can win on balance while one part, like the selfie camera, is only average.

whyNot.fal_composition: Ollie moves from the whole phone down to one feature; composition would go from the features up to the phone.

items.source: Board member Carl Hughes · Ridgeview HOA meeting
items.passage: I know a $1,200 special assessment for the new roof isn't welcome news, and we're offering a payment plan. But look at the numbers: Ridgeview's median household income is over $110,000, one of the highest in the county. Our residents can clearly afford this, including the folks in the Maple Court units who've been calling.
items.cue: Our residents can clearly afford this, including the folks in the Maple Court units
items.explanation: Carl uses the neighborhood's high median income to conclude every household can pay. A median says nothing about the households below it, including the Maple Court residents raising concerns.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Carl isn't building a rule from a few cases; he applies a figure about the whole neighborhood to particular households.

items.title: New math program lifts district scores by six points
items.passage: Average math scores across the Orland district rose six points in the first year of the MathSprout program, the largest gain in a decade. Speaking to reporters, principal Grace Holloway said the result means every student at her school has benefited, and she plans to cut after-school tutoring as no longer needed.
items.cue: the result means every student at her school has benefited
items.explanation: A district-wide average can rise while some students stay flat or fall behind. Ms. Holloway treats the district's overall gain as true of each student, then cuts help some may still need.

whyNot.fal_composition: This runs from the district's overall result down to each individual student, which is division, not composition.

items.title: Q3 reviews: great news
items.passage: Team, what a quarter: our region finished at 120% of target, the best result in the company. I've completed the Q3 reviews, and I've rated all eleven of you 'exceeds expectations,' since we smashed the goal as a team. You should all be proud. Bonus letters go out Friday, and lunch is on me next week.
items.cue: I've rated all eleven of you 'exceeds expectations,' since we smashed the goal as a team
items.explanation: Renata treats the region's total as proof that every rep performed well. A team can beat its target thanks to a few big sellers while others fall short.

whyNot.fal_composition: Renata reasons from the team's result down to each member, not from members up to the team, so it's division rather than composition.

items.passage: My English teacher keeps writing 'be more critical' on my essays. Fine. My next essay on the assigned novel trashes it from the first page to the last: boring plot, flat characters, terrible ending. Being critical is literally what she asked for, so this one better get an A.
items.cue: Being critical is literally what she asked for
items.explanation: Jaylen's teacher means 'critical' as in careful analysis; Jaylen takes it as 'negative.' A one-sided takedown isn't what she asked for just because the same word covers both.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: Jaylen isn't distorting an argument to attack it; he's sliding between two meanings of the word 'critical.'

items.passage:
Customer: I'm on your Unlimited plan, but after 25GB my speed dropped so low I can't even load a map.
Agent: I understand. But the plan is unlimited: you can keep using data all month and we never cut you off.
Agent: So you're getting exactly what Unlimited promises.
items.cue: the plan is unlimited: you can keep using data all month and we never cut you off
items.explanation: The customer reads 'unlimited' as full-speed data with no cap; the agent switches to 'never fully cut off.' The conclusion only works because the word changes meaning mid-argument.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: The agent isn't misrepresenting the customer's complaint so much as quietly redefining 'unlimited' to make the plan look honest.

items.title: Re: Should we run the Delmar story?
items.passage: Thanks for flagging the concerns, Pia. I agree the restaurant-review angle is weak and the photos need work. But the teaser about Chef Delmar's divorce got 40,000 clicks in an hour. When the public is this interested, running it is in the public interest. Let's publish at noon.
items.cue: When the public is this interested, running it is in the public interest.
items.explanation: Grant slides from 'the public is interested' (people are curious) to 'the public interest' (what benefits the community). Lots of clicks show curiosity, not that the story serves the public.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: The clicks aren't offered as proof the story is true or good because it's popular; the trick is the shift from 'interested' to 'the public interest.'

items.title: Beat the 3 p.m. slump
items.passage: Feeling drained by mid-afternoon? Each can of Kickwell Fizz delivers 210 calories of pure energy, more energy than four cups of black coffee combined. Lightly sparkling, real citrus flavor, no artificial colors. When you need energy to finish the day strong, why settle for less?
items.cue: 210 calories of pure energy, more energy than four cups of black coffee combined
items.explanation: Kickwell uses 'energy' in the calorie sense, then sells it as the feeling of being alert. Coffee has almost no calories but plenty of caffeine; more calories doesn't mean more pep.

whyNot.fal_false_analogy: The ad isn't comparing two unlike things on shared features; it's swapping the calorie meaning of 'energy' for the alertness meaning.

items.title: Superintendent cites 'significant' sleep study in phone ban push
items.passage: In a randomized trial at two high schools, students asked to put phones away at 9 p.m. slept an average of four minutes longer, a statistically significant difference. Superintendent Rhonda Kaplan said the study shows late-night phones have a significant effect on students' health, large enough to justify a district-wide ban.
items.cue: late-night phones have a significant effect on students' health, large enough to justify a district-wide ban
items.explanation: 'Statistically significant' means the result is unlikely to be chance, not that it's big. Kaplan treats it as meaning important, but four extra minutes of sleep is a small effect.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: The trial was randomized, so cause isn't the weak spot; the slip is reading 'statistically significant' as 'large.'

items.passage:
Corinne: The Halcyon invoice went out two weeks late. Finance says their billing system was down.
Mark: Lena's responsible for the Halcyon account, right?
Corinne: Yes, since March.
Mark: Then she's responsible for the late invoice. I'll note it in her review.
items.cue: Then she's responsible for the late invoice.
items.explanation: Mark moves from 'responsible' meaning in charge of the account to 'responsible' meaning at fault. Lena can own the account without being to blame for Finance's system outage.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: Mark isn't distorting anyone's argument; his conclusion rests on the word 'responsible' changing meaning between lines.

items.passage: Unpopular opinion: running a household is basically running a small business. And businesses borrow money to grow all the time; that's how the economy works. So no, I don't feel guilty putting our beach week on the credit card. Think of it as an investment in the family brand.
items.cue: businesses borrow money to grow all the time
items.explanation: Jared compares his household to a business, but business loans usually pay for things that earn money back. A beach week on a credit card brings in no income to cover the interest.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: Jared doesn't just call the two the same; he carries a conclusion (borrowing is fine) across a comparison that fails on that very point.

items.passage:
Rhea: Can we cap the planning meeting at 30 minutes? Last week's ran two hours.
Tomasz: Think of it like the gym. Nobody gets stronger from a 10-minute workout. The more time we put in, the more we get out of it.
Rhea: We spent 40 minutes on the font for one slide.
items.cue: Think of it like the gym. Nobody gets stronger from a 10-minute workout.
items.explanation: Tomasz assumes meetings work like exercise, where more time builds more strength. But a meeting's value comes from decisions made, and Rhea's example shows extra time can simply be wasted.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: Tomasz isn't claiming meetings and workouts are equal; he infers "longer is better" from a comparison that doesn't hold.

items.source: Trustee Gordon Abernathy · Fennwick Public Library board meeting
items.passage: Our acquisitions budget is down 12% this year, so we have to make choices, and I appreciate the staff report. My view is simple. A library works like a grocery store: when a product doesn't move, you clear the shelf for something that will. Poetry has our lowest checkout rate, so it should be the first section we cut.
items.cue: A library works like a grocery store: when a product doesn't move, you clear the shelf
items.explanation: The budget pressure is real, but Gordon borrows a grocery store's logic. A store stocks what sells for profit; a public library exists to give access to a wide range of material, including less popular books.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: Gordon isn't saying a library and a store are equal; he imports a store's rule into a library, where the purpose differs.

items.title: Cute kit, but it didn't survive
items.passage: The jar is sturdy and the flour it came with is lovely. The instructions say to feed the starter twice a day, but I figured a starter is basically a houseplant, and my houseplants do fine with a weekly watering, so I fed it on Sundays. It was dead by week two. Two stars.
items.cue: a starter is basically a houseplant, and my houseplants do fine with a weekly watering
items.explanation: Sunita assumes the starter needs houseplant-style care because both are alive. But the yeast and bacteria in a starter eat through their food within hours, which is why the kit says twice a day.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: Sunita doesn't just call them equal; she infers a feeding schedule from a comparison that fails on how fast each uses up food.

items.title: Re: AI policy for the persuasive essay
items.passage: Hi Ms. Lindgren, thanks for sending the essay guidelines home. I respect that you want original work, but I'd push back on the chatbot ban. Thirty years ago people worried calculators would ruin math, and now every student uses one in class. A chatbot is just the next calculator, so it belongs in the essay assignment too. Best, Ravi
items.cue: A chatbot is just the next calculator, so it belongs in the essay assignment too
items.explanation: Ravi's comparison breaks on the key point: calculators are allowed when arithmetic isn't what's being tested, but this essay exists to test the student's own writing and reasoning.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: Ravi's error isn't just calling the tools equal; he draws a classroom rule from a comparison that fails on what the assignment measures.

items.title: Fresh passwords, every season
items.passage: Your passwords work like a toothbrush: the longer you use one, the more worn out it gets. That's why Lockwillow reminds you to swap every password every 90 days and generates a strong new one in a single tap. Start your free 30-day trial today and keep every account fresh.
items.cue: Your passwords work like a toothbrush: the longer you use one, the more worn out it gets
items.explanation: Lockwillow implies passwords wear out with use, like bristles. A strong, unique password doesn't weaken over time; the main reason to change one is that it may have been exposed.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: The ad doesn't just equate the two; it infers a 90-day schedule from a comparison that fails on whether passwords actually wear out.

items.passage: Pulled the numbers from our gym's check-in app this month. Members who train before 7 a.m. have the lowest average body fat of any time slot, and it's not close. Early sessions just burn more fat, simple as that. Stuck on a plateau? Move your workouts to the morning and watch what happens. 5:30 crew, see you tomorrow.
items.cue: Early sessions just burn more fat, simple as that.
items.explanation: Brandon sees that early trainers are leaner and decides the early hour causes it. People who show up at 5:30 may differ in diet, routine or experience, so the link alone can't show the clock is doing the work.

whyNot.fal_post_hoc: Brandon isn't saying one event followed another; he's comparing groups of members and reading a correlation as cause.

items.title: Councillor says more cafés could make Millbrook wealthier
items.passage: Presenting a regional comparison on Tuesday, Councillor Dana Whitfield noted that the five towns with the most independent coffee shops per resident also have the highest median household incomes. She proposed rent relief to attract new cafés, arguing that more coffee shops would help lift local wages.
items.cue: arguing that more coffee shops would help lift local wages
items.explanation: Whitfield treats the link between cafés and incomes as if cafés create wealth. The arrow may point the other way: towns where people already earn more can support more coffee shops.

whyNot.fal_texas_sharpshooter: She didn't sift data for a lucky cluster; she took a plain correlation across towns and assumed which way the cause runs.

items.title: Proposal: Quillmoor for every team
items.passage: Hi all, quick follow-up on Q2. The five teams that chose to adopt Quillmoor closed about 30% more tickets per person than the teams that stayed on spreadsheets. Licenses are cheap and onboarding takes an afternoon. Given the gap, I'm confident the tool is what's driving the extra output, so I'd like to make it mandatory from September. Comments welcome before Friday.
items.cue: I'm confident the tool is what's driving the extra output
items.explanation: Gareth credits the tool for the gap, but teams chose whether to adopt it. Teams eager to try new tools may already have been the faster ones, so the comparison can't show the tool caused the difference.

whyNot.fal_post_hoc: There's no before-and-after story here; Gareth compares adopters with non-adopters and treats that group difference as the tool's doing.

items.source: Principal Ortega · Westfield High parent evening
items.passage: We looked closely at last year's report cards, and one pattern stood out: students who sat in the first two rows averaged almost a full letter grade higher than students at the back. Our teachers work hard to reach every row, and they'll keep doing that. But starting this term, we'll seat students who are struggling up front so they get the same boost.
items.cue: we'll seat students who are struggling up front so they get the same boost
items.explanation: Principal Ortega assumes the front row produces the higher grades. Students who are already keen often choose to sit up front, so moving others there may not deliver the same 'boost'.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: A full year of report cards is a decent sample; the problem is assuming the seat causes the grades when keen students may simply pick the front.

items.title: Green tea drinkers catch fewer colds, survey of 12,000 finds
items.passage: Adults who drank at least two cups of green tea a day reported 20% fewer colds over the winter than those who drank none, even after researchers adjusted for age and smoking. Lead author Dr. Mirela Sandu said the result shows compounds in the tea strengthen the immune system, and recommended a daily cup through flu season.
items.cue: the result shows compounds in the tea strengthen the immune system
items.explanation: Dr. Sandu moves from an association to a cause. Daily tea drinkers may also exercise more, eat differently or report symptoms differently, and adjusting for age and smoking doesn't rule those out.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: With 12,000 people, sample size isn't the issue; the leap is from an adjusted correlation to the tea itself doing the protecting.

items.passage:
Imani: Went through my shop stats last night. Listings with 8+ photos sell about twice as often as the ones with 3 or 4.
Theo: makes sense, people want to see what they're buying
Imani: Right?? So I'm reshooting all my cheap listings with 8 photos each. That should double their sales.
Theo: worth a weekend for sure
items.cue: I'm reshooting all my cheap listings with 8 photos each. That should double their sales.
items.explanation: Imani assumes the extra photos caused the extra sales. The listings she photographed most may be her best items, which sell well anyway, so adding photos to cheaper ones may not double anything.

whyNot.fal_texas_sharpshooter: Imani didn't hunt through her data for a lucky cluster; she noticed one plain pattern and assumed photos are what drive it.

items.passage: Hot take after six years of coaching: there are two kinds of gym-goers. Either you commit to heavy barbell work, or you accept staying exactly where you are. Cardio machines and light dumbbells are fine for warming up, but that's about it. Who's starting a real program Monday?
items.cue: Either you commit to heavy barbell work, or you accept staying exactly where you are
items.explanation: Dani allows only two paths, heavy barbell work or no progress at all, skipping bodyweight training, machines, classes, sport, or a mix of approaches.

whyNot.fal_middle_ground: Dani isn't claiming a compromise is right; the problem is that only two options are allowed to exist.

items.passage:
Marisol: QA found two bugs in checkout. Small, but customers will definitely hit them.
Kofi: Then we have a choice. We ship Thursday as announced, or we tell the whole company this team can't deliver.
Ines: How long would the fixes actually take?
items.cue: We ship Thursday as announced, or we tell the whole company this team can't deliver
items.explanation: Kofi frames it as ship on schedule or admit failure, ignoring a short delay, a phased release, or shipping with checkout turned off until it's fixed.

whyNot.fal_loaded_question: Kofi isn't asking a question with a built-in assumption; he's presenting a choice with too few options.

items.title: Re: Grade 7 math placement
items.passage: Hi Ms. Adeyemi, thanks for the detailed placement report. I agree Noor's quiz scores dropped this term, and I appreciate you flagging it early. That said, I don't want her moved. As I see it, she stays in accelerated math, or she decides she's 'not a math person' for good. We'd like to keep her where she is. Best, Hana
items.cue: she stays in accelerated math, or she decides she's 'not a math person' for good
items.explanation: Hana reduces the decision to two outcomes, staying accelerated or giving up on math forever, leaving out tutoring, a temporary move with a review date, or extra support.

whyNot.fal_slippery_slope: Hana doesn't describe a chain of steps leading somewhere bad; she presents just two possible outcomes as if nothing else could happen.

items.source: Councillor Rina Castellanos · Millcaster council meeting
items.passage: Thank you all for coming out tonight. The Harlow Street pool is sixty years old, and the engineers' report confirms the filtration system is failing. I won't pretend that's cheap to fix. But let's be honest about what's in front of us: we approve the full $4 million rebuild this spring, or Millcaster kids spend their summers without a pool.
items.cue: we approve the full $4 million rebuild this spring, or Millcaster kids spend their summers without a pool
items.explanation: Rina's report shows a real problem, but she skips everything between a full rebuild and no pool, such as replacing just the filtration system or rebuilding in phases.

whyNot.fal_middle_ground: Rina isn't saying the halfway option is right; she's hiding the fact that halfway options exist at all.

items.title: Quiet and long-lasting, but I sent it back
items.passage: Battery life is great and it's quiet enough to run during video calls. The issue is navigation. Robot vacuums come in two kinds: lidar models that map your home, and cheap ones that bounce around at random. There's no lidar turret on this one, so you can guess which camp it's in. Mine went back after a week.
items.cue: come in two kinds: lidar models that map your home, and cheap ones that bounce around at random
items.explanation: Tobias sorts every robot vacuum into lidar mapping or random bouncing, overlooking camera- and sensor-based models that clean in planned rows without a lidar turret.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Tobias isn't generalizing from a few cases; he starts from a two-category split that leaves out other ways of navigating.

items.title: Hospital board weighs $9M ER expansion as visits climb 18%
items.passage: Board chair Wen Moreau told Tuesday's meeting that Larkwell General's emergency department saw 18% more visits this year than last. "The math is simple," she said. "We find $9 million to expand the ER, or residents accept waits that keep getting longer." A vote is expected in March.
items.cue: We find $9 million to expand the ER, or residents accept waits that keep getting longer
items.explanation: The rise in visits is real, but Wen treats expansion as the only fix for waits, leaving out options like an urgent-care clinic for minor cases, more night staff, or better triage.

whyNot.fal_middle_ground: Wen isn't pushing a compromise as automatically right; she leaves out the alternative fixes entirely.

items.passage:
Lin: IT says the server room door was propped open all weekend. They're running a full audit.
Gus: Honestly, that's no worse than someone leaving their laptop unlocked while they grab a coffee. A lapse is a lapse.
Lin: That room holds the payroll and customer databases, Gus.
items.cue: that's no worse than someone leaving their laptop unlocked while they grab a coffee
items.explanation: Gus treats a weekend-long open door to the payroll and customer servers as equal to a laptop left unlocked for a few minutes. Both are lapses, but the risk is nowhere near the same.

whyNot.fal_false_analogy: Gus isn't drawing a new conclusion from a comparison; he flatly declares two very differently sized lapses equally serious.

items.source: Student driver to his instructor · Hollowmere Driving School
items.passage: I know, I know, no phone while driving. But honestly, reading a text while you're driving is no worse than reaching over to change the radio station. Either way your eyes leave the road for a second. I'll keep my replies short, I promise.
items.cue: reading a text while you're driving is no worse than reaching over to change the radio station
items.explanation: The student equates reading a text with tapping a radio button. Both take your attention off the road, but reading and replying usually takes far longer than a quick tap.

whyNot.fal_false_analogy: He isn't transferring a conclusion from one case to another; he claims two very different distractions are equally risky.

items.title: Do cold plunges ward off colds? The evidence is split
items.passage: A two-year trial of 2,000 adults found that daily cold-water immersion made no difference to how many colds participants caught. Meanwhile, a poll by wellness blogger Saffi Lund found that 70% of her followers feel healthier since they started plunging. With evidence pointing both ways, it may be a while before we know for sure.
items.cue: With evidence pointing both ways, it may be a while before we know for sure
items.explanation: The article gives a large two-year trial and a follower poll equal weight, as if they were comparable evidence. They aren't: one measured colds carefully, the other asked fans how they feel.

whyNot.fal_middle_ground: The article doesn't settle on a halfway answer; it treats a large trial and an informal poll as equally strong evidence.

items.title: Great value for commuters
items.passage: Bought these to replace the $350 pair I left on a train. The battery easily lasts the advertised 30 hours and they fold up small. The noise canceling is a lot weaker (I can still hear the bus engine and people talking), but both have active noise canceling, so these are basically the same as headphones four times the price. Five stars.
items.cue: both have active noise canceling, so these are basically the same as headphones four times the price
items.explanation: Odette notices the noise canceling is much weaker, then calls these the same as a pair four times the price because both list the feature. Sharing a feature doesn't make them equal at it.

whyNot.fal_false_analogy: Odette isn't carrying a conclusion over from a different case; she declares two very unequal products the same because they share a feature.

items.passage: Day 212 of my walking streak! A few people asked why I skip the HIIT classes at my gym. Honestly, 30 minutes of strolling and 30 minutes of HIIT are both 30 minutes of movement, so the calorie burn ends up about the same. I'll take the version where I can finish my podcast, thanks.
items.cue: 30 minutes of strolling and 30 minutes of HIIT are both 30 minutes of movement
items.explanation: Bea treats a gentle stroll and a high-intensity session as equal because they last the same time, but intensity changes calories burned a lot. Walking is great; it just isn't the same workout.

whyNot.fal_false_analogy: Bea isn't carrying a conclusion over from a comparison; she declares two very unequal workouts the same because they share a duration.

items.title: Re: Question about my fund fees
items.passage: Hi Grace, great question, and I'm glad you're reading your statements. Our managed fund charges 1% a year; the index fund you mentioned charges 0.05%. Honestly, at that level the difference is a rounding error, since both are low-cost by any reasonable standard. What matters most is staying invested. Best, Warren
items.cue: at that level the difference is a rounding error, since both are low-cost
items.explanation: Warren lumps 1% and 0.05% together as "low-cost," but one fee is twenty times the other. Over decades of compounding, that gap can add up to a big share of someone's savings.

whyNot.fal_false_analogy: Warren isn't reasoning from a comparison to some other case; he simply declares two very different fees equivalent.

items.passage:
Rhea: Okay, we've decided: we're going to try for one more baby!
Aunt Mira: Wonderful news! Still hoping for a girl?
Rhea: After three boys, the odds have to be on our side this time. It's basically our turn. Already looking at names.
items.cue: After three boys, the odds have to be on our side this time.
items.explanation: Rhea feels a girl is owed after three boys, but each pregnancy's odds are about the same no matter what came before. Past births don't tilt the next one.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: Rhea isn't claiming one thing causes another; she's treating three independent outcomes as if they make a different one more likely.

items.passage: Board game night update: I have rolled exactly zero sixes in fifteen turns of Harbor Barons. Fifteen! Everyone else is building cities while I'm stuck with two roads and a sheep. The dice owe me at this point, so next round I'm going all in on the strategy that needs a six. Wish me luck.
items.cue: The dice owe me at this point
items.explanation: Jess expects her luck to even out, but each roll of the dice is independent. Fifteen turns without a six doesn't make a six any more likely on the next roll.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Jess isn't drawing a broad rule from her rolls; she expects past bad luck to push the next roll her way.

items.title: 41 weeks without a winner. This could be the night.
items.passage: Our Saturday Mega Jackpot now stands at $48,000, the biggest in our hall's history. Nobody has hit it in 41 straight weeks, which means a winner has to be coming soon. Doors open at 6, cards are $10, and the snack bar has new pizza. Come early, grab your lucky seat and be there when it finally drops!
items.cue: Nobody has hit it in 41 straight weeks, which means a winner has to be coming soon
items.explanation: The hall implies a long dry spell makes a win more likely, but each week's game is independent. Forty-one weeks without a winner doesn't raise the odds for this Saturday.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: The ad doesn't claim one event causes another; it suggests a streak of losses makes a win likelier, which isn't how chance works.

items.title: Official says town is safe from major flooding for decades
items.passage: With repairs to the east levee now on schedule, Riverside's emergency manager told residents Thursday that the 2024 flood was the area's 'hundred-year flood.' Since that one has now happened, he said, another flood that size is very unlikely for several generations, and the flood insurance program can wind down.
items.cue: Since that one has now happened, he said, another flood that size is very unlikely for several generations
items.explanation: A 'hundred-year flood' has about a 1% chance in any given year, every year. Having one in 2024 doesn't use up the odds, so another could come next year.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: He isn't generalizing from a few cases; he's treating a past rare event as if it lowers the yearly chance of the next one.

items.passage: The forecast has said 30% chance of rain every single day this week, and we haven't had a drop. Five 'maybes' in a row that never happened. At this point today's 30% is practically guaranteed, the odds have to catch up eventually. Moving the picnic to Sunday and packing the big umbrella for work.
items.cue: today's 30% is practically guaranteed, the odds have to catch up eventually
items.explanation: Wes treats the dry days as if they make rain owed. Each day's 30% forecast is its own estimate, and rain not showing up earlier in the week doesn't push today's chance toward certainty.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: Wes points to no change in the weather causing rain; he simply expects the odds to 'catch up' after a run of dry days.

items.passage:
Olu: Reminder that IT's random laptop compliance checks start Monday. They pick 10% of staff by lottery each quarter.
Bea: I got picked in Q1, so I'm basically safe for the rest of the year.
Olu: Must be nice. Still updating my antivirus tonight, just in case.
items.cue: I got picked in Q1, so I'm basically safe for the rest of the year
items.explanation: Bea assumes being picked once lowers her chances, but each quarter's lottery starts fresh. She has the same 10% chance as everyone else.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Bea isn't generalizing from a sample; she's assuming an earlier random pick changes the odds of the next one.

items.passage: My study group keeps pushing that timer method: 25 minutes of work, a 5-minute break, repeat. I looked it up, and it started with one university student and a tomato-shaped kitchen timer. That's a dorm-room hack, not a real study method, so I'm not reorganizing finals week around it. Back to the library.
items.cue: That's a dorm-room hack, not a real study method
items.explanation: Maddie dismisses the timer method because it began as one student's kitchen-timer trick. Humble beginnings don't tell us whether timed work blocks help people focus; only how well it works can.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Maddie isn't attacking the student who invented it or her study group; she judges the method purely by how it started.

items.passage:
Sofia: Feeling rough. Making Grandma's ginger-lemon tea and staying in tonight.
Leo: That tea thing is just village folklore from before anyone knew what germs were. Hard to take seriously.
Sofia: The warm drink is soothing my throat right now, Leo.
Leo: Folklore is folklore.
items.cue: just village folklore from before anyone knew what germs were
items.explanation: Leo dismisses the tea because the remedy began as old folk practice. Where a remedy started doesn't settle whether a warm drink soothes a sore throat; that's a question about its effects.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Leo isn't attacking Sofia or Grandma personally; he rejects the remedy because of where it came from.

items.title: Re: No-meeting Wednesdays
items.passage: Hi all, I'm open to fewer meetings, and Felipe's survey (68% of us say meetings break up deep work) deserves a real look. But I should mention that this whole idea started as a joke slide at last year's offsite. I'm wary of reorganizing our week around something that began as a punchline. Maybe we revisit next quarter? Hana
items.cue: I'm wary of reorganizing our week around something that began as a punchline
items.explanation: Hana acknowledges the survey, then sets the proposal aside because it first appeared as a joke. How an idea started doesn't tell us whether it would help the team now.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Hana isn't attacking Felipe or whoever made the slide; she judges the idea by its joking origin.

items.title: Comfy ring, silly score
items.passage: The Orbet ring is comfortable enough to sleep in and the battery really does last a week. The app's 'readiness score' is mostly built on heart rate variability, though, and HRV was first used to monitor babies during labor. I'm a 42-year-old adult, not a fetus. Not letting that number tell me whether to run. Three stars.
items.cue: HRV was first used to monitor babies during labor
items.explanation: Andre likes the hardware but rejects the score because heart rate variability was first used in monitoring births. A measure's first use doesn't decide whether it's useful for adults today.

whyNot.fal_guilt_by_association: Andre isn't objecting to who uses or promotes HRV now; he dismisses it because of where it was first applied.

items.source: Resident Clara Osei · Larkmoor planning meeting
items.passage: I've looked at the county's crash data for Mill Road, and I agree that intersection is a problem. But remember how this roundabout plan began: Vellacott Homes drew it up in 2019 to speed traffic into their new subdivision. A plan born to sell houses isn't a plan for this neighborhood, however the county's engineers have dressed it up since.
items.cue: A plan born to sell houses isn't a plan for this neighborhood
items.explanation: Clara rejects the roundabout because a developer first drew it up for its own reasons. The county's engineers have since reworked it, so its origin doesn't show whether it would fix the crash problem.

whyNot.fal_guilt_by_association: Vellacott isn't a current backer tainting the plan; Clara rejects it because of how it originated in 2019.

items.title: Second trial backs afternoon naps for memory in older adults
items.passage: An independently funded trial at Marrowfield University has confirmed earlier findings that a 20-minute afternoon nap improved recall in adults over 60. Sleep coach Martin Feld isn't persuaded: 'This whole line of research was started by a mattress company looking for a marketing hook. I don't care how many times they rerun it.'
items.cue: This whole line of research was started by a mattress company looking for a marketing hook
items.explanation: Martin waves off an independent replication because the research line began with a mattress maker. Funding worries are fair for a single sponsored study, but this new trial had no such ties.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Martin doesn't attack the Marrowfield researchers; he rejects their result because of how the research area began.

items.passage: Guess who's backing the community garden plan for the old Pine Street lot? The Brindle Street Neighbors Association. Same group that spent all last summer trying to ban leaf blowers. I don't need to read the proposal to know where this is headed. Hard no from me.
items.cue: Same group that spent all last summer trying to ban leaf blowers
items.explanation: Doug rejects the garden plan because a group he dislikes supports it, and admits he hasn't read the proposal. The plan's merits depend on its details, not on who's cheering for it.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Doug isn't attacking whoever proposed the plan; he taints the plan through a disliked group that happens to back it.

items.passage:
Ines: The review sheet says to focus on chapters 6 and 7. Want to split them?
Ravi: Isn't that what the Thursday-night group keeps telling everyone? The crew that got caught sharing quiz answers last term? If they're on board, I'm out. Chapter 9 for me.
Ines: Ravi, it's on the professor's sheet.
items.cue: The crew that got caught sharing quiz answers last term? If they're on board, I'm out.
items.explanation: Ravi drops the study advice because a group with a cheating scandal is also passing it around. Who else repeats the tip doesn't change what the professor's review sheet says.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Ravi doesn't attack Ines, who suggested the plan, or anything about her; he rejects the advice because a group he distrusts backs it too.

items.title: Re: Moving to Trellisboard for project tracking
items.passage: Thanks, Omar. The per-seat price is reasonable and I like that it exports to CSV, which would make reporting easier. My hesitation: Trellisboard is the Ostrander team's favorite tool, and they champion it at every all-hands. Honestly, anything that crowd gets excited about makes me nervous. Could we look at a couple of alternatives first?
items.cue: anything that crowd gets excited about makes me nervous
items.explanation: Beatriz weighs real factors like price and CSV export, then counts the tool against itself because a team she distrusts loves it. Their enthusiasm says nothing about how well it would work for her.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Beatriz isn't attacking Omar, who proposed the tool; she judges the tool by the team it's associated with.

items.title: Good food, but I'm out
items.passage: Three weeks in: the produce shows up fresh, portions are generous, and the Thai basil chicken is a weeknight hero. Then I learned the founder spoke at the same wellness summit as the guy selling 'detox' foot pads. That told me what kind of company this is, so I've canceled. Two stars for the food.
items.cue: spoke at the same wellness summit as the guy selling 'detox' foot pads
items.explanation: Carmen's own experience with the meal kit is positive, but she condemns the company because its founder shared a stage with a dubious seller. Sharing a lineup isn't evidence about this company.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Carmen doesn't point to anything the founder did wrong; she tars the company through someone else at the same event.

items.passage: The Lantern Phonics program has solid pilot numbers; I've read them. What gives me pause is who has lined up behind it. It's the flagship curriculum at Corvane Academies, the chain fined last year for inflating graduation rates. When an organization like that champions a program, I think parents deserve better, and I can't support it for Fenmoor.
items.cue: It's the flagship curriculum at Corvane Academies, the chain fined last year for inflating graduation rates
items.explanation: Trustee Holloway accepts the pilot results, then rejects the program because a discredited school chain uses it. Corvane's misconduct doesn't change how Lantern Phonics performed in the pilot.

whyNot.fal_genetic_fallacy: Corvane didn't create the program; the trustee rejects it because of who uses and promotes it now, not because of where it came from.

items.title: Standing desks show no back-pain benefit in 900-person trial
items.passage: Researchers at the Wexmoor Institute found office workers with standing desks reported the same back pain after a year as those who sat. Ergonomics blogger Tessa Vane urged readers to ignore the results, noting the study 'is being cheered on by every office-chair company in the country.' The trial was publicly funded.
items.cue: is being cheered on by every office-chair company in the country
items.explanation: Tessa dismisses the trial because chair makers are celebrating it. Their applause came after a publicly funded study was finished, so it says nothing about whether the results are sound.

whyNot.fal_genetic_fallacy: The chair companies didn't fund or run the study; Tessa rejects it because of who's cheering now, not because of where it came from.

items.title: Port Ellis is a tourist trap
items.passage: Stopped in Port Ellis for one night on our road trip. The two restaurants we tried by the harbor were overpriced, and one waiter barely looked at us. The sunset from the pier was gorgeous, I'll give it that. But the whole town is clearly built to squeeze tourists. Save your money and keep driving.
items.cue: the whole town is clearly built to squeeze tourists
items.explanation: Marcus judges an entire town from one night and two harbor restaurants, which are the places most likely to cater to tourists. That's far too small and skewed a sample to describe the whole town.

whyNot.fal_anecdotal_evidence: Marcus isn't brushing aside any data with his story; he simply stretches a tiny sample into a verdict on the whole town.

items.passage:
Rachel: Our sitter from the Hatchsit app canceled an hour before date night. Again.
Ben: Ugh, sorry. That's the worst.
Rachel: That's both sitters we've booked through it, and both bailed. App sitters are just unreliable. I'm only asking the neighbors' teenagers from now on.
items.cue: both bailed. App sitters are just unreliable.
items.explanation: Rachel writes off every sitter on the app after two cancellations. Two people can't tell her much about the hundreds of sitters who use it.

whyNot.fal_anecdotal_evidence: Rachel isn't setting her experience against ratings or data; the flaw is generalizing from just two sitters.

items.title: Poll: our readers are done with flat phones
items.passage: In our weekend poll, 82% of the 3,400 readers who voted said their next phone will be a foldable. Folding screens have come a long way, with sturdier hinges and fewer creases than early models. With numbers like these, it's clear the mainstream market is ready to leave flat phones behind.
items.cue: it's clear the mainstream market is ready to leave flat phones behind
items.explanation: Circuit Weekly treats its own poll as a picture of the whole market. People who read a gadget site and vote in its polls are enthusiasts, not typical phone buyers, so 3,400 votes can't speak for the mainstream.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: The poll isn't used to argue foldables are good because they're popular; it's used to predict the whole market from a skewed sample of fans.

items.source: Principal Dawn Achebe, Cedar Grove Elementary
items.title: Update on the new homework policy
