items.passage: Dear families, thank you for your patience as we tried our new nightly reading log this month. I've now heard from three parents, and all three say their children feel overwhelmed. It's clear the policy isn't working for our families, so we'll pause it from Monday. Teachers will share a lighter plan next week.
items.cue: It's clear the policy isn't working for our families
items.explanation: Principal Achebe decides for the whole school based on three emails. Parents who write in are often the most unhappy ones, so three messages can't show how most families feel.

whyNot.fal_anecdotal_evidence: No survey or data is being overridden here; the problem is treating three self-selected emails as the voice of all families.

items.source: CEO Lauren Mbeki · Fernwood all-hands meeting
items.passage: Six weeks ago our design team, all eight of them, piloted a four-day week. Output held steady, deadlines were met and satisfaction scores jumped. I want to thank them for being our guinea pigs. Results like that tell us the four-day week will work across Fernwood, so support, sales and the warehouse will switch over in January.
items.cue: Results like that tell us the four-day week will work across Fernwood
items.explanation: Lauren extends one small team's pilot to the whole company. Eight designers with flexible project work may tell her little about support lines, sales targets or warehouse shifts.

whyNot.fal_composition: Composition assumes the parts' traits belong to the whole; here one unusual team is treated as a fair sample of very different teams.

items.passage: Big news! At our farmers' market stall on Saturday, 47 out of 50 tasters picked our new oat-milk vanilla over our classic dairy version. Even allowing for people being polite, that's a landslide. So starting next month, we're going fully dairy-free at the shop, because that's clearly what our customers want now.
items.cue: that's clearly what our customers want now
items.explanation: Scoop & Spoon assumes Saturday's market tasters speak for all its customers. A farmers' market crowd stopping for a free sample may differ a lot from the regulars who come in for dairy scoops.

whyNot.fal_anecdotal_evidence: This is an actual tally, not a personal story outweighing data; the trouble is that the 50 tasters may not represent the shop's customers.

items.passage:
Sofia: Found the perfect dress for Ana's wedding! $280 though.
Jules: Ouch.
Sofia: Here's the thing: Marlowe's lets you return anything within 30 days, worn or not. So I'll wear it Saturday and send it back Monday. If their policy allows it, there's nothing wrong with doing it.
items.cue: If their policy allows it, there's nothing wrong with doing it.
items.explanation: Sofia moves from what the store's policy permits to what's ethically fine. A rule allowing returns tells you what you can get away with, not whether wearing and returning is fair to the store.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Sofia isn't citing custom or how it's always been done; she leaps from a fact about the policy to a moral verdict.

items.passage: Psychologists have found that people form a first impression of someone within a few seconds of meeting them. Seconds! So stop feeling guilty about judging people fast. If someone gives you a bad vibe in the first ten seconds, you're right to write them off. Trust the first impression.
items.cue: So stop feeling guilty about judging people fast.
items.explanation: Derek turns a finding about how people do form impressions into advice about how they should judge others. That snap judgments happen doesn't make them accurate or fair.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Derek doesn't praise snap judgments as natural; he moves from a research finding about what people do to what they ought to do.

items.title: Re: Starting salary gap
items.passage: Thanks for raising this, Aaliyah. You're right that new hires who negotiated earn about 7% more than those who took our first offer for the same role, and I'd encourage everyone to negotiate. But that's simply where everyone's pay ended up, and where it ended up is where it should be. I don't see a reason to adjust anyone's pay.
items.cue: that's simply where everyone's pay ended up, and where it ended up is where it should be
items.explanation: Bruce treats the gap's existence as its own justification: pay is where it landed, so that's where it should stay. Whether equal work deserves equal pay needs an actual reason, not just a description.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Bruce doesn't appeal to long-standing custom; he goes straight from how pay stands right now to how it should stand.

items.source: Trustee Marion Feld · Lakeshore school board
items.passage: The new student laptops are a great investment, and teachers tell me they're already using them well. They also come with software that can log every website a student visits, around the clock. That capability is right there on every machine. So yes, I believe staff should review every student's browsing history each week.
items.cue: So yes, I believe staff should review every student's browsing history each week
items.explanation: Marion moves from what the software can do to what staff should do. Being able to monitor every site doesn't settle whether weekly reviews of students' browsing are right.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Nothing here appeals to how things have always been done; the leap is from a technical fact, 'it can log', to a 'should'.

items.passage:
Seraphine: The cooks asked again this week whether they could get a share of the nightly tips.
Tobiah: Tips get left on the servers' tables, and the servers collect them at the end of every shift.
Tobiah: That's where the money ends up, so that's who it should belong to. The kitchen has its hourly wage.
items.cue: That's where the money ends up, so that's who it should belong to
items.explanation: Tobiah goes straight from how tips currently flow, onto the servers' tables, to who should own them. Where the money lands describes the setup; whether the cooks deserve a share needs an actual reason.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Tobiah doesn't claim tips have always gone to servers; he leaps from where the money lands right now to who it ought to belong to.

items.title: Flickwell defends autoplay, including on kids' profiles
items.passage: Asked about criticism of autoplay at an industry conference, Flickwell product chief Harold Banks said viewers watch about 40% longer when the next episode starts automatically, including on children's profiles. 'The data tells us what serves our viewers,' he said, adding that keeping autoplay on by default is the right thing to do.
items.cue: The data tells us what serves our viewers
items.explanation: Banks treats a fact about viewing time as proof of what's good for viewers. Watching longer shows autoplay holds attention, not that it's right, especially for kids.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Banks never says autoplay is natural; he slides from a measured fact about behavior to a claim about what's right.

items.passage:
Leah: Morning! Inventory sync finished overnight with no errors.
Darnell: Nice. Bilal, why do you keep ignoring the reorder alerts?
Bilal: I've acknowledged every alert in the queue this week. Happy to share the log if that helps.
items.cue: why do you keep ignoring the reorder alerts?
items.explanation: Darnell's question assumes Bilal has been ignoring alerts, which nobody has shown. Any direct answer about "why" would concede the accusation.

whyNot.fal_circular_reasoning: Darnell isn't arguing in a loop; he slips an unproven accusation into a question and asks Bilal to explain it.

items.source: Resident Owen Tremblay · Thornvale school board, public comment
items.passage: Good evening. I've had two kids at Thornvale Elementary, and I want to thank the teachers, who have been wonderful. But I have one question for the board tonight, and I'd like a straight answer: why did you keep the mold problem in the east wing hidden from parents for a whole year?
items.cue: why did you keep the mold problem in the east wing hidden from parents
items.explanation: Owen's question takes for granted that there is a mold problem, that the board knew about it, and that it hid it for a year. None of that has been established.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: Owen doesn't limit the board to two options; he asks a single question that already assumes the cover-up happened.

items.title: One-question survey before our meeting
items.passage: Hi neighbors, the tenants' committee meets with the management company next month about the overnight concierge, which they plan to cut in January. Please answer one quick question by Sunday: How much safer do you feel with a concierge on duty overnight? (Much safer / Somewhat safer / Slightly safer) Thanks so much, Ngozi
items.cue: How much safer do you feel with a concierge on duty overnight?
items.explanation: Ngozi's question assumes the concierge makes residents feel safer. Every answer choice records some benefit, so a resident who notices no difference can't say so.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: There are three choices, not two; the real issue is that all of them accept the question's built-in assumption.

items.title: Downtown meters: three months in
items.passage: Main Street's $2-an-hour parking meters went live in June, and the city says revenue is on target. So why are the new fees driving shoppers out of downtown? We asked three shop owners and a parking consultant. Foot-traffic counts from the business association won't be released until September.
items.cue: why are the new fees driving shoppers out of downtown?
items.explanation: The standfirst asks why the fees are driving shoppers away before showing that they are. The foot-traffic numbers that could answer that aren't even out yet.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: The paper doesn't infer a cause from a pattern in the data; it assumes the effect inside a question, with no data at all.

items.source: Corinne Vasquez · hosting the Quiet Variables podcast
items.passage: Thanks for joining us, Dr. Pell. Your team's sweetener study got a lot of attention this spring, and it's already been cited in two follow-up papers. So let's start right there, because I think listeners are curious: when did your lab first realize the results were flawed?
items.cue: when did your lab first realize the results were flawed?
items.explanation: Corinne's friendly opener hides an assumption: that the study's results are flawed. Nothing she says supports that, yet any direct answer about "when" would accept it.

whyNot.fal_circular_reasoning: Corinne isn't using a conclusion as its own proof; she tucks an unsupported claim, that the results are flawed, into a question.

items.passage: We're trying to be more intentional about tablets in our house this year, and I'd love input from parents who've been through it. Honest question: at what age did you start noticing screen time shortening your kid's attention span? Trying to figure out whether we're already late. Thanks in advance!
items.cue: at what age did you start noticing screen time shortening your kid's attention span?
items.explanation: Priya's sincere-sounding question assumes screen time shortens attention spans and only asks when it showed up. Parents who saw no such effect have no way to answer.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: Priya doesn't reason from a pattern to a cause; she presumes the effect exists and asks only when it appeared.

items.passage:
Callum: Thermometer says the chicken's at 130°F. The recipe says it needs to hit 165°F.
Aiyana: I always pull mine at 120. It stays way juicier.
Callum: Okay, let's compromise and take it out at 145. Somewhere between the two has to be about right.
items.cue: Somewhere between the two has to be about right.
items.explanation: Callum picks 145°F only because it falls between the recipe and Aiyana's habit. A safe cooking temperature is a fact to look up, not a number to negotiate.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: Callum isn't limiting the choices to two; he assumes the midpoint between two claims must be correct.

items.source: A dad at family movie night
items.passage: Okay, okay, both of you stop. Lena says the movie is rated for teens and up, Marcus says it's fine for everyone. I'm not looking it up again. Let's just say it's somewhere in the middle, like ten and up, so Marcus can watch the first half and we'll see how it goes.
items.cue: Let's just say it's somewhere in the middle, like ten and up
items.explanation: The movie's rating is a checkable fact, and one child is right. Dad settles on an in-between rating that nobody actually claimed, just because it splits the difference.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: Dad doesn't argue that the two claims are equally strong; he invents a rating halfway between them instead of checking.

items.source: Councillor Teodor Basu · Ashwyn council session
items.passage: I want to thank everyone who wrote in about the new signals on Kessler Avenue. Some residents tell me their commute has doubled. Our traffic engineer's data says travel times are down ten percent. My guess is reality sits between those two, which would mean the signals haven't changed much either way, so I see no reason to revisit them this year.
items.cue: My guess is reality sits between those two
items.explanation: Teodor has measured data and personal reports, but instead of weighing them he assumes the answer lies halfway and concludes the signals changed nothing.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: Teodor isn't limiting the options to two; he takes two accounts and assumes the truth sits halfway between them.

items.passage: My DMs are split: half of you say kill the credit card first, half say max out retirement savings first. Both camps are so confident that the smart move must be doing a bit of each. So the plan is a 50/50 split of every extra dollar starting this month. (Card is at 24% APR, for anyone wondering.)
items.cue: Both camps are so confident that the smart move must be doing a bit of each
items.explanation: Tasha picks a 50/50 split because it sits between two confident camps, not because she compared them. With a 24% APR card, the numbers may clearly favor one side.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: Tasha does consider a third option; her error is assuming the in-between one wins just because both sides sound sure.

items.title: Migration timeline for the board deck
items.passage: Hi Jonas, quick note on the timeline before Thursday. Our engineer, Sunil, estimates the database migration at six weeks, based on the last two we ran. The vendor's sales rep says it can be done in two. I've put four weeks in the deck, since reality usually lands somewhere between the optimistic and the cautious estimate. Let me know if that works. Renée
items.cue: reality usually lands somewhere between the optimistic and the cautious estimate
items.explanation: Renée's four weeks sounds prudent, but she picks it for being in the middle. Sunil's estimate rests on two past migrations; the sales rep's doesn't, and splitting them ignores that.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: Renée never declares the two estimates alike; her leap is choosing the midpoint without weighing which estimate is better supported.

items.title: Is the new diet-soda sweetener safe? Our columnist weighs in
items.passage: Two recent papers reach opposite conclusions about alluvose, the sweetener now in many diet sodas: one finds no effects at typical doses, the other reports headaches in a small trial. Columnist Hollis Mwangi's take: with researchers this divided, the sensible view is that it's mildly risky, so a can or two a week is probably fine.
items.cue: with researchers this divided, the sensible view is that it's mildly risky
items.explanation: Hollis lands on "mildly risky" because it sits between "no effects" and "causes headaches," not because any evidence points there. Weighing the two studies is the step he skips.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: Hollis's key leap isn't calling the two papers alike; it's concluding the truth must sit halfway between their findings.

items.passage:
Zara: You said if I got at least a B on the chemistry final, I'd get my phone back. I got a B+!
Dad: Great job, honey, really. Now let's see you keep that up through the end of the semester.
Zara: That was not the deal!!
items.cue: Now let's see you keep that up through the end of the semester.
items.explanation: Dad set a clear bar, at least a B on the final, and Zara cleared it. Instead of keeping his word, he adds a new condition after the fact.

whyNot.fal_special_pleading: Dad isn't exempting himself from a rule; he swaps in a tougher condition once the first one was met.

items.passage: Couch update, since people asked: the buyer said he'd pay my $300 asking price if I delivered it. I borrowed my brother's truck and got it to his building. Then it was 'only if you can carry it up to the fourth floor.' Did that too. Now, standing in his living room, he says the cushions are softer than he expected and offers $220.
items.cue: Then it was 'only if you can carry it up to the fourth floor.'
items.explanation: The buyer agreed to $300 with delivery. Each time Tamika met his condition, he set a new one: first the stairs, then a lower price once the couch was already in his living room.

whyNot.fal_special_pleading: The buyer isn't exempting himself from a rule; he keeps setting a new condition each time Tamika meets the last one.

items.title: Re: Promotion conversation
items.passage: Hi Tariq, congratulations again on the Larkin launch. In March we agreed that leading a client project end to end, with strong feedback, would make your case, and the client's feedback was glowing. Before I put your name forward, though, I'd like to see you lead a second project and present it at the spring all-hands. Let's revisit in the fall. Best, Harriet
items.cue: Before I put your name forward, though, I'd like to see you lead a second project
items.explanation: Harriet confirms the agreed bar from March and that Tariq met it, then adds two new conditions anyway. The warm tone doesn't change that the target moved after he hit it.

whyNot.fal_no_true_scotsman: Harriet doesn't redefine who counts as a real leader; she adds new conditions after Tariq met the one they agreed on.

items.title: Food truck owners say city changed permit rules mid-review
items.passage: Fourteen vendors submitted applications in August that met every item on the city's posted permit checklist. In September, the licensing office quietly updated the online checklist to add a $2 million insurance minimum, then rejected all fourteen. A spokesperson said the applicants "simply don't meet the current requirements."
items.cue: quietly updated the online checklist to add a $2 million insurance minimum, then rejected all fourteen
items.explanation: The vendors met the checklist as it was written when they applied. The office then rewrote it and judged them against the new version, so the bar moved after they had cleared it.

whyNot.fal_special_pleading: The office isn't exempting a favored applicant; it raises the standard after these vendors had already met the original one.

items.source: Commissioner Arturo Benn · Marrowdale Basketball League press conference
items.passage: I understand the frustration from Ms. Ortega's camp. Our written criteria for the Rookie of the Year shortlist are 15 starts and a top-ten finish in assists, and yes, she met both. But the selection committee feels a shortlist spot should reflect a full season's body of work, so we've asked that nominees also have 25 starts. She has 21.
items.cue: so we've asked that nominees also have 25 starts
items.explanation: Ortega met both written criteria. The committee's appeal to a "full season's body of work" sounds principled, but it appears only after she qualified and is applied to her right away.

whyNot.fal_no_true_scotsman: The committee doesn't declare Ortega not a "real" rookie; it adds a requirement after she met the written criteria.

items.title: Update: battery fixed, still three stars
items.passage: Update: the firmware patch fixed the battery drain, just like support promised, and the watch now lasts the full three days. I said I'd bump this to five stars if they fixed it. But honestly, a bug like that should have been caught in testing, so I'm holding at three until the next model proves they've sorted out their QA.
items.cue: I'm holding at three until the next model proves they've sorted out their QA
items.explanation: Farid's worry about testing sounds reasonable, but he named the condition for five stars himself, the battery fix, and it was met. He then sets a new test the current product can never pass.

whyNot.fal_special_pleading: Farid isn't exempting himself from a rule; he set the bar for five stars, saw it met, and swapped in a new one.

items.passage:
Keiko: Serious runners never walk during a race. You push through or you don't bother.
Sam: My sister walked through a few water stations at the Brackwater Marathon and still finished under four hours.
Keiko: Then with respect, she's not a serious runner.
items.cue: Then with respect, she's not a serious runner.
items.explanation: When Sam offers a counterexample, Keiko doesn't revise her claim; she declares Sam's sister not a "serious runner," using the very walking break in question as the reason.

whyNot.fal_special_pleading: Keiko isn't exempting anyone from a rule; she redefines who counts as a serious runner so the counterexample no longer counts.

items.passage: Every week someone says I'm wrong about this, so let's settle it: homemade bread stays fresh for a full week on the counter. Yes, Marco, I saw your comment about your loaf going stale in two days. Respectfully, if it went stale that fast, it wasn't real homemade bread.
items.cue: if it went stale that fast, it wasn't real homemade bread
items.explanation: Marco's loaf is a counterexample to Hollie's claim. Instead of revising the claim, she rules his loaf "not real" homemade bread, and her only reason is that it went stale.

whyNot.fal_moving_the_goalposts: Hollie isn't demanding more proof from Marco; she redefines "homemade bread" so his loaf no longer counts.

items.title: Re: Q3 delivery review
items.passage: Hi Omar, thanks for pulling the delivery numbers together; that's really useful. On the Harbor project slipping three weeks: I'd gently push back on reading that as a knock on the framework. Teams that genuinely run our sprint process don't miss dates like that, so if Harbor slipped, they weren't truly running it. Happy to talk Thursday. Bettina
items.cue: if Harbor slipped, they weren't truly running it
items.explanation: Harbor is a counterexample: a team that used the process and still slipped. Bettina decides it wasn't "truly" using the process, judged only by the fact that it slipped.

whyNot.fal_special_pleading: Bettina isn't exempting the framework from a rule; she redefines who counts as using it so the miss can't count against it.

items.source: Nutrition coach Imogen Hale · Wexbridge community health fair
items.passage: Great question. You're saying your father has eaten fish, olive oil and vegetables every day for decades and still has high cholesterol. I'd say that tells us he isn't truly eating the Mediterranean way, because people who genuinely follow it don't end up with high cholesterol. That's how powerful this diet is.
items.cue: he isn't truly eating the Mediterranean way, because people who genuinely follow it don't end up with high cholesterol
items.explanation: The father matches every usual description of the diet. Imogen rules him out as not "truly" following it only because his cholesterol is high, which shields her claim from any counterexample.

whyNot.fal_moving_the_goalposts: Imogen isn't raising a bar for evidence; she redefines who counts as following the diet so the counterexample disappears.

items.title: Sturdy, quiet, and worth learning to use
items.passage: Sturdy frame, quiet motor, and the memory presets are handy. I've noticed a few one-star reviews from people whose back pain got worse after switching. With respect, that just means they weren't using it correctly. Anyone who uses a standing desk the right way ends up with a healthier back; that's the whole point of them.
items.cue: that just means they weren't using it correctly
items.explanation: Paolo dismisses reviewers whose pain got worse by saying they used the desk wrong, but his only sign of wrong use is the pain itself. No reviewer could ever count against his claim.

whyNot.fal_special_pleading: Paolo isn't exempting himself or the desk from a rule; he defines "correct use" so any counterexample is excluded automatically.

items.source: Director Felicity Amadi · Quillfield Learning Center parent night
items.passage: That's a fair question, and I'm glad you asked it in front of everyone. Yes, a student from last spring's group scored 1150 after attending every session. But our results speak for themselves: students who fully commit to our program score above 1300. If she didn't get there, she wasn't fully committed, whatever her attendance sheet says.
items.cue: If she didn't get there, she wasn't fully committed, whatever her attendance sheet says
items.explanation: Felicity faces a student who did everything and scored 1150. Rather than soften her claim, she declares the student not "fully committed," with the low score as the only evidence.

whyNot.fal_moving_the_goalposts: Felicity isn't raising the bar for proof in a debate; she redefines who counts as a committed student so the 1150 can't count.

items.title: Knocked out my cold in a week!
items.passage: I started taking Zincora lozenges the morning my throat got scratchy, four a day as directed. By the following weekend I was completely back to normal. These things work. They taste a bit chalky and the tin is tiny for the price, but I'm keeping a pack in my bag from now on.
items.cue: By the following weekend I was completely back to normal. These things work.
items.explanation: Gail credits the lozenges because she recovered after taking them. But colds usually clear up within a week or so on their own, so getting better afterward doesn't show the lozenges did it.

whyNot.fal_anecdotal_evidence: Gail isn't using her story to override studies or data; her mistake is reading cause into the order of events.

items.passage: Five straight losses, so on Saturday I dug out my grandad's old green scarf and wore it to the match for the first time. Final score: 3-0, our best performance all year. That scarf turned our season around and it's coming to every game from now on. Harbor City, you can thank me later.
items.cue: That scarf turned our season around
items.explanation: Danny credits the scarf because the win came right after he wore it. One win following a new scarf is easily coincidence, and the team's form has far more likely causes.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: Danny isn't comparing many games with and without the scarf; he's reading cause into a single 'this, then that' sequence.

items.passage:
Nadia: We put the Thermalyn smart thermostat in at the start of November, and December's heating bill was the biggest we've ever had.
Owen: Ugh. Those things aren't cheap either.
Nadia: Exactly. It's obviously costing us money, so it's going back while we're still inside the return window.
items.cue: It's obviously costing us money
items.explanation: Nadia blames the thermostat because the big bill came after installing it. December is usually much colder than the months before, so a higher bill would be expected with or without the new device.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: Nadia isn't comparing many homes with and without the device; she's going purely on the order of events in her own house.

items.source: Councillor Teodora Quintero · Eastbrook town hall
items.passage: In March we finished installing the new LED streetlights along Harbor Road. By the end of June, reported burglaries in the area were down by a third. The energy savings alone justify the project, and our maintenance crews love them. But that burglary number tells you the lights work, and I'll be asking council to fund LEDs across the entire east side.
items.cue: that burglary number tells you the lights work
items.explanation: Councillor Quintero credits the lights because burglaries fell after they went up. Crime numbers rise and fall between seasons and for many reasons, so a drop that follows the lights doesn't show they caused it.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: No comparison with similar streets is offered; the case rests entirely on the drop coming after the installation.

items.title: Larkfield Bank expands coaching after branch turnaround
items.passage: Larkfield Bank sent performance coaches to its ten lowest-scoring branches after a record-bad first quarter. By the second quarter, nine of the ten had improved their customer scores. Regional director Felipe Arancibia called it clear proof the coaching works, and the bank will roll it out to 40 more branches this fall.
items.cue: called it clear proof the coaching works
items.explanation: Arancibia credits coaching because improvement came after it. Branches picked for a record-bad quarter tend to drift back toward normal on their own, so a rebound was likely with or without coaches.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: There's no comparison group here; the bank infers cause simply because the improvement followed the coaching.

items.title: Caching change: great results
items.passage: Hi team, we shipped the new caching layer Tuesday night, and Wednesday's average page load was 1.2 seconds, down from 2 seconds last week. Traffic has been lighter since the spring sale ended Monday, so the servers had a quiet week too. Still, I've told leadership the caching change cut load times by 40%. Great work, everyone!
items.cue: I've told leadership the caching change cut load times by 40%
items.explanation: Mei credits the whole speedup to caching because it came right after the release. Traffic also dropped that week, so the faster pages may be partly or mostly due to lighter load.

whyNot.fal_cherry_picking: Mei mentions the lighter traffic herself rather than hiding it; her slip is crediting the change just because the speedup followed it.

items.passage:
Mariam: Can we talk about why the kids got one water break in a 90-minute practice on Saturday? It was 88 degrees.
Coach Greg: Honestly, the bigger issue is that a third of the team still hasn't paid the uniform fee. Let's get that sorted first.
Mariam: That's separate. I'm asking about water.
items.cue: the bigger issue is that a third of the team still hasn't paid the uniform fee
items.explanation: Coach Greg answers a question about water breaks in the heat by switching to unpaid uniform fees. The fees may matter, but they don't explain or justify one water break at 88 degrees.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: Greg doesn't misstate Mariam's concern; he skips it entirely and raises a different issue.

items.passage: You're asking why the heat was out for six days in January. What I'd like everyone to appreciate is that we just repainted the entire lobby and installed new mailboxes. Honestly, this building has never looked better. Okay, next question?
items.cue: we just repainted the entire lobby and installed new mailboxes
items.explanation: The manager responds to six days without heat by talking up the lobby paint and mailboxes. Those upgrades don't explain the outage or what will prevent the next one.

whyNot.fal_tu_quoque: The manager doesn't point at the tenants' own behavior; he simply switches to a more flattering topic.

items.title: Re: Homework load in grade 7
items.passage: Dear Mr. Abara, thank you for raising your concern about the amount of nightly homework in grade 7. I'll share your note with the grade 7 team. I'd also like to highlight that our grade 7 math scores rose 11 points this year, the best gain in the district. Our teachers are doing remarkable work, and I hope families feel proud of that. Warm regards, Lorraine Hughes
items.cue: our grade 7 math scores rose 11 points this year
items.explanation: The principal politely acknowledges the homework concern, then pivots to rising test scores. Better scores don't tell Mr. Abara whether the nightly workload is reasonable.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: She doesn't twist his complaint into something weaker; she steers the conversation to a different, more positive topic.

items.passage: We've seen your questions about why some customers' email addresses were visible to other users last week, and we hear you. Security is always our priority. Meanwhile, we're thrilled to announce dark mode, offline sync and 40 new templates, free for everyone! Update today and tell us what you think.
items.cue: we're thrilled to announce dark mode, offline sync and 40 new templates
items.explanation: Quillpad acknowledges questions about exposed email addresses, then jumps to new features. Dark mode doesn't answer what went wrong or whether customers' data is safe now.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: The company doesn't misrepresent the customers' question; it leaves the question behind for a happier announcement.

items.source: HOA president Glen Moritz · Cedarline Commons annual meeting
items.passage: Several of you have asked whether the 12% fee increase was passed without the member vote our bylaws require. I understand the frustration. Let me tell you what that money is doing: the pool filters are twenty years old, the clubhouse roof leaks every spring, and our reserve fund was dangerously low. These repairs can't wait, and I think most of you agree.
items.cue: Let me tell you what that money is doing
items.explanation: Glen is asked whether the increase skipped a required vote and answers by explaining why the money is needed. The repairs may be urgent, but that doesn't show the bylaws were followed.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: Glen doesn't distort the members' question; he swaps a question about process for one about need, which is easier to answer.

items.title: Worth it, and here's why
items.passage: Three months with the Driftway X2 e-bike. A few reviewers say the battery only manages about 20 miles, not the advertised 45. What they don't mention is that the X2 is assembled in a solar-powered factory and the company plants a tree for every bike sold. That's the kind of brand I'm proud to ride, so take the range complaints with a grain of salt.
items.cue: the X2 is assembled in a solar-powered factory and the company plants a tree for every bike sold
items.explanation: Nate answers complaints about short battery range by praising the company's green practices. Those may be good reasons to like the brand, but they don't show the range complaints are wrong.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: Nate states the range complaint accurately; instead of distorting it, he changes the subject to the factory and the trees.

items.passage:
Kemi: Ava asked again about getting a phone for her 11th birthday. She mostly wants to text her cousins.
David: If she gets a phone now, next it's social media, then she's up all night messaging strangers, and by high school her grades are in the gutter.
Kemi: I was thinking a basic one with parental controls.
items.cue: next it's social media, then she's up all night messaging strangers
items.explanation: David jumps from a basic phone to strangers and failing grades without showing why each step would follow. Parents can set limits at every stage, so the chain is far from inevitable.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_fear: David does stir up worry, but the core move is a step-by-step chain from one phone to disaster, with no support for the links.

items.source: Walt Brennan, resident · Linden Park board meeting
items.passage: I've lived across from Linden Park for thirty years, and I love what the volunteers have done with the gardens. But this food truck proposal worries me. Today it's two trucks on Saturdays. Next year it's a dozen every day, then permanent stalls, and before long the park is just a parking lot for a strip mall.
items.cue: Next year it's a dozen every day, then permanent stalls
items.explanation: Walt leaps from two weekend trucks to a strip mall with no reason to think each step would follow. The board would have to approve every expansion, so nothing here makes the slide automatic.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: Walt isn't misreading a correlation; he strings together a series of unsupported steps that end with the park disappearing.

items.title: Re: Early-finish Fridays
items.passage: Thanks for putting the proposal together, Sam. I agree morale has been low, and I support flexibility in principle. My concern is where it leads: leave at 3 on Fridays, and soon Thursdays go the same way, then clients notice nobody picks up after lunch, and we lose the Hartley account. Can we talk Monday?
items.cue: soon Thursdays go the same way, then clients notice nobody picks up after lunch
items.explanation: Harriet grants the morale problem but then predicts a slide from Friday afternoons to losing a major client. She gives no evidence for each step, and the team could set coverage rules to stop it.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_fear: Harriet's worry isn't just emotional pressure; she builds a chain from one early Friday to a lost account without backing any link.

items.passage: Our department is debating whether to allow spellcheck on in-class essays. I get the case for it, especially for students with dyslexia, and that matters. But once spellcheck is in, students stop learning to spell, then they stop proofreading altogether, and in a few years we'll have graduates who can't write a sentence without an app.
items.cue: students stop learning to spell, then they stop proofreading altogether
items.explanation: Ms. Iqbal moves from spellcheck on essays to graduates who can't write, with no evidence for each link. Students still read, write and get feedback in many other ways, so the slide isn't shown.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: She isn't inferring cause from a correlation; she predicts a run of escalating effects without showing any of them is likely.

items.passage:
Marco: Can my team use our own deploy script for the mobile release? The shared pipeline doesn't support the new signing step yet.
Liz: If we make an exception for you, every team will want one. That's how the logging rules fell apart last year. Then nobody can cover anyone's on-call, and the first big outage takes days to fix.
items.cue: Then nobody can cover anyone's on-call, and the first big outage takes days to fix
items.explanation: Liz cites one past case, which makes the first step plausible, but then jumps to an outage nobody can fix. A temporary exception for a missing feature doesn't make that whole chain likely.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_fear: Liz isn't only raising alarm; she offers a chain of steps and supports just the first, letting the rest ride on it.

items.title: Trustee warns fine-free plan could unravel library lending
items.passage: Library trustee Hal Benedetti opposed the proposal to scrap overdue fines at Tuesday's meeting. Without fines, he argued, fewer books will come back, waitlists will grow, frustrated patrons will stop visiting, and falling visits will hand the county a reason to cut the library's budget. The board votes next month.
items.cue: fewer books will come back, waitlists will grow, frustrated patrons will stop visiting
items.explanation: Benedetti strings together four steps that each sound plausible, but offers no evidence for any of them, such as return rates at libraries that dropped fines. Small doubts at each link add up.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: He isn't drawing a cause from a correlation; he predicts a cascade from one policy change without supporting the links.

items.passage:
Kofi: Our panels cut our power bill by 70%! Happy to refer anyone, I install for Solvane now.
Jess: Love that, but since Kofi sells them, I checked the utility's public savings data instead. Homes on our street average about 35%, so still worth it for south-facing roofs, just not 70% for most of us.
Arun: Good to know. Ours faces north.
items.cue: I checked the utility's public savings data instead
items.explanation: Jess treats Kofi's sales job as a reason to verify, then relies on independent utility data. She doesn't call him a liar; the evidence sets the realistic figure.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Jess uses Kofi's interest only as a cue to check, and her conclusion rests on the utility's data, not on attacking Kofi.

items.title: Fence line dispute: my view before Tuesday
items.passage: The only evidence that the Dale fence predates 2019 is Mr. Dale's memory. Last year, Mr. Dale told this board he never received the parking notice that we have on file with his signature. Without a survey, permit or dated photo, I don't think his recollection alone can settle this, so I'd ask him for one of those before we rule.
items.cue: The only evidence that the Dale fence predates 2019 is Mr. Dale's memory
items.explanation: Teresa questions Mr. Dale's reliability only because the claim rests entirely on his word. She doesn't say he's wrong; she asks for documents that could settle it either way.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Credibility matters when testimony is the only evidence, and Teresa asks for proof instead of rejecting the claim because of who made it.

items.passage: Two weeks with the Corvel 14 laptop. On normal workdays (browser, docs, video calls) I'm getting about nine hours per charge. That lines up with the 9.5 hours the Benchline Labs team measured in its standardized test, so I'm fairly convinced the 'all-day battery' claim holds up for office work. Gaming, I'd guess, is a different story.
items.cue: That lines up with the 9.5 hours the Benchline Labs team measured
items.explanation: Hana shares her own experience but checks it against a standardized lab test, and she limits her conclusion to office work. Her story supports the data instead of replacing it.

whyNot.fal_anecdotal_evidence: Hana's experience agrees with systematic testing and she claims only what both support, so her story isn't outweighing the evidence.

items.title: Does NOT fit every phone
items.passage: The listing says this car mount 'fits every phone.' Mine measures 3.4 inches across in a slim case, and it won't fit no matter how I adjust it. The included manual lists the clamp's maximum opening as 3.2 inches. So whatever else is true, 'every phone' is simply wrong. It's sturdy and holds my partner's smaller phone well, hence two stars.
items.cue: The included manual lists the clamp's maximum opening as 3.2 inches
items.explanation: Noor uses her experience only to test an 'every phone' claim, and the manual's own specs confirm it. A single real counterexample is enough to show an absolute claim is false.

whyNot.fal_anecdotal_evidence: Noor isn't setting a story against broad data; one confirmed counterexample is exactly what it takes to refute an 'every' claim.

items.passage:
Camila: The crack in the basement wall is freaking me out. Do we need underpinning?
Diego: Both the structural engineer we hired and the city inspector said it's shrinkage, not settling, and they wrote their reports separately. Two independent experts who looked at the actual wall agree, so no underpinning.
Camila: Okay, I can breathe.
items.cue: Both the structural engineer we hired and the city inspector said it's shrinkage, not settling
items.explanation: Diego relies on two relevant experts who examined the actual crack and reached the same conclusion independently. That's exactly the kind of authority worth trusting.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_authority: Both sources are experts in foundations, both inspected this wall, and they agree independently, so deferring to them is reasonable.

items.source: Parks director Wendell Ames · Kestrel Point council
items.passage: Three certified arborists have now examined the Founders Oak, including one hired by the residents who want it saved. All three found extensive decay in the trunk, and their resistance-drill readings show less than a third of the wood is sound. When every expert, including the one hired by its defenders, reaches the same verdict, we have to accept that the tree is at serious risk of failing.
items.cue: including one hired by the residents who want it saved
items.explanation: Wendell defers to arborists, the right experts, who all examined the tree and agree, including one with every reason to disagree. He also cites their measurements, not just their titles.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_authority: These are relevant experts in agreement, backed by drill measurements, and one was hired by the other side, so the appeal is strong, not fallacious.

items.passage:
Tomasz: Inspection rated the Mill St bridge deck 'poor', with spalling on two spans.
Renee: Agreed, it's in bad shape. A full closure adds about 15 minutes to east-side ambulance runs. A 10-ton limit keeps ambulances (around 6 tons) moving while banning the gravel trucks that cause most of the wear, so a weight limit is the better call until repairs.
items.cue: Agreed, it's in bad shape.
items.explanation: Renee accepts the inspection's finding, then weighs the consequences of different responses. Using outcomes to choose an action, not to deny a fact, is exactly where consequences belong.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_consequences: Renee doesn't deny the bridge is in poor shape; she uses consequences only to decide what to do about it.

items.passage: Our shopper survey is in, and it's not what we hoped: 41% say the market is too expensive to visit weekly. We'd love to call that a fluke, but it matches the 18% drop in attendance since spring. Raising stall fees again would push prices even higher, so we're freezing fees for next season and inviting more budget-friendly vendors.
items.cue: We'd love to call that a fluke, but it matches the 18% drop in attendance
items.explanation: The market accepts an unwelcome finding because it fits the attendance data, then uses consequences only to choose next steps. Wishes don't override the evidence here.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_consequences: The market resists wishful thinking about the survey and applies consequences only to the fee decision, where they belong.

items.source: Music teacher Elena Vasquez · Brookside school board
items.passage: When Mateo played his first solo at the spring concert, his grandmother cried in the front row. Moments like that matter, but they're not my main argument. Band costs $38 per student, the lowest of any elective, and it's the only course that fills the arts credit students need to graduate. Cutting it would save little and leave students with no way to earn that credit.
items.cue: Band costs $38 per student, the lowest of any elective
items.explanation: Elena opens with a moving story, then rests her case on cost and graduation requirements. The emotion frames the argument; the facts carry it.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_emotion: The story isn't doing the work: Elena's conclusion follows from the low cost and the arts credit, which hold however you feel.

items.title: Hear every word at the dinner table again
items.passage: Remember catching every joke at family dinners? Auralis dual-microphone aids were tested by the independent Halden Audiology Lab, where wearers understood 34% more words in noisy rooms than with standard single-mic aids. That's the difference between nodding along and joining in. Try a pair free for 45 days.
items.cue: where wearers understood 34% more words in noisy rooms than with standard single-mic aids
items.explanation: The ad uses warm family imagery, but its claim rests on an independent test of understanding speech in noise, which is exactly what dinner-table listening needs.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_emotion: The feeling matches what the evidence supports: an independent test shows better understanding in noisy rooms, the very benefit the ad describes.

items.title: CO detectors: replacing expired units this week
items.passage: Hi residents, our annual inspection found expired carbon monoxide detectors in 6 of our 40 units. Every unit here has a gas furnace, and carbon monoxide has no smell or color, so a working detector is the only practical warning if a furnace malfunctions. That's why replacing the expired ones matters, and we'll install new units free this Thursday.
items.cue: carbon monoxide has no smell or color, so a working detector is the only practical warning
items.explanation: Rhea warns of a real hazard and ties it to specific facts: gas furnaces in every unit, an odorless gas and expired detectors. The action directly reduces that risk.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_fear: The danger is real, specific to this building and actually addressed by the action, not exaggerated to frighten.

items.title: Boil-water advisory issued after north-side main break
items.passage: Halverton Water says pressure in the north district fell below 20 psi for six hours after Tuesday's main break. Low pressure can let groundwater seep into pipes, so the utility says tap water there may not be safe to drink until two rounds of bacteria tests come back clean, likely by Friday. Boiling water for one minute kills the bacteria of concern.
items.cue: Low pressure can let groundwater seep into pipes
items.explanation: The utility names a specific event, explains how it could contaminate the water and says when the warning should end. The concern is sized to real evidence.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_fear: The warning rests on a measured pressure drop and a known contamination route, with a clear end point, not on exaggerated dread.

items.title: Inspection results
items.passage: Hi Daniel and Sofia, good news from this morning. The inspector spent two hours probing every accessible beam in the basement, crawlspace and attic and found no termite damage, droppings or mud tubes. If termites were active, those are exactly the signs she'd expect to see, so I'm comfortable saying there's no sign of an active infestation. Keisha
items.cue: If termites were active, those are exactly the signs she'd expect to see
items.explanation: The absence of evidence means something here: a thorough search looked for the specific signs termites leave, and Keisha keeps her conclusion appropriately modest.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_ignorance: This isn't just "no one proved otherwise"; a careful search that would have found termite signs came up empty.

items.passage:
Ola: The leaked password belonged to an old admin account. Did anyone actually use it?
Kwame: I went through every authentication log since the account was created. Every login attempt is recorded, and there's not one from that account in two years.
Ola: Then it hasn't been used to get in. Let's disable it and close the ticket.
items.cue: Every login attempt is recorded, and there's not one from that account in two years
items.explanation: Ola's conclusion rests on a complete record: every login attempt is logged, so if the account had been used, Kwame's search would have found it.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_ignorance: The missing evidence is meaningful because a full search of complete logs would have revealed any use of the account.

items.title: Finally, no more stinging eyes
items.passage: Switched my daughter to a mineral sunscreen this summer. Zinc oxide blocks both UVA and UVB, and our pediatrician pointed out that mineral formulas are less likely to irritate sensitive skin and sting eyes, which was exactly our problem with the old one. Two months in, no more tears at the pool. For her, this is the better pick.
items.cue: mineral formulas are less likely to irritate sensitive skin and sting eyes
items.explanation: Rania picks the mineral sunscreen for specific reasons: broad UV protection and less irritation, which matched her daughter's problem. The choice rests on effects, not on 'mineral' sounding natural.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Rania never claims mineral means better in general; she chooses it for specific, supported effects that fit her daughter's skin.

items.source: City engineer Mehmet Aydin · Fenmoor flood forum
items.passage: Restoring the 40-acre marsh along Fen Creek sounds like a feel-good idea, so here are the numbers. Our model shows it would hold about 30 million gallons in a 100-year storm, roughly what the proposed concrete basin holds, at a third of the cost and with lower upkeep. On capacity and cost, restoration is simply the better flood plan for Fenmoor.
items.cue: Our model shows it would hold about 30 million gallons in a 100-year storm
items.explanation: Mehmet prefers the marsh, but not because it's natural: he compares storage capacity, cost and upkeep with the concrete option. The evidence carries the conclusion.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Mehmet's case rests on modeled capacity and cost, not on the marsh being natural; if the numbers flipped, so would his conclusion.

items.title: Extension request: Lab 4 report
items.passage: Dear Dr. Ferreira, I'm requesting a one-week extension on the Lab 4 report due Friday. I was hospitalized Monday through Wednesday (discharge note attached), and the syllabus allows extensions of up to seven days for documented medical absences. I've already finished the data analysis, so a week is enough to complete the write-up. Thank you, Kai
items.cue: the syllabus allows extensions of up to seven days for documented medical absences
items.explanation: Kai's hospital stay is relevant because the syllabus makes documented illness the standard for extensions. He shows he meets that standard instead of asking for sympathy.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_pity: Kai's hardship is exactly what the rule asks about, and he documents it, so it's a reason, not a bid for sympathy.

items.source: Caseworker Imani Carter · Wrenford housing committee
items.passage: The emergency rent fund is for households facing eviction after a sudden loss of income. The Abebe family meets both conditions: Mr. Abebe was laid off in August, with the letter on file, and they received a notice to vacate on October 2. Their story is hard to hear, but that's not why I'm recommending approval. It's because they meet the fund's criteria.
items.cue: It's because they meet the fund's criteria.
items.explanation: Imani's case involves real hardship, but she ties it to the fund's written criteria and documents both. Need is the very thing this fund is meant to decide on.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_pity: The fund exists for this kind of hardship, and Imani shows the family meets its documented conditions instead of just evoking sympathy.

items.passage: People ask why we still use a 40-year-old wood-fired oven when a convection oven would be cheaper to run. We tried one for a month last winter: crust complaints tripled and our Saturday sellouts stopped. So the old oven stays, and not for nostalgia's sake. The bread is measurably better in it.
items.cue: We tried one for a month last winter: crust complaints tripled and our Saturday sellouts stopped.
items.explanation: The bakery keeps its old oven because of a real test: when it switched, complaints rose and sales fell. The reason is results, not age.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: The bakery doesn't keep the oven because it's old; it keeps it because a direct comparison showed better results.

items.title: Re: Removing the Dover St. turn restriction
items.passage: Before we remove the 'no left turn, 7 to 9 a.m.' sign on Dover Street because it 'has been there forever,' I pulled the history. It was added in 1998 after five crashes in two years at that corner, all during school drop-off. The school is still there and morning traffic has grown. The reason for the rule still holds, so I'd keep it.
items.cue: I pulled the history. It was added in 1998 after five crashes in two years
items.explanation: Maya checks why the rule exists and whether that reason still applies today. The rule survives because its safety purpose remains, not because it's old.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Maya doesn't defend the sign for its age; she finds its original safety reason and shows it still applies.

items.title: Trusted the reviews, no regrets
items.passage: I was torn between two hiking boots. The Cairnstep has 4,800 reviews averaging 4.7 stars, and the main complaint is that it runs small, which I handled by going up half a size. For something like comfort, thousands of people actually wearing a boot tell me more than any spec sheet. Fifty trail miles in, zero blisters.
items.cue: For something like comfort, thousands of people actually wearing a boot tell me more than any spec sheet
items.explanation: Tobias uses lots of reviews as evidence about comfort, something each wearer can judge directly, and checks the main complaint. Many independent firsthand reports are real evidence here.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Tobias treats popularity as evidence about something every reviewer experienced firsthand, not as proof of a claim the crowd can't judge.

items.title: Story hour time slot for winter
items.passage: Hi team, we surveyed 220 families about story hour. 64% prefer Saturday mornings, 21% weekday evenings, and the rest had no preference. Since the whole point of story hour is to reach as many families as possible, the slot most families can attend is the right one. Let's move it to Saturdays at 10 starting in January.
items.cue: the whole point of story hour is to reach as many families as possible
items.explanation: Farah uses majority preference because the question is which time families want. When the goal is attendance, what most people prefer is exactly the relevant evidence.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Popularity is the very thing being decided here, so counting preferences is evidence, not a substitute for it.

items.passage:
Hamza: The vendor says this water filter removes 99% of microplastics. Want to order one for the office?
Amira: Did they share any test results? It's $3,000.
Hamza: Not yet.
Amira: Since it's their claim and real money, let's ask for the lab report before we buy.
items.cue: Since it's their claim and real money, let's ask for the lab report
items.explanation: Amira places the burden where it belongs: the vendor made the claim, so it should supply evidence, and the $3,000 price makes checking worthwhile.

whyNot.fal_burden_of_proof: Amira asks the claimant to support its own claim; she isn't making a claim and demanding others disprove it.

items.title: Re: Reviewer comments on the smart-meter study
items.passage: Dear Dr. Ruiz, thank you for your careful comments. Our claim that the meters cut household energy use by 6% rests on the attached three-year dataset of 4,200 households and two independent replications. If you believe the effect is an artifact, could you point to the specific flaw or data that suggests it? We'd genuinely like to test it.
items.cue: rests on the attached three-year dataset of 4,200 households and two independent replications
items.explanation: Mei-Ling asks the reviewer for specifics only after laying out substantial evidence for her claim. Her request is an invitation to test it, not a way to avoid supporting it.

whyNot.fal_burden_of_proof: Mei-Ling has already carried her burden with data and replications, so asking a critic to name a flaw is fair.

items.title: Engagement survey: final numbers
items.passage: Hi all, final numbers are in. Following the rule we agreed on before launch, I removed 14 responses completed in under 30 seconds. With them excluded, 62% of staff rate their workload as manageable; with them included, it's 61%. Either way the conclusion holds: most staff say their workload is manageable, though a sizable minority don't.
items.cue: Following the rule we agreed on before launch
items.explanation: Dana did leave some data out, but by a rule set before anyone saw the results, and she shows the answer barely changes with it included. That's transparent, not selective.

whyNot.fal_cherry_picking: The exclusion rule was fixed in advance and the full-data result is reported too, so nothing inconvenient is being hidden.

items.passage: Lots of you asked whether the Mindloom app improves concentration. I found 20 studies. Fourteen had no control group, so I set those aside, following my usual rule. The six randomized trials found small or no effects, averaging out to almost nothing. So my honest answer: the app probably doesn't do much for focus, whatever its ads claim.
items.cue: Fourteen had no control group, so I set those aside, following my usual rule
items.explanation: Sam does narrow the evidence, but by a quality rule he applies consistently, and the result cuts against the product rather than toward an answer he wanted. Filtering by study quality is fair.

whyNot.fal_cherry_picking: Sam filters by a stated quality standard, not by which results he likes, and reports what the stronger studies actually found.

items.passage:
Kenji: How do we know the new rain gauge is accurate enough for the watering log?
Sofia: I mounted it right next to the extension office's calibrated gauge for a month. On all nine rainy days, the two readings were within a millimeter of each other.
Kenji: Okay, that's a real check. Let's start using it.
items.cue: I mounted it right next to the extension office's calibrated gauge for a month
items.explanation: Sofia tested the new gauge side by side with a calibrated one, so both caught the same rain. Close agreement on every rainy day is independent evidence that the new gauge is accurate.

whyNot.fal_circular_reasoning: Sofia checks the gauge against a separate, calibrated instrument rather than against its own readings, so nothing loops back on itself.

items.passage: People ask why I trust the reviews on the marketplace I use more than on other shopping sites. Two reasons: you can only review an item after a verified purchase, and last year an outside audit flagged fewer than 1% of its reviews as fake. That doesn't make every review right, but it's why I weigh them more.
items.cue: you can only review an item after a verified purchase
items.explanation: Lucia backs the reviews' trustworthiness with two independent facts, purchase verification and an outside audit, rather than with the reviews themselves, and she keeps her conclusion modest.

whyNot.fal_circular_reasoning: Lucia's reasons come from outside the reviews (purchase checks and an audit), so her conclusion isn't assumed in her premises.

items.title: Finally, a bakery I can trust
items.passage: I have celiac disease, so I asked a lot of questions before ordering. Every ingredient in the birthday cake is certified gluten-free, and the bakery's kitchen is dedicated: no wheat flour comes through the door at all. Since nothing in it contains gluten and there's no way for it to sneak in, the cake is gluten-free. And it tasted amazing.
items.cue: the bakery's kitchen is dedicated: no wheat flour comes through the door at all
items.explanation: Being gluten-free is a trait that does pass from ingredients to cake, as long as nothing else adds gluten. Avery checks that too, by confirming the kitchen is dedicated.

whyNot.fal_composition: Here the trait really transfers: if every ingredient is gluten-free and cross-contamination is ruled out, the whole cake is too.

items.title: Lead test results for our building
items.passage: Good news, neighbors. The city tested the kitchen tap in every one of our 48 units, and all 48 came back below the lead action level. The building's service line was also replaced with copper last year. Since every unit's tap tested below the limit, we can say the building's tap water passed the city's lead test.
items.cue: The city tested the kitchen tap in every one of our 48 units
items.explanation: The claim about 'the building's tap water' just sums up every unit's result, and all 48 passed. Because the conclusion covers exactly what was tested, the trait does carry from the parts to the whole.

whyNot.fal_composition: 'Passed' here simply means every unit passed, so going from all the parts to the whole is valid rather than a leap.

items.title: Pull all of this week's muffins
items.passage: Our flour supplier just recalled lot 4471 because it may be contaminated with E. coli. I checked the logs: every muffin we've baked since Monday used flour from that lot. So every one of this week's muffins is covered by the recall, including the ones already wrapped for the café. Please pull them all and set them aside for disposal.
items.cue: every muffin we've baked since Monday used flour from that lot
items.explanation: The recall covers the whole lot, and Hector confirms each muffin was made from it. A risk that applies to all of the flour does carry down to each muffin made with it.

whyNot.fal_division: The recall applies to all the flour in the lot, so every muffin made from it is covered; here the trait genuinely transfers to each part.

items.passage:
Aiko: The movers chipped Grandma's blue vase. Is it covered?
Ken: Her collection is insured under one policy, and the policy schedule lists every item individually, the vase included, at appraised value.
Aiko: So the vase itself is covered, not just the collection overall. I'll file the claim tonight.
items.cue: the policy schedule lists every item individually, the vase included
items.explanation: Aiko isn't assuming the vase is covered just because the collection is. The policy lists each item individually, so the coverage really does apply to the vase itself.

whyNot.fal_division: The coverage is written to apply to each listed item, so concluding the vase is covered follows from the policy, not just from the whole.

items.title: Re: Is the new onboarding flow worth it?
items.passage: Short answer: the improvement is real but small. The test result was statistically significant (p = 0.01), which tells us it's unlikely to be chance. 'Significant' in that sense doesn't mean large, though: completion rose from 71% to 72.5%. Given the $80,000 rebuild cost, I don't think the gain justifies a full rollout yet.
items.cue: 'Significant' in that sense doesn't mean large, though
items.explanation: Dr. Renn spots the two meanings of 'significant' and keeps them apart: real (unlikely to be chance) versus big. His conclusion follows from the size of the effect, not from the word.

whyNot.fal_equivocation: Instead of sliding between meanings, Dr. Renn names both senses of 'significant' and reasons from the right one.

items.passage:
Ngozi: The site says free shipping on orders over $35. My cart was $38, but with the coupon it's $31.
Alex: Doesn't the $38 count as the order?
Ngozi: I checked the terms: they define the order total as the amount after discounts. So I'm under the threshold and won't get free shipping.
items.cue: they define the order total as the amount after discounts
items.explanation: 'Order total' could mean before or after the coupon, but Ngozi looks up how the store defines it and sticks to that meaning. Her conclusion follows.

whyNot.fal_equivocation: Ngozi settles the ambiguous phrase with the store's own definition and uses it consistently, so no meaning shifts mid-argument.

items.title: Rolling out the new picking route at Corrow Hill
items.passage: Hi all, the new picking route cut walking time by 20% at the Brennick warehouse over the past quarter. Corrow Hill has the same floor layout, the same shelving system and similar daily order volume, so I expect a comparable improvement there. We'll measure the first month to confirm. Thanks, Hyun-woo
items.cue: the same floor layout, the same shelving system and similar daily order volume
items.explanation: Hyun-woo compares two warehouses that match on the things that determine walking time: layout, shelving and volume. He also plans to check the result.

whyNot.fal_false_analogy: The warehouses are alike in exactly the ways that affect walking routes, so the comparison holds on the relevant point.

items.passage: Six months of 15-minute daily piano practice took me from zero to playing simple songs. Now I'm trying the same approach with Spanish. Different skills, sure, but both build through spaced, repeated practice, and research on spacing finds short daily sessions beat occasional cramming for both. So I'm expecting steady progress, not miracles.
items.cue: both build through spaced, repeated practice
items.explanation: Piano and Spanish are different skills, but Imani compares them on the point that matters (both improve with spaced practice), cites research for it, and keeps her expectations modest.

whyNot.fal_false_analogy: The two skills share the feature that drives the conclusion, benefiting from spaced practice, so the analogy holds where it counts.

items.source: Dr. Leila Haddad, Brookside Family Clinic
items.title: Results of our reminder-text pilot
items.passage: Hi everyone, here are the pilot results. For three months, patients booking appointments were randomly assigned to get a text reminder the day before or no reminder. The no-show rate was 8% with texts and 14% without, across about 1,900 appointments. Since the groups were split by chance, the texts are the likely reason for the drop, so I suggest we keep them.
items.cue: randomly assigned to get a text reminder the day before or no reminder
items.explanation: Dr. Haddad's groups were split at random, so other differences between patients should even out. That makes the reminders a fair explanation for the lower no-show rate.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: This isn't a bare correlation: random assignment rules out the usual hidden third factors, so crediting the texts is reasonable.

items.title: Asthma ER visits fell along electric bus routes, study finds
items.passage: After Dunmore replaced its diesel buses with electric ones in 2024, asthma-related ER visits fell 11% the next year, while neighboring Carver, which kept its diesel fleet, saw no change. The drop was largest in blocks along bus routes. Researchers say the pattern points to cleaner air from the new buses as a likely contributor.
items.cue: while neighboring Carver, which kept its diesel fleet, saw no change
items.explanation: The researchers don't rely on timing or one correlation alone. A similar town without the change acts as a comparison, and the effect is strongest nearest the buses, so 'likely contributor' is a fair conclusion.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: A comparison town plus a stronger effect near the routes helps rule out other explanations, and the claim is suitably modest.

items.title: Garden grant deadline
items.passage: Hi all, quick update on the city garden grant. The application portal closes this Friday at 5 p.m., and it only opens once a year. So our real options are to submit by Friday or wait until next fall. Waiting would cost us the spring planting season, and the draft is nearly done, so I think we should finish it Thursday night. Amara
items.cue: it only opens once a year
items.explanation: Amara's two options really are the only ones: the portal opens once a year, so it's submit by Friday or wait a year. She then gives a reason to prefer submitting.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: The two choices are exhaustive because of a stated fact, a single yearly window, not because other options were ignored.

items.passage:
Coach Tamsin: Reminder: Saturday's semifinal is single elimination. Win and we play the final on the 14th; lose and the season's over.
Rafael: What if it ends in a draw?
Coach Tamsin: Draws go straight to penalty kicks, so there's no third result. Please keep the 14th free just in case.
items.cue: Draws go straight to penalty kicks, so there's no third result
items.explanation: Tamsin's either/or is genuine: in a knockout game decided by penalty kicks, every match ends in a win or a loss, so planning around both outcomes makes sense.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: Tamsin checks the possible third outcome, a draw, and shows the rules rule it out, so the two options really are exhaustive.

items.passage:
Marta: Plan A is $35 a month with 20GB. Plan B is also $35 with 20GB, same contract length, same overage fee.
Femi: And the coverage maps look identical for our street. I checked both.
Marta: Then they're basically the same deal, so let's just pick whichever store is closer.
items.cue: the coverage maps look identical for our street. I checked both
items.explanation: Marta and Femi compare the plans on everything that matters to them (price, data, contract, fees and coverage) before calling them the same deal.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: The two plans really do match on every relevant point they checked, so treating them as equivalent is accurate.

items.passage: Quick one from behind the counter: the store-brand ibuprofen on the bottom shelf has the same 200 mg of the same active ingredient as the name-brand box, and generics have to meet the same standards for how the drug is absorbed. So for the active ingredient, you're getting the same thing for about a third of the price.
items.cue: generics have to meet the same standards for how the drug is absorbed
items.explanation: Nadia calls the two pills equivalent on the point that matters, the active dose, and backs it with the absorption standards generics must meet. She doesn't claim every detail is identical.

whyNot.fal_false_equivalence: The products match in dose and in the required absorption standards, so the parity Nadia claims is real, not a surface resemblance.

items.passage:
Lou: 20 cards left in the deck and none of the four aces have shown up yet.
Grace: We're not reshuffling until the deck runs out, right?
Lou: Right, so all four aces are somewhere in those 20 cards. That's a 1-in-5 shot at an ace on the next draw, way better than the 1-in-13 we started with.
items.cue: all four aces are somewhere in those 20 cards
items.explanation: Lou's odds really have changed: dealt cards aren't put back, so the four aces now sit among just 20 cards. With draws like this, history matters.

whyNot.fal_gamblers_fallacy: These draws aren't independent; without reshuffling, every card dealt changes what's left, so the odds of an ace genuinely rise.

items.title: Schedule pump 3 seal replacement
items.passage: Pump 3 has run 5,400 hours since its seals were last replaced. The manufacturer's data shows seal failure rates climb sharply after 5,000 hours of use, and our own logs show pumps 1 and 2 both failed between 5,200 and 5,800 hours. It's increasingly likely to fail soon, so I'd like to replace the seals during next week's shutdown.
items.cue: seal failure rates climb sharply after 5,000 hours of use
items.explanation: Kwame isn't saying a failure is owed by luck. Seals wear out with use, so the chance of failure genuinely rises with hours, and both the manufacturer's data and local logs back that up.

whyNot.fal_gamblers_fallacy: Wear makes each hour depend on the ones before, unlike a coin toss, so 'more likely to fail soon' is a fair reading of the data.

items.passage:
Gabe: Is school really closing at noon Friday? My sister-in-law forwarded a screenshot.
Priti: That screenshot is from an account nobody can identify, and the district website and Ms. Tran's newsletter both list normal hours. So a normal day is far more likely.
Gabe: Fair enough, I'll plan for regular pickup.
items.cue: the district website and Ms. Tran's newsletter both list normal hours
items.explanation: Priti discounts the screenshot because its source can't be identified, then checks two official sources that contradict it. Her conclusion rests on that evidence, not on origin alone.

whyNot.fal_genetic_fallacy: For an unverified rumor the source is the evidence, and Priti backs her doubt with official sources instead of dismissing it by origin alone.

items.title: Phone ban in Lab 2: time to retire it?
items.passage: Our no-phones rule in Lab 2 dates to 1998, when the old spectrometers were sensitive to radio interference. Those units were replaced in 2021, and the new manufacturer's spec sheet says phones at normal distance have no measurable effect. I asked around and no one knows of any other reason for the rule, so it no longer serves its purpose.
items.cue: the new manufacturer's spec sheet says phones at normal distance have no measurable effect
items.explanation: Ngozi traces the rule's origin, then checks whether that reason still applies and looks for other reasons. The rule falls because current evidence removes its only justification.

whyNot.fal_genetic_fallacy: Ngozi doesn't reject the rule for its origin; she tests the original reason against current evidence and finds nothing else supporting it.

items.title: Dana Price deal: why I want an audit first
items.passage: Dana co-founded her last two companies with Victor Reese, and both were shut down after regulators found misreported revenue. That doesn't make Dana guilty of anything. But we're being asked to invest on her unaudited figures alone, and that history is a real risk signal. An independent audit before we commit is a reasonable price for confidence.
items.cue: we're being asked to invest on her unaudited figures alone
items.explanation: Wen treats Dana's repeated partnership with a misreporting co-founder as a reason to verify, not a verdict. Because the deal rests on unaudited numbers, checking them is a fair, proportionate step.

whyNot.fal_guilt_by_association: Wen explicitly doesn't call Dana guilty; the link justifies an audit of the actual figures, which will settle the question.

items.passage:
Marisol: Should we run the playground fundraiser through Pitchpot again?
Keon: It's the same platform that sat on the Pell Street drive's money for months. I checked: their terms let them hold payouts for up to 90 days on new campaigns. If we need equipment ordered by March, donations might not arrive in time.
Marisol: Good catch.
items.cue: their terms let them hold payouts for up to 90 days on new campaigns
items.explanation: Keon mentions another drive's bad experience, but his real reason is the platform's published payout terms, which directly clash with the March deadline.

whyNot.fal_guilt_by_association: Keon doesn't reject the platform for its reputation alone; he checked its actual payout terms, which bear directly on the deadline.

items.title: Most residents back longer library hours, city survey finds
items.passage: The city mailed surveys to 2,400 randomly selected households across all 12 wards and received 1,650 responses. Of those, 68% supported extending weekday library hours to 9 p.m., with majorities in every ward. With a margin of error of about 2 points, staff told council most residents favor the change.
items.cue: 2,400 randomly selected households across all 12 wards
items.explanation: The survey drew a large random sample from every ward, and support was a majority everywhere. That's a sound basis for saying most residents favor longer hours.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: The sample is large, random and spread across the whole city, so generalizing to residents as a whole is justified.

items.passage:
Jae: That cable shipment from Quorvex came in. I pulled 5 cables at random from five different boxes and tested them.
Renee: And?
Jae: All 5 failed the charge test. If only a few in the shipment were bad, hitting five failures in a row would be really unlikely. I'm rejecting the whole lot and filing a return.
items.cue: If only a few in the shipment were bad, hitting five failures in a row would be really unlikely
items.explanation: Five is a small sample, but Jae picked at random from different boxes, and every one failed. If defects were rare, that result would be very unlikely, so concluding the shipment is badly flawed is reasonable.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: The sample is small but random, and five out of five failures is too extreme to blame on chance, so rejecting the lot is justified.

items.title: Afternoon air quality on floor 2
