items.passage: Our new monitors show CO2 on floor 2 above 1,400 ppm most afternoons. Our facilities policy commits us to keeping indoor CO2 under 1,000 ppm, the level we adopted as our ventilation standard. Since we've agreed that's the standard we should meet, we ought to raise the air handler's fresh-air setting, which the vendor says will bring us back under.
items.cue: Our facilities policy commits us to keeping indoor CO2 under 1,000 ppm
items.explanation: Aisha's 'ought' doesn't come from the readings alone. She states the value premise openly, the policy's commitment, and then shows the facts fall short of it.

whyNot.fal_is_ought: The step to 'should' is bridged by a stated, agreed standard, so the conclusion isn't drawn from facts alone.

items.source: Dr. Kenji Watanabe, pediatrician · Halden school board
items.passage: During puberty, teens' sleep cycles shift later, so many can't fall asleep before 11 p.m. With our 7:20 a.m. start, most of our students get under seven hours a night, well short of what pediatric guidelines recommend. This board has said its schedule should support students' health and learning. Given that commitment, we ought to move the start to 8:30.
items.cue: This board has said its schedule should support students' health and learning
items.explanation: Dr. Watanabe pairs facts about teen sleep with a value the board has already endorsed. With that premise stated, the case for a later start follows.

whyNot.fal_is_ought: He doesn't jump from facts straight to 'should'; the board's stated commitment to student health supplies the value premise.

items.passage:
Rosa: The inspector's report confirmed the roof leak over unit 3 back in March. I attached it above.
Theo: And the landlord wrote back saying he'd fix it, right?
Rosa: Yes. Both facts are on paper, so I'm not asking whether there's a leak anymore. I'll ask him when the repair is booked.
items.cue: Both facts are on paper, so I'm not asking whether there's a leak anymore
items.explanation: Rosa's question "when is the repair booked?" does assume a leak, but the inspector's report and the landlord's written reply already establish it.

whyNot.fal_loaded_question: The assumption inside Rosa's question is documented and admitted, not slipped in unproven.

items.title: Backup failures: agenda for Tuesday
items.passage: Hi team, the server logs show the backup job failed on nine of the last thirty nights (log attached). Since that's established, the useful question for Tuesday isn't whether our backups are unreliable. It's why they fail and what a fix would take. Please come with ideas, even half-formed ones. Thanks, Yusuf
items.cue: the server logs show the backup job failed on nine of the last thirty nights
items.explanation: Yusuf's question "why do they fail?" presumes the backups fail, but he shows the evidence first: nine failures in thirty nights, with the log attached.

whyNot.fal_loaded_question: The assumption behind Yusuf's question is backed by attached logs, so he isn't sneaking in an unproven claim.

items.title: Thermostat update
items.passage: Hi everyone, after the thermostat back-and-forth, we ran a two-week test at 71°F instead of 68 or 74. In the follow-up survey, 82% of you said you were comfortable, up from 41% before the test. Since the middle setting actually worked better for most people, we'll keep it at 71. Thanks for your patience! Gloria
items.cue: In the follow-up survey, 82% of you said you were comfortable, up from 41%
items.explanation: Gloria didn't pick 71°F just because it's in the middle. She tested it and kept it because the survey showed far more people were comfortable.

whyNot.fal_middle_ground: The compromise is justified by test results, not assumed to be right because it sits between two positions.

items.passage:
Abebe: The quote for the new fence is $1,800. I was hoping you'd cover it, since Biscuit knocked the old one down.
Wren: Fair, but that fence was 25 years old and already leaning, and the survey puts it exactly on our property line.
Abebe: True. It was due anyway and we both get the same fence, so $900 each seems fair.
items.cue: It was due anyway and we both get the same fence
items.explanation: Abebe agrees to split the cost for stated reasons: the old fence needed replacing regardless, and the new one sits on the line and benefits both yards equally.

whyNot.fal_middle_ground: The even split is backed by relevant facts about age and shared benefit, not chosen merely because it's halfway.

items.source: Luisa Marchetti (Hollow Creek Youth Baseball board)
items.title: Re: Treasurer's statements
items.passage: Hi Pat, thank you for sending the bank statements so quickly. One thing: they run through August, but the shortfall we flagged at the meeting is from September to November. Since those are the months in question, I'd ask for just those three statements, and then I'm happy to close this out. Thanks, Luisa
items.cue: the shortfall we flagged at the meeting is from September to November
items.explanation: Luisa asks for more because the original request wasn't actually met: the statements Pat sent stop before the months under question. She also says what would settle it.

whyNot.fal_moving_the_goalposts: Luisa's standard hasn't changed; the documents sent simply didn't cover the period she asked about in the first place.

items.passage:
Noor: You said we'd switch to the new antivirus if it passed the independent lab test. It scored 99%.
Felix: It did, and I meant it. But yesterday the lab withdrew that report: the vendor had sent them a special build, not the version customers get.
Noor: Oh, I hadn't seen that.
Felix: Same deal as before, then. If the retest on the public version holds up, I'm in.
items.cue: the lab withdrew that report: the vendor had sent them a special build
items.explanation: Felix keeps exactly the same standard, an independent lab test. The lab itself withdrew the result because it tested a special build, so the condition was never really met by the product they'd buy.

whyNot.fal_moving_the_goalposts: Felix's bar hasn't moved: the evidence that seemed to meet it was withdrawn, and he asks for the same test on the real product.

items.title: Delicious, but please fix the label
items.passage: The texture is great and the frosting isn't too sweet. But the "vegan" label needs to go: the ingredient card at the counter lists butter and honey. Vegan means no animal products, and both of those come from animals, so this cupcake doesn't qualify, however tasty it is. Please relabel it for those of us who check.
items.cue: Vegan means no animal products, and both of those come from animals
items.explanation: Tamar excludes the cupcake using the standard, agreed definition of vegan and the listed ingredients, not a definition invented to dodge a counterexample.

whyNot.fal_no_true_scotsman: The definition Tamar applies existed beforehand and is widely shared, so excluding the cupcake isn't an after-the-fact redefinition.

items.title: Gullhaven marathon course found 2.1 miles short
items.passage: A certified remeasurement found that Sunday's route was only 24.1 miles. Because a marathon is defined as 26.2 miles, race officials say finish times can't be listed as marathon results or used to qualify for other races, though every finisher will still receive a medal.
items.cue: Because a marathon is defined as 26.2 miles
items.explanation: Officials say the race didn't count as a marathon because it failed a fixed, official distance confirmed by a certified measurement, not because of an awkward result.

whyNot.fal_no_true_scotsman: The 26.2-mile standard was set long before the race, so excluding the results applies a prior definition rather than inventing one.

items.passage: Update on my stomach cramps: they showed up after dinner most days for a month. My doctor suggested cutting dairy for three weeks, and they stopped. Then I added it back and they returned within two days. Cut it again, gone again. One coincidence I'd doubt, but on-off-on-off is pretty convincing. Getting tested for lactose intolerance next week.
items.cue: Then I added it back and they returned within two days
items.explanation: Rosa didn't stop at 'it got better after I quit dairy.' She brought dairy back and the cramps returned, then removed it again. That repeated on-and-off pattern is much stronger evidence than timing alone.

whyNot.fal_post_hoc: One improvement after a change would be weak, but symptoms that come and go with dairy across repeated switches point to a real link.

items.title: Root cause of Thursday's checkout errors
items.passage: Errors started at 14:02, the minute release 2.3 went live. Timing alone wouldn't settle it, so we checked: rolling back at 14:40 stopped the errors immediately, redeploying 2.3 to staging reproduced them, and the stack traces all point to its new address parser. We're confident 2.3 caused the outage and have a fix in review.
items.cue: redeploying 2.3 to staging reproduced them
items.explanation: Arjun treats the timing as a lead, not proof. The rollback stopped the errors, a redeploy reproduced them, and the traces point to specific code, so blaming the release is well supported.

whyNot.fal_post_hoc: The release isn't blamed just for coming first; removing it fixed the errors, restoring it brought them back, and the logs show how.

items.passage:
Simone: The shop says the transmission repair is $3,200. Should we just do it?
Ade: Before deciding: the same report says it needs brakes and a timing belt within six months, about $1,400 more. That's $4,600 on a car worth roughly $4,000, so replacing it is the better deal.
Simone: Ugh, fair.
items.cue: the same report says it needs brakes and a timing belt within six months
items.explanation: Ade brings in other repairs, but they bear directly on Simone's question: whether fixing the car is worth it. Adding up the total against the car's value answers exactly that.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: The extra repairs aren't a distraction; they change the answer to the very question Simone asked.

items.title: Why the Westside pool closed early this summer
items.passage: The pool closed in early August because we couldn't staff it: we needed 14 certified lifeguards and had 8. Pay was the main reason. Neighboring towns pay $4 more an hour, and three of our applicants told us they took those jobs. Raising lifeguard wages is therefore the most direct way to keep the pool open all summer next year.
items.cue: The pool closed in early August because we couldn't staff it
items.explanation: Marcus answers the question directly, then turns to wages, which can look like a change of topic. But pay is the cause he identifies, backed by applicants' own reasons.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: The wage discussion follows a direct answer and explains the cause of the closure, so it addresses the question instead of dodging it.

items.title: Please don't skip this year's fire inspection
items.passage: I know the inspection is a hassle during audit season, but it can't slide. Our insurance policy (section 4.2) requires a current annual fire certificate, and without it the policy lapses at renewal on March 1. Our lease, clause 11, requires active coverage at all times. So skipping the inspection would put us in breach of the lease.
items.cue: Our insurance policy (section 4.2) requires a current annual fire certificate
items.explanation: Tomasz traces a chain of consequences, but each link is backed by a specific document: the policy clause, the renewal date and the lease clause. That makes his conclusion a fair warning, not a scare.

whyNot.fal_slippery_slope: Every step from skipped inspection to lease breach is tied to a written requirement, so the chain is documented rather than assumed.

items.source: Transit planner Ana Oyelaran · Carver city council
items.passage: Cutting Route 9 from every 15 minutes to every 30 will cost us riders. When Halden made the same cut in 2023, weekday ridership fell 18% within a year, and in our own survey a third of Route 9 riders said they'd switch to driving if waits doubled. Fewer riders also means a smaller state transit grant, which is paid per rider.
items.cue: When Halden made the same cut in 2023, weekday ridership fell 18% within a year
items.explanation: Ana's chain of consequences is backed at each step: a comparable city's results, local survey data and the grant formula. That makes her warning a supported prediction rather than a slide into fantasy.

whyNot.fal_slippery_slope: Each link, from fewer buses to fewer riders to a smaller grant, comes with evidence instead of being simply asserted.

items.title: Late fees this month
items.passage: Hi everyone, our lease charges a $50 fee for rent paid after the 5th. This month I'm waiving it for every tenant who paid late, because the payment portal was down from the 3rd to the 6th, so nobody could pay on time, which is what the fee exists to encourage. The fee applies as usual next month. Odalys
items.cue: the payment portal was down from the 3rd to the 6th, so nobody could pay on time
items.explanation: Odalys makes an exception for a reason tied to the fee's purpose: the outage made paying on time impossible. It applies to every affected tenant, and the rule returns next month.

whyNot.fal_special_pleading: The exception rests on a relevant, stated difference and covers everyone affected, not just a favored person.

items.passage:
Mom: Phones in the basket, everyone, dinner's ready.
Ayesha: Mine stays on the table tonight. I'm the on-call vet this weekend, and if the clinic calls, an animal could be in trouble.
Jun: You're always the strictest about the basket!
Ayesha: And I still am. Anyone who's on call gets the same pass.
items.cue: I'm the on-call vet this weekend
items.explanation: Ayesha exempts herself, but for a reason that matters (she may be needed for an emergency) and she offers the same exception to anyone in her position.

whyNot.fal_special_pleading: Ayesha's exception rests on a relevant difference and applies to anyone on call, so it isn't a double standard.

items.passage:
Luis: I think we should only take clients with budgets over $20k from now on.
Yasmin: Just so I've got it right: no projects under $20k at all? Last year 9 of our 14 projects were under that, and they covered most of summer payroll. So that rule would have cut most of our income in our slowest season.
Luis: Hm. Fair.
items.cue: Just so I've got it right: no projects under $20k at all?
items.explanation: Yasmin checks that her summary matches Luis's proposal before responding, then tests it against last year's actual projects. She argues against what he really said.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: Yasmin restates Luis's rule accurately and confirms it, so her objection targets his real position, not a distorted one.

items.source: Business association chair Halina Varga · Main Street parking forum
items.passage: Mr. Brandauer's letter says, and I'm quoting, 'the new parking meters will hurt small shops on Main Street.' That's a fair worry. But when Oak Street added meters last year, shop revenue rose 6%, because spaces turned over instead of being taken all day by commuters. Main Street has the same commuter problem, so I expect meters to help our shops too.
items.cue: Mr. Brandauer's letter says, and I'm quoting,
items.explanation: Halina quotes Mr. Brandauer's exact objection and answers that version with evidence from a comparable street. She engages his real argument, not a weaker one.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: Halina quotes Mr. Brandauer word for word and answers that exact claim, so nothing has been distorted.

items.title: Recommendation on the warehouse robot pilot
items.passage: Hi all, I know we've already spent $200,000 on the robot pilot, and that's painful. But that money is gone whichever way we decide. Finishing would cost another $500,000 for about $120,000 a year in savings, and the hardware lasts about three years. That doesn't pay back, so my recommendation is to stop here. Ingrid
items.cue: that money is gone whichever way we decide
items.explanation: Ingrid sets aside the $200,000 already spent and compares only what's ahead: $500,000 more for roughly $360,000 in savings over the hardware's life. Stopping follows from those numbers.

whyNot.fal_sunk_cost: Ingrid explicitly sets aside past spending and decides on future costs and benefits alone.

items.passage:
Carmen: Honestly, I'm sick of this renovation. Should we just stop and list the house as is?
Diego: Our agent says a kitchen without counters will scare buyers off, and finishing adds about $15,000 to the price. The counters cost $4,000.
Carmen: So forget the $40,000 we've already spent. That last $4,000 pays for itself. Okay, let's finish.
items.cue: finishing adds about $15,000 to the price. The counters cost $4,000
items.explanation: Carmen decides to keep going, but not because of past spending: she sets the $40,000 aside and finishes because the last $4,000 should add about $15,000 in value.

whyNot.fal_sunk_cost: The decision to continue rests on future costs and benefits, and Carmen explicitly sets aside what's already been spent.

items.title: Bus lanes cut Route 4 commute times, as planners predicted
items.passage: Before the bus lanes opened, city planners published their prediction: average Route 4 trips would fall by at least five minutes. Six months on, trips are 6.5 minutes faster, while Route 7, which got no lanes, is unchanged. The transport office says the results support keeping the lanes and adding them to Route 7.
items.cue: Before the bus lanes opened, city planners published their prediction
items.explanation: The target was drawn first: planners stated a specific prediction in advance, then checked it against a route without lanes. A hit on a target set beforehand is real evidence.

whyNot.fal_texas_sharpshooter: The prediction was published before the results came in, so the target wasn't painted around the outcome afterward.

items.source: Dr. Imogen Clarke, Westvale Health Department
items.title: Update: stomach illness cluster
items.passage: Last week we flagged a cluster of 12 stomach illness cases. Rather than assume a source, we interviewed every case and a matched group of healthy residents: 11 of the 12 sick people had eaten at the Ferry Street food stall, versus 2 of 40 healthy people. The lab then matched patients' bacteria to samples from the stall, so we're confident it's the source.
items.cue: we interviewed every case and a matched group of healthy residents
items.explanation: Dr. Clarke treats the cluster as a lead, then tests it by comparing sick and healthy residents and confirming with lab results. That turns a noticed pattern into solid evidence.

whyNot.fal_texas_sharpshooter: The cluster wasn't taken as proof; it was tested with a comparison group and lab matching before any conclusion.

items.title: In-office Fridays and the leadership exemption
items.passage: The new policy asks all staff to be in the office on Fridays because in-person time improves collaboration. Leadership has exempted itself. If that reasoning holds, it applies most to the people we collaborate with most, and that's leadership. So either the rule should include them, or the collaboration case is weaker than the memo suggests.
items.cue: If that reasoning holds, it applies most to the people we collaborate with most
items.explanation: Rosa points to leadership's exemption to test the policy's own rationale. She isn't dodging a criticism; she shows the stated reason and the exemption can't both stand.

whyNot.fal_tu_quoque: Rosa isn't deflecting criticism of herself; she uses the inconsistency to examine whether the policy's justification really holds.

items.passage: My brother told me to quit vaping. He still smokes a pack a week, which is honestly kind of funny. But his point stands: I get winded on two flights of stairs now, my cough hangs around for weeks, and I'm spending about $90 a month on pods. Him not following his own advice doesn't make any of that less true. Day 3 without it.
items.cue: Him not following his own advice doesn't make any of that less true
items.explanation: Jonah notices his brother's inconsistency but judges the advice on its merits, citing his own breathing, cough and costs. That's the opposite of dismissing a point because the critic does it too.

whyNot.fal_tu_quoque: Jonah raises his brother's smoking and then sets it aside, accepting the criticism based on his own evidence.

items.passage:
Pilar: Friendly reminder that quiet hours start at 10. Someone's been running a washer at midnight.
Dev: Agreed, that's really inconsiderate. Heads-up though, I'm having people over Saturday and it'll probably go until 1. It's my birthday, so that's different.
Ruth: Noted, I guess.
items.cue: It's my birthday, so that's different.
items.explanation: Dev agrees quiet hours matter, then exempts himself because it's his birthday. A neighbor trying to sleep is kept awake just the same, whatever the occasion.

whyNot.fal_moving_the_goalposts: Dev isn't raising a bar someone already cleared; he keeps the rule for others and waives it for himself.

items.passage: Real talk for my coaching clients: if you want results, you log every single bite, weekends included. No excuses, no "I'll remember it later." (I don't track on weekends myself, but weekends are family time for me, so that's a different situation.) Consistency is everything!
items.cue: weekends are family time for me, so that's a different situation
items.explanation: Marisa demands that clients log every bite, then excuses herself because weekends are family time. Her clients have family weekends too, and that doesn't change what anyone eats.

whyNot.fal_no_true_scotsman: Marisa isn't redefining who counts as a real client; she holds others to a rule and gives herself a pass.

items.title: Office days starting next month
items.passage: Hi team, thanks for your patience while we reviewed the hybrid pilot. The survey showed handoffs slowed when people were rarely in the same room, so starting next month everyone will be in the office Monday through Thursday. I'll keep working from home on Tuesdays, since a lot of my work is focused planning. Thanks, Celeste
items.cue: I'll keep working from home on Tuesdays, since a lot of my work is focused planning
items.explanation: Celeste's rule rests on handoffs between people, and she's part of those handoffs. "Focused planning" isn't a relevant difference; much of her team does focused work too.

whyNot.fal_no_true_scotsman: Celeste isn't redefining who counts as part of the team; she applies a rule to everyone but herself without a relevant reason.

items.source: Mayor Constance Ilori · Dunmarrow drought briefing
items.passage: The reservoir is at 31%, its lowest level in fifteen years, so starting Monday, residential lawn watering is limited to one day a week. I know that's hard. The one exception will be the Copperbeck golf course, which keeps its daily schedule. That course has been the pride of this town for fifty years, and I won't see it go brown.
items.cue: That course has been the pride of this town for fifty years
items.explanation: The limit exists because water is scarce, and a golf course uses far more than a lawn. Constance exempts it out of civic pride, which has nothing to do with how much water is left.

whyNot.fal_moving_the_goalposts: No one met a standard that then got raised; Constance sets one rule for residents and waives it for a favored course.

items.source: Lars Whitfield, senior engineer · Tuesday standup
items.passage: Quick reminder, everyone: two approvals on every pull request, no exceptions, because that's how we catch the bugs we can't see in our own code. For tonight's billing hotfix I'm going to merge on my own review, though. I wrote that module, so I know it better than anyone who'd be reviewing it.
items.cue: I wrote that module, so I know it better than anyone who'd be reviewing it
items.explanation: Lars says reviews exist because authors miss bugs in their own code, and writing the module makes him exactly that author. His expertise sounds relevant, but the rule's purpose still applies to him.

whyNot.fal_moving_the_goalposts: Lars isn't changing the standard after someone met it; he keeps the review rule for everyone else and waives it for himself.

items.title: Still my favorite, even on an off night
items.passage: Regular readers know my rule: I review the meal I got, not the meal a place is capable of, and excuses don't count. Tonight at Trattoria Belvane the pasta came out cold and the service was slow, but they were down two cooks, and I've been coming here for nine years. I'm going on what I know this kitchen can do. Five stars.
items.cue: I'm going on what I know this kitchen can do
items.explanation: Desmond's own rule is to rate the meal served and ignore excuses. For his longtime favorite, he accepts the staffing excuse and rates what the kitchen can do instead.

whyNot.fal_no_true_scotsman: Desmond doesn't redefine what counts as a real restaurant; he suspends his own reviewing rule for a place he loves.

items.passage:
Ezra: Could we swap a couple of the soda options for sparkling water? A bunch of people asked for it in the survey.
Bianca: Great, let's just ban snacks entirely and hand out celery sticks at the door.
Ezra: I said a couple of sodas, Bianca.
items.cue: let's just ban snacks entirely and hand out celery sticks at the door
items.explanation: Ezra suggests swapping a couple of sodas, and Bianca mocks a far more extreme plan he never proposed. Her joke doesn't address the actual, modest request.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: Bianca stays on the topic of the kitchen; she just inflates Ezra's suggestion into something easy to ridicule.

items.passage: Saw a physio post that runners should add two short strength sessions a week to cut injury risk. Sorry, but I'm not giving up running to become a gym rat. Some of us actually like being outside. Ten miles along the river this morning and it was glorious.
items.cue: I'm not giving up running to become a gym rat
items.explanation: The physio suggested adding two short strength sessions, not quitting running. Kay rejects a far bigger change than the one proposed, so the actual advice goes unanswered.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: Kay's main move isn't limiting the choices to two; it's arguing against a version of the advice the physio never gave.

items.title: Re: Proposed in-office days
items.passage: Hi Sandra, thanks for laying out the plan for two office days a week for teams that collaborate daily. I agree onboarding has been harder remotely, and our new hires have said as much. But if leadership's position is that remote employees can't be trusted and need to be watched, I think that's a real step backward for this team. Happy to talk it through. Malik
items.cue: remote employees can't be trusted and need to be watched
items.explanation: Sandra proposed two office days for teams that collaborate daily. Malik agrees about onboarding, then argues against a claim about distrust and surveillance that her plan never made.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: Malik stays on the in-office plan; the problem is that he recasts its reasoning as distrust, which is easier to oppose.

items.passage: We all want children safe. I have two grandkids at Ridgeview myself. But the proposal before us, a 20 mph limit near schools during school hours, would essentially have every driver in Halverton crawling along at 20 all day, every day. That's not a safety plan; that's a traffic jam.
items.cue: every driver in Halverton crawling along at 20 all day, every day
items.explanation: Councillor Pruitt describes the proposal accurately, then attacks a much broader version: a citywide, all-day limit. The real plan covers school zones during school hours only.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: He doesn't claim there are only two choices; he exaggerates the scope of the actual proposal so it's easier to dismiss.

items.title: Moving, but too sweeping
items.passage: In 'The Quiet Hour', Dr. Ilse Moss argues that heavy recreational scrolling after 9 p.m. is linked to poorer sleep in teens. The interviews are moving and she writes beautifully. But her view that screens are simply bad for kids ignores how many teens use them for homework, coding and staying close to friends. A more careful book would have been stronger.
items.cue: her view that screens are simply bad for kids
items.explanation: Odette summarizes the book's narrow claim about late-night scrolling, then criticizes a much broader 'screens are bad' view. Homework and coding don't touch the claim Moss actually made.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: Homework and coding are on topic; the flaw is that Odette critiques a broader position than the one she just described.

items.title: Swap some city lawns for native plants, researchers urge
items.passage: A Pellham Institute study recommends converting 20% of city-owned lawns in parks and medians to native plantings, which it estimates would cut municipal irrigation by 15%. Landscaping association head Rob Kessler pushed back Monday, saying residents 'shouldn't be told to tear out the yards their kids play in.'
items.cue: shouldn't be told to tear out the yards their kids play in
items.explanation: The study is about city-owned lawns in parks and medians, but Rob responds as if it targeted families' backyards. He argues against a proposal nobody made.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: Rob stays on lawns and plantings; he shifts the target from city land to family yards, which misrepresents the study.

items.passage:
Lena: I'm so full I can barely move. That last plate was a mistake.
Corbin: We paid $42 each for this buffet. Go get one more plate so we at least get our money's worth.
Lena: Making myself sick isn't going to get the $42 back, Corbin.
items.cue: We paid $42 each for this buffet. Go get one more plate
items.explanation: Corbin wants Lena to keep eating because of what they already paid. The $42 is spent whether she eats more or not, so the only real question is whether another plate helps her now.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_consequences: Corbin isn't judging a claim by whether its outcome is pleasant; he's letting money already spent drive what Lena does next.

items.passage: Confession: I can't stand spin class. The music gives me a headache and my knees ache for days afterward. But I prepaid $900 for a full year of classes in January, so I'm dragging myself there four mornings a week until December. Not letting that money go to waste!
items.cue: I prepaid $900 for a full year of classes in January, so I'm dragging myself there
items.explanation: Jules keeps going to a class that hurts her knees because of money she can't get back. The $900 is gone either way; the real choice is about how she spends her mornings from now on.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Jules isn't continuing because it's how things have always been done; she's continuing because of what she already paid.

items.title: Re: Should we switch CRMs?
items.passage: Hi Noemi, thanks for the comparison sheet. You're right that the off-the-shelf option covers nearly everything we need for about $40k a year. Still, we've put eighteen months and $1.2 million into our in-house system. Walking away now would mean all of that was wasted, so I want to push on and finish it. Let's discuss Monday. Graham
items.cue: Walking away now would mean all of that was wasted, so I want to push on
items.explanation: Graham accepts that the cheaper tool does the job, then decides to continue because of the $1.2 million already spent. That money is gone either way; only the remaining costs should count.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Graham isn't defending the in-house system as the way things have always been done; his reason is past spending.

items.source: Mayor Delphine Achterberg · Port Ellery council session
items.passage: I've read the consultant's report, and I won't sugarcoat it: finishing the Riverside arena will cost another $30 million, and the operating forecast shows losses for at least a decade. But this town has already put $14 million into that site. We cannot let that investment go to waste. We finish what we started.
items.cue: But this town has already put $14 million into that site.
items.explanation: Delphine accepts the report's grim forecast, then argues to continue because of the $14 million already spent. That money is gone either way; the vote should weigh the $30 million still to come.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_consequences: Delphine doesn't dispute the report because she dislikes its conclusion; she argues for continuing because of money already spent.

items.source: Customer at the service counter · Pinchbeck Auto Repair
items.passage: I know, I know, the car's only worth about two grand and the transmission is another $2,500. But I put $3,000 into it this year already: new brakes, new tires, the alternator. If I scrap it now, all of that was for nothing. Go ahead and do the transmission.
items.cue: If I scrap it now, all of that was for nothing.
items.explanation: The recent repairs feel like a reason to keep going, but that $3,000 is spent either way. The real choice is $2,500 for a car worth about $2,000 versus the alternatives.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_consequences: The customer isn't rejecting a claim because its outcome feels bad; past repair bills are driving a decision about future spending.

items.title: Honest, patient, and knows the market
items.passage: Marisol was fantastic: honest pricing advice and gorgeous photos. She recommended listing at $435k based on recent sales nearby. But we paid $480k two years ago, and we're not taking a loss on our home, so we've decided to wait until the market gets us back to $480k, even if that means carrying two mortgages a while longer.
items.cue: we paid $480k two years ago, and we're not taking a loss on our home
items.explanation: Lucas and Mei anchor on what they paid, but buyers don't care about that number, and it can't be recovered by waiting. Their choice is today's price versus months of extra mortgage payments.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_consequences: They aren't rejecting the agent's advice as false because it's unpleasant; their reason to wait is the price they paid in the past.

items.source: Big Mike Danvers · Harbor City sports radio
items.passage: Folks, back in August I told you this would be a season of surprises, and look what happened. A rookie scored a hat trick in his first start, the coach got fired in October, and we beat the defending champs on the road. I called it, plain and simple. Next week I'll give you my playoff predictions, so stay tuned.
items.cue: I told you this would be a season of surprises, and look what happened
items.explanation: Mike's prediction was so vague that almost any season would fit it. He's choosing the surprising moments afterward and drawing his target around them.

whyNot.fal_cherry_picking: Mike isn't just hiding inconvenient games; his 'prediction' only becomes a hit because he defines it after seeing what happened.

items.passage: OK, look at the new album's tracklist. Take the first letter of tracks 2, 5, 7 and 11: T, O, U, R. TOUR! They hid the announcement right in front of us. I've been refreshing their site all morning. Fall tour dates incoming, calling it now.
items.cue: Take the first letter of tracks 2, 5, 7 and 11
items.explanation: The fan page chose which tracks to read only after hunting for a word. With a dozen titles to pick from, you can spell plenty of words by chance, so finding one proves nothing.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: No cause is being read into a correlation; the 'message' exists only because the tracks were chosen after the word was found.

items.passage:
Asha: I went through all six outages this year and tried every angle I could think of: weekday, time of day, deploys, weather, traffic, data center, vendor, who was on call.
Ryan: And?
Asha: Nothing lined up until on-call: four of the six were in Dmitri's weeks. That's our pattern. He's the common thread, and I'm flagging it to his manager.
items.cue: Nothing lined up until on-call: four of the six were in Dmitri's weeks. That's our pattern.
items.explanation: Asha sliced the outages eight different ways and kept the one slice that happened to fit. Check enough factors and one will line up by chance, so her 'pattern' is a target drawn around the hits.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: The deeper flaw isn't reading cause into a correlation; Asha found the 'link' only by testing factor after factor until one fit.

items.passage: We mapped all 40 dead songbirds reported in Fenwick County this spring, then circled the tightest bunch on the map: twelve birds in the northeast corner, around Millpond Road. Twelve in one small patch is way too many to be chance. Something there is harming birds, and we've asked the county to test the soil. Volunteers welcome for weekend counts!
items.cue: then circled the tightest bunch on the map: twelve birds in the northeast corner
items.explanation: The birders found the densest patch first and then drew their boundary around it. Scattered points always bunch up somewhere, so a circle drawn to fit the dots can't show that anything unusual is going on.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: No suspect is being blamed from a correlation; the 'hot spot' exists only because the circle was drawn around the dots after the fact.

items.title: Born in March? You may be destined for accounting
items.passage: Analyzing records of 50,000 workers in 60 professions, a team at the Halvorsen Institute compared every birth month against every job and found that people born in March were 18% more likely to become accountants. The researchers say early-spring births may shape a detail-oriented temperament.
items.cue: compared every birth month against every job
items.explanation: Comparing 12 months against 60 jobs makes 720 comparisons, and some are bound to stand out by chance. The team found its 'pattern' by searching, then told a story about why it fits.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: The causal story is a problem, but the deeper one is that the March link was picked out of hundreds of comparisons after the fact.

items.title: New sales forecast model
items.passage: Hi Tom, good news on the forecasting front. I tuned the new model on our last ten years of sales, adjusting the weights until it fit, and it now matches nine of those ten years almost exactly. That track record gives me a lot of confidence in its forecast of 14% growth next year. Happy to walk the team through it Thursday.
items.cue: adjusting the weights until it fit, and it now matches nine of those ten years
items.explanation: Priyanka shaped the model to fit the same ten years it now 'predicts', so matching them was guaranteed. That's drawing the target around past data, not a test of how well it forecasts.

whyNot.fal_cherry_picking: No unfavorable years are hidden; the model was simply fitted to the very data it's being credited with predicting.

items.passage:
Noor: Can we stick to the cleaning rota? There have been dishes in the sink since Sunday and the kitchen is starting to smell.
Callum: You left a pot soaking for three days last month, so I'm not taking a lecture on dishes from you.
Noor: Fair, and I cleaned it. The pans in there now are still yours though.
items.cue: You left a pot soaking for three days last month
items.explanation: Callum answers Noor's complaint by pointing to her own past mess. Even if Noor slipped up once, the current pans are still unwashed and the rota still applies.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Callum isn't attacking Noor's character in general; he's saying she did the same thing, so she can't complain.

items.source: Teen to parent · car ride home
items.passage: Mom, you can't tell me to put my phone away at dinner. You answered work emails through Grandma's entire birthday party. So honestly, I don't think screens at the table are that big a deal. Can we stop for tacos?
items.cue: You answered work emails through Grandma's entire birthday party
items.explanation: The teen decides screens at dinner are fine because Mom also uses her phone at family events. Mom's habit doesn't change whether phones at the table are a problem.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: This isn't a random change of topic; it turns the criticism back onto Mom's own behavior to escape it.

items.title: Re: Q3 expense reports
items.passage: Hi Joanne, thanks for the reminder. Two receipts are missing because the hotel's billing system was down, and I've asked them for copies. On deadlines more generally, I'd gently point out that my June reimbursement sat in your approval queue for five weeks, so I'm not sure strict timelines are a fair ask of our team. Best, Tariq
items.cue: my June reimbursement sat in your approval queue for five weeks
items.explanation: Tariq gives a fair reason for two missing receipts, then deflects the deadline issue onto Joanne's slow approvals. Her delays don't make late reports from his team acceptable.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Tariq doesn't attack Joanne's character; he argues that her own lateness means she can't hold his team to deadlines.

items.passage: To the neighbor leaving one-star reviews about our patio heaters 'wasting energy': we've seen your SUV idling outside the school for twenty minutes every afternoon. Maybe start there. Our heaters stay on through March, and the spiced cider is back this week. Come in and warm up!
items.cue: we've seen your SUV idling outside the school for twenty minutes every afternoon
items.explanation: The café answers the energy complaint by pointing at the critic's idling SUV. That may be inconsistent of the neighbor, but it says nothing about whether the patio heaters waste energy.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: The SUV isn't just a new topic; it's aimed at the critic's own habits to deflect the complaint about the heaters.

items.passage: Councillor Mbeki has raised concerns that the library renovation is running 18% over budget, and I take budget discipline seriously. But I'd remind my colleague that the community pool she championed in 2022 came in 30% over, and no one on this side of the chamber demanded an inquiry then. I'd ask that the library receive the same good faith.
items.cue: the community pool she championed in 2022 came in 30% over
items.explanation: Councillor Vance answers a concern about the library overrun by citing Councillor Mbeki's own over-budget pool. Her past project doesn't explain or excuse the library's 18%.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: The pool isn't an unrelated detour; it's aimed squarely at the critic's own record to neutralize her concern.

items.title: Running app maker hits back at privacy watchdog
items.passage: Strydo, whose running app was found sharing users' location history with advertisers, responded Tuesday by noting that the watchdog behind the report, the Clearfield Privacy Project, 'tracks its own website visitors with third-party ad cookies' and questioned whether the group should 'lecture anyone on data.' Strydo said it would review its settings.
items.cue: tracks its own website visitors with third-party ad cookies
items.explanation: Strydo meets a report about its location sharing by pointing at the watchdog's own cookies. Even if the group is inconsistent, its findings about Strydo still need an answer.

whyNot.fal_ad_hominem: Strydo isn't attacking the group's character broadly; it claims the critic does similar tracking and so can't criticize.
